## Appendix A Strong Coupling Perturbation Theory

In this appendix we analyze the splitting of strong coupling states in h-HTG upon moving away from the chiral, dispersion-free limit where they are all degenerate. Before doing so it is useful to review some notation. We will use the “hatted” notation for second quantized operators $\hat{A}$ in terms of their first quantized versions $A$ . Hatting preserves commutators:

$$ \hat{A}=\sum_{I,J}c^{\dagger}_{I}A_{IJ}c_{J},\qquad\hat{[A,B]}=[\hat{A},\hat{B}]. $$

Here, $I,J$ label all states in the band-projected single-particle Hilbert space: they are multi-indices that combine both momentum ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ , spin, valley, and sublattice. For example, $\hat{\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}=\sum_{IJ}c^{\dagger}_{I}\rho_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}IJ}c_{J}$ is the second quantized version of the first quantized $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ where

$$ \rho_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}IJ}=(\rho_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}})_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}^{\tau\tau^{\prime},\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}}=\Lambda_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}^{\tau,\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\delta_{ss^{\prime}},\qquad\Lambda^{\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{\sigma}^{\prime}}_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\innerproduct{u_{\bk\tilde{\sigma}}^\tau}{u_{\bk+\bq\tilde{\sigma}'}^\tau}. $$

Here $\tau=\pm=K,\bar{K}$ labels the graphene valley, $\tilde{\sigma}=\pm=A,B$ labels the sublattice band, and $s=\pm=\uparrow,\downarrow$ labels the spin. For the appendices, from now on, we we will drop the tildes on the sublattice band labels and Pauli matrices for convenience: we will not have to refer to the microscopic sublattice. Since unperturbed strong coupling states are exact Slater determinants, we will be interested in expectation values of Slater determinant states in this section. These may be evaluated by Wick’s theorem

$$ \langle\hat{A}\rangle=\Tr PA,\qquad\langle\hat{A}\hat{B}\rangle=\Tr PAB-\Tr APBP+\Tr AP\Tr BP=\frac{1}{2}\Tr[A,P][P,B]+\Tr AP\Tr BP, $$

where $P_{IJ}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{J}c_{I}\rangle$ is the Hartree Fock projector: $P^{2}=P$ . Here, we are using a capital $\Tr$ to denote traces over the multiindices $I,J$ . For traces over band indices, that don’t include sums over momenta, we use $\tr$ .

The full Hamiltonian is

$$ \mathcal{H}=\hat{h}+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}, $$

where $A=N_{M}A_{M}$ is the sample area in terms of the number of unit cells $N_{M}$ and the unit cell area $A_{M}$ . We have used

$$ \delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}=\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}-4\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},\qquad\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\tau\sigma}\overline{\rho}^{\tau\sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},\qquad\overline{\rho}^{\tau\sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}},{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\Lambda^{\tau,\sigma\sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}) $$

which is the density measured relative to half filling of the flat bands in a periodic gauge $c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}=c_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}$ . The background density $-4\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ , where $\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ is the average density of a fully filled band, is only nonzero if ${{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ is a reciprocal lattice vector, by translation symmetry. The factor of four arises because at charge neutrality four out of eight bands are filled.

### A.1 Symmetric, Dispersion-Free, Limit

We begin with the idealized limit of symmetric form factors, $[\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}),\sigma_{z}]=0$ from chiral symmetry, such that $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{\tau,\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\Lambda^{\tau,\sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}$ and zero dispersion $\hat{h}$ . Then, the form factors $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ are $8\times 8$ diagonal matrices, with diagonal elements $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{\tau\sigma}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ (we leave the spin index implicit, since $\Lambda$ is spin-independent). Note that we are only neglecting the sublattice off-diagonal part of the form factor here; we include the $\kappa=w_{AA}/w_{AB}>0$ contributions to the diagonal form factor in practice. In this idealized limit the form factors, and the interacting Hamiltonian, have a $U(2)\times U(2)\times U(2)\times U(2)$ symmetry consisting of spin and charge rotations within each sublattice and valley sector.

Since the form factor is diagonal in sublattice and valley, we will shortly see that all many-body states $\ket{\Psi}$ that consist of completely filling some number of sublattice and valley diagonal bands are exact eigenstates. Such states are described by translationally symmetric, ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ -independent, Hartree-Fock projectors $P$ that are flavor and sublattice diagonal. We will use the notation

$$ P=\sum_{\tau\sigma}P^{\tau}_{\sigma}\frac{1+\tau\tau_{z}}{2}\frac{1+\sigma\sigma_{z}}{2},\qquad P_{\sigma}=\sum_{\tau}P^{\tau}_{\sigma}\frac{1+\tau\tau_{z}}{2},\qquad P^{\tau}=\sum_{\sigma}P^{\tau}_{\sigma}\frac{1+\sigma\sigma_{z}}{2} $$

and

$$ P_{\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q_{\sigma}),\quad P^{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q^{\tau}),\quad P_{\sigma}^{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q_{\sigma}^{\tau}). $$

The matrix $Q^{\tau}_{\sigma}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that describes the spin-occupations in valley $\tau$ and sublattice $\sigma$ . It is acted on by the $U(2)$ spin and charge rotation associated to this spin and valley: $Q^{\tau}_{\sigma}\to(U_{\sigma}^{\tau})^{\dagger}Q^{\tau}_{\sigma}U_{\sigma}^{\tau}$ , though the sublattice and valley occupations

$$ \nu^{\tau}_{\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}\tr Q^{\tau}_{\sigma} $$

are invariant under this action.

The states described by (15) are distinguished by the fact that they commute with $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ , so that the density operator cannot scatter occupied states to deoccupied states. To see that these states are exact eigenstates, we note that $\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\ket{\Psi}=0$ unless ${{\boldsymbol{q}}}={{\boldsymbol{G}}}$ is a reciprocal lattice vector, since all other scattering is Pauli blocked. For reciprocal lattice wavevectors, we have

$$ \delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau\sigma}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\left(c^{\dagger}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau\sigma}c_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau\sigma}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{\sigma\tau}\nu_{\sigma}^{\tau}\rho_{{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}^{\tau\sigma}\ket{\Psi} $$

Since the only opertor in the disperisonless Hamiltonian is the density operator, (18) implies that $\ket{\Psi}$ is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian. We now assess which states have the smallest energy and what this energy depends on.

The form factors for different sublattices are not symmetry related since the associated bands have different $\absolutevalue{C}$ , but the form factors for different valleys are related by time reversal: $\Lambda^{(-\tau)\sigma}_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\overline{\Lambda^{\tau\sigma}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}})}=\Lambda^{\tau\sigma}_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}-{{\boldsymbol{q}}})$ . This implies that the background density is the same for the bands in each valley related by time reversal, as one would expect: $\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}^{(-\tau)\sigma}=\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}^{\tau\sigma}=\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}^{\sigma}$ . We also now have $\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\sigma=\pm}\overline{\rho}^{\sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}$ . Thus, only the sublattice polarization affects the eigenvalue (18). In particular we have

$$ \delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\ket{\Psi}=\left(\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\nu+\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\nu_{z}\right)\ket{\Psi} $$

where we have defined $\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\sigma=\pm}\sigma\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}^{\sigma}$ , the filling $\nu=\frac{1}{2}\tr Q$ , and sublattice polarization $\nu_{z}=\frac{1}{2}\tr Q\sigma_{z}$ . The total energy is then

$$ \mathcal{H}\ket{\Psi}=E_{0}\ket{\Psi},\qquad E_{0}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}(\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\nu+\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\nu_{z})(\overline{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\nu+\overline{\rho}^{z}_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\nu_{z}). $$

At charge neutrality, $\nu=0$ , we see that any state that has zero sublattice polarization, $\nu_{z}=0$ , has the ground state energy $E_{0}=0$ .

### A.2 Off-diagonal Form factors

Away from the chiral limit, the sublattice-bands are not perfectly sublattice polarized, such that the form factors $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ are not diagonal in sublattice. We can isolate the off diagonal piece $\Lambda^{o}$ from the chirally-symmetric diagonal piece $\Lambda^{d}$

$$ \Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})+\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{o}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}),\qquad\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{d/o}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\frac{1}{2}(\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\pm\sigma_{z}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\sigma_{z}), $$

and define the associated density operators

$$ \displaystyle\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\Lambda^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})c_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}-4\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}, \displaystyle\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle=\hat{\rho}^{A}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\Lambda^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})c_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}}} $$

such that the Hamiltonian now reads

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H} \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{d}+\mathcal{H}_{o} \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{d} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\left(\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}+\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}+\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\right). $$

The Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{d}$ , with densities corresponding to sublattice diagonal form factors, was studied in the previous section. We will now compute the effect of $\mathcal{H}_{o}$ at first order in perturbation theory. We will use $\langle\cdot\rangle$ to denote an expectation value in one of the ground states of $\mathcal{H}_{d}$ . For the first term of $\mathcal{H}_{o}$ , we have

$$ \langle\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle\propto\langle\delta\hat{\rho}^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle=\Tr P\rho^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}P\Lambda^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=0 $$

where we used that ground states of $\mathcal{H}_{d}$ are eigenstates of $\rho^{d}$ and that $\Lambda^{o}$ is off-diagonal in sublattice while $P$ is diagonal. The same argument may be applied to the second term of $\mathcal{H}_{o}$ . We therefore have

$$ \displaystyle E_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\langle\mathcal{H}_{o}\rangle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\langle\rho^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rho^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{2}\Tr[\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{o},P][P,\rho^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{8}\Tr[\rho^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},Q][Q,\rho^{o}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{16A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tr[\Lambda^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}),Q][Q,\Lambda^{o{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})] \displaystyle=\text{const.}+\frac{1}{8A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\tr Q^{\tau}\Lambda^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})Q^{\tau}\Lambda^{{\dagger}o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}). $$

In the last step we have expanded the commutators and used $Q^{2}=1$ to write the terms involving $\tr QQ\Lambda^{o}\Lambda^{o{\dagger}}$ as irrelevant additive constants that we now drop.

To move forward, we comment on the structure of $\Lambda^{o}$ . Since $\Lambda^{o}$ is off-diagonal in sublattice and diagonal in valley, we can write $\Lambda^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\sigma_{x}F^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})e^{i\Phi^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\sigma_{z}}$ where $\tau$ labels the valley. Time reversal symmetry implies

$$ \Lambda^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\Lambda^{o(-\tau)}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}),\qquad\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\left(F^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right)^{2}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\left(F^{o(-\tau)}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right)^{2} $$

which we will shortly use.

Using the fact that $Q$ is sublattice and valley diagonal, we have

$$ \displaystyle E_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\tr Q^{\tau}\Lambda^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})Q^{\tau}\Lambda^{{\dagger}o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\tr Q\sigma_{x}F^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})Q\sigma_{x}F^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{\tau}\left[\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\left(F^{o\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right)^{2}\right]\tr Q^{\tau}\sigma_{x}Q^{\tau}\sigma_{x} \displaystyle=N_{M}\sum_{\tau}\frac{\lambda}{4}\tr Q^{\tau}\sigma_{x}Q^{\tau}\sigma_{x} \displaystyle=N_{M}\frac{\lambda}{4}\tr Q\sigma_{x}Q\sigma_{x}=N_{M}\frac{\lambda}{2}\tr Q_{A}Q_{B} $$

where we have defined

$$ \lambda=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{N_{M}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\left(F^{o\tau_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{N_{M}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\frac{1}{8}\tr\Lambda^{o{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{o}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}) $$

which is independent of the valley $\tau$ due to (26).

### A.3 Superexchange correction from Dispersion

We now compute the leading correction from the single-particle dispersion $\hat{h}$ . We split $h$ into its sublattice diagonal and off-diagonal parts as

$$ h=h_{d}+h_{o},\qquad h_{d,o}=\frac{1}{2}(h+\sigma_{z}h\sigma_{z}). $$

The dispersion is diagonal in valley, and the dispersions in each valley are related by time-reversal symmetry

$$ h^{-\tau}_{o,d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\overline{h^{\tau}_{o,d}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}})}, $$

where the complex conjugation flips the sign of the part of the off-diagonal dispersion, $h_{o}=h_{x}\sigma_{x}+h_{y}\sigma_{y}$ , that is proportional to $\sigma_{y}$ . Furthermore particle-hole-inversion symmetry implies

$$ h^{\tau}_{o,d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=-h^{\tau}_{o,d}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}), $$

The unperturbed states are eigenstates of $h_{d}=h_{0}+h_{z}\sigma_{z}$ , since all such states correspond to filling bands of definite sublattice and valley,

$$ \displaystyle\hat{h}_{d}\ket{\Psi_0}=\left(\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tr h_{d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})P\right)=\tr P\left(\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}h_{d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right)\ket{\Psi}=0 $$

where we used that $\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}h_{d}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=0$ due to particle-hole inversion symmetry (31). We will therefore ignore the diagonal dispersion, as it annihilates all unperturbed states.

To split the unperturbed states with dispersion, we must therefore focus on $\hat{h}_{o}$ . Since all unperturbed states are sublattice diagonal, $\langle\hat{h}_{0}\rangle=\Tr h_{o}P=0$ . However, the unperturbed states are not all eigenstates of $\hat{h}_{o}$ , since $\hat{h}_{o}$ will create particle-hole excitations between the A,B sublattices. For states that have partiallly filled spin and valley flavors, these excitations are not Pauli blocked, and the ability to have such excitations will favor these states within second-order perturbation theory as we shall see.

In order to perform the second-order perturbation theory, we must invert the unperturbed Hamiltonian within the space of excitations and compute

$$ E_{2}=-\bra{\Psi_0}\hat{h}(\mathcal{H}_{0}-E_{0})^{-1}\hat{h}\ket{\Psi_0} $$

While the full space of excitations on top of a state $\ket{\Psi_0}$ is enormous and hard-to control, and inverting $\mathcal{H}$ in this full space would be challenging, we can use the fact that $\hat{h}_{o}$ only creates particle-hole excitations on top of $\ket{\Psi_0}$ ; we will soon recall[11, 64] that the Hamiltonian leaves this block invariant. Such excitations, on top of a particular choice of $\ket{\Psi_0}$ , form a Hilbert space spanned by

$$ \hat{\phi}\ket{\Psi_0},\qquad\{\phi,Q\}=\{\phi,\sigma_{z}\}=[\phi,\tau_{z}]=0, $$

that is, the creation of particle-hole pairs that are not Pauli Blocked, between sublattices, and within the same valley.

It is straightforward to check that the unperturbed Hamiltonian preserves the Hilbert-space (34); to do so we use that $\delta\hat{\rho}^{d}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\ket{\Psi_0}=\lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\ket{\Psi_0}$ . For brevity, we will drop the superscript “ $d$ ” in this section as we have dealt with the $\Lambda^{o}$ form factors in the previous section. We have

$$ \displaystyle\delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\hat{\phi}\ket{\Psi_0} \displaystyle=\delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\left([\hat{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},\hat{\phi}]+\hat{\phi}\lambda_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\right)\ket{\Psi} \displaystyle=\left(\widehat{[\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},[\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},\phi]]}+\lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\widehat{[\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},\phi]}+\lambda_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\widehat{[\rho_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},\phi]}\right)\ket{\Psi_0}. $$

The operator acting on $\ket{\Psi_0}$ above is a two-body operator that anticommutes with $Q$ if $\phi$ does (note that $[Q,\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]=0$ : both matrices are diagonal in sublattice and valley, $\rho$ is the identity in spin-space, and $Q$ is ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ -independent). Thus, the state (35) lies in the Hilbert space spanned by (36). We can therefore invert the Hamiltonian by computing the matrix elements $(H_{\text{eh}})_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}\nu,{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mu}=\bra{\Psi_{\bk' \nu}}(\mathcal{H}-E_{0})\ket{\Psi_{\bk\mu}}$ , where $\ket{\Psi_{\bk\mu}}$ form a basis of particle hole excitations, and then inverting $H_{\text{eh}}$ [11]. The second order correction then reduces to

$$ E_{2}=-\bra{\Psi_0}\hat{h}H_{\text{eh}}^{-1}\hat{h}\ket{\Psi_0}. $$

Here however we will take a slightly different approach, which is somewhat less algebraically intensive than computing (36) directly. In particular we will write

$$ \ket{\Psi_M}=(1+i\hat{M})\ket{\Psi_0}\approx e^{i\hat{M}}\ket{\Psi_0},\quad\{M,Q\}=\{M,\sigma_{z}\}=0,\quad(M)_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}\tau^{\prime}}=M^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}, $$

where $\tau$ labels valley, and $M_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\tau}$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix in spin and sublattice space. The state (37) should be regarded as a fully-general ansatz for the first-order perturbed wavefunction; $\hat{M}$ should be thought of as $O(\hat{h})$ , and it is kept to linear order in the state $\ket{\Psi_M}$ corresponding to the fact that first order perturbations in the wavefunction lead to second order corrections in the energy. The true first order wavefunction corresponds to (37) with the $M$ that minimizes the total energy

$$ E_{M}=\bra{\Psi_M}(\mathcal{H}_{0}-E_{0}+\hat{h})\ket{\Psi_M}. $$

The simplification that this restructuring leads to is that $\ket{\Psi_M}=e^{i\hat{M}}\ket{\Psi_0}$ is a Slater determinant with $P_{M}=e^{-iM}Pe^{iM}$ . The first order correction does not take us out of the Slater determinant space of states, and we can make use of this to evaluate (38).

We proceed to evaluate and minimize (38). To do the minimization over the space of matrices $M_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\tau}$ , we will use that they are off diagonal in sublattice

$$ M_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\tau}=\begin{pmatrix}0&m_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\tau}\\
m_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\tau{\dagger}}&0\end{pmatrix}_{A,B}, $$

and expand in a matrix basis

$$ m_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}=\sum_{\mu}m_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}r_{\tau}^{\mu},\qquad r^{\mu}_{\tau}=-Q^{\tau}_{A}r_{\tau}^{\mu}Q^{\tau}_{B},\qquad\tr r_{\tau}^{\mu}r_{\tau}^{\nu}=\delta^{\mu\nu} $$

Here, $r^{\mu}_{\tau}$ are a basis of $4\times 4$ matrices that span the subspace of matrices that are odd under the map $m\to Q^{\tau}_{A}mQ^{\tau}_{B}$ (which squares to the identity).

We begin with the interaction term

$$ \displaystyle E_{\text{int}}[M] \displaystyle=\bra{\Psi_M}(\mathcal{H}_{0}-E_{0})\ket{\Psi_M}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\langle\delta\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\hat{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle_{M}-E_{0}, \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{8}\Tr[Q_{M},\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}][\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},Q_{M}]+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{4}\Tr Q_{M}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Tr Q_{M}\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}-E_{0}. $$

We must now expand two second order in $M$ via $Q_{M}=e^{-iM}Qe^{iM}=e^{i\ad_{M}}Q=Q+i\ad_{M}Q-\frac{1}{2}\ad^{2}_{M}Q+\cdots$ where $\ad_{M}Q=[M,Q]=2MQ$ since $M$ anticommutes with $Q$ . The zeroth order terms reproduce the ground state energy $E_{0}$ .

#### A.3.1 Charge Neutrality Superexchange

We will begin with the first, Fock, term. We will later see that the Hartree term, the second term in the final line of (41), vanishes at charge neutrality. Away from charge neutrality, this term leads to a minor, quantitative, change to the superexchange scale that we compute in the next subsection. For now, however, we will focus on charge neutrality and the Fock term.

In the Fock term, we must expand each of $[Q_{M},\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]$ to at least linear order because $[Q,\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]=0$ . We therefore have, to second order in $M$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{8}\Tr[Q_{M},\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}][\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},Q_{M}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-)\frac{1}{8}\Tr[[M,Q],\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}][\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}},[M,Q]], \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\left(\frac{1}{4}\Tr MM(\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}+\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rho_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}})-\frac{1}{2}\Tr M\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}M\rho_{-bq}\right), \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tr\left(M_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{2}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})-M_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})M_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\Lambda_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})\right), \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\bigg(\tr(m^{\tau\dag}_\bk m_\bk^\tau)\left(\Lambda^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{A\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})+\Lambda^{B\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})\right) \displaystyle-\tr(m^{\tau\dag}_\bk m^\tau_{\bk+ \bq})\Lambda^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})-\tr(m^{\tau\dag}_{\bk+ \bq} m^\tau_{\bk})\Lambda^{A\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\bigg), \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\tr(m^{\tau\dag}_\bk m_\bk^\tau)\frac{1}{2}\left(\Lambda^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{A\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})+\Lambda^{B\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\right) \displaystyle-\tr(m^{\tau\dag}_\bk m^\tau_{\bk+ \bq})\Lambda^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime},\tau}\overline{m}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}R^{F,\tau}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}m_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}^{\tau}, $$

where

$$ R^{F,\tau}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\left(\frac{1}{2}\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}(\absolutevalue{\Lambda^A_\bq(\bk)}^{2}+\absolutevalue{\Lambda^B_\bq(\bk)}^{2})-\Lambda^{A\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\Lambda^{B\tau}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}})\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\right), $$

is a Fock Hamiltonian that describes the exchange energy penalty for creating particle-hole pairs in valley $\tau$ . In simplifying (42), we repeatedly used $[Q,\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]=\{M,Q\}=0$ , the cyclic property of the trace, and $V({{\boldsymbol{q}}})=V(-{{\boldsymbol{q}}})$ . The Fock Hamiltonians in the two valleys are related by time reversal symmetry. Indeed, using that the form factors satisfy $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{\tau}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=\overline{\Lambda_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}(-{{\boldsymbol{k}}})}$ we have

$$ R^{\tau}_{F{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=\overline{R}^{-\tau}_{F-{{\boldsymbol{k}}},-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=R^{\tau}_{F-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime},-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}=\left(T\left(R_{F}^{(-\tau)}\right)^{T}T\right)_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}, $$

where $T_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}},-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}$ is the matrix that takes ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}\to-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ and we have written the action of time reversal ultimately as a transpose, related to complex conjugation by the, verifiable, hermiticity of $R$ .

We now compute the dispersion term, which contributes at first order in $M$ and thus favors a nonzero perturbative correction $M$ of the appropriate direction and sign. We will write

$$ h_{o\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&z_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\\
\overline{z}_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}&0\end{pmatrix} $$

such that

$$ \langle\hat{h}_{o}\rangle_{M}=\frac{i}{2}\Tr h_{o}[M,Q]=-i\Tr QMh_{o}=-i\sum_{\mu\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\left(m_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}\overline{z}_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}-\overline{m}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}z_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu{\dagger}}_{\tau}\right). $$

In total, the energy as a function of $m_{\mu}$ is

$$ E[M]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime},\tau}\overline{m}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}R^{F,\tau}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}m_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}^{\tau},-i\sum_{\mu\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\left(m_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}\overline{z}_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}-\overline{m}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}^{\tau}z_{\tau{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu{\dagger}}_{\tau}\right). $$

As discussed above, the energy in second order perturbation theory corresponds to the minimum of (47) over all $m_{\mu}$ because our variational space encompasses all possible perturbative corrections. The minimum energy is then

$$ E_{\text{SE}}=\min_{M}E[M]=-2\sum_{\tau}\sum_{\mu}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\overline{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}(R_{F}^{\tau})^{-1}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}z_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}. $$

We now define

$$ J_{\nu=0}=\frac{2}{N_{M}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\overline{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}(R_{F}^{\tau})^{-1}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}z_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau} $$

as the superexchange energy per unit cell at charge neutrality, where $N_{M}$ is the number of unit cells and number of ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ -points. While (49) has $\tau$ dependence, in fact $J$ is independent of the valley $\tau$ due to the time reversal symmetries (44) and (30), the latter of which implies $z_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}=\overline{z}_{-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}-\tau}=(T\overline{z}_{-\tau})_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ .

We must now deal with the sum over generators $r^{\mu}_{\tau}$ using an appropriate Fierz identity for the space of matrices odd under $m\mapsto-Q^{\tau}_{A}mQ^{\tau}_{B}$ . This identity can be derived from the usual Fierz identity of all matrices, $\tr Xt^{\mu}\tr Yt{{\dagger}\mu}$ together with the projection $t^{\mu}\to-Q^{\tau}_{A}t^{\mu}Q^{\tau}_{B}=r^{\mu}$ :

$$ \sum_{\mu}\tr Xr^{\mu}\tr Yr^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}(\tr XY-\tr Q_{B}XQ_{A}Y). $$

Substituting $X=Y=Q_{A}$ we have

$$ E_{\text{SE}}=\frac{1}{2}J_{\nu=0}\sum_{\tau}(\tr Q^{\tau}_{A}Q^{\tau}_{B}-2)=\frac{1}{2}J_{\nu=0}(\tr Q_{A}Q_{B}-4) $$

as the superexchange energy at charge neutrality

#### A.3.2 Superexchange Away from Charge Neutrality

We now perform a full calculation that includes the Hartree term and is valid at all integer fillings. We must compute the Hartree energy, the second term in the second line of (41). We use that $\Tr[M,Q]\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}=0$ since $M$ is off-diagonal in sublattice while $Q$ and $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ are diagonal. Then, the terms contributing to second order are, again using $V({{\boldsymbol{q}}})=V(-{{\boldsymbol{q}}})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle E_{H}[M]=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{4}\Tr Q_{M}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Tr Q_{M}\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{4}\Tr[M,[M,Q]]\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Tr Q\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\left(\Lambda^{0\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\tr([M^\tau_\bk,[M^\tau_\bk,Q^\tau]])+\Lambda^{z\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\tr([M^\tau_\bk,[M^\tau_\bk,Q]]\sigma_z )\right) \displaystyle\times\left(\nu\overline{\rho}_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}+\nu_{z}\overline{\rho}^{z}_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\right) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\Lambda^{z\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\tr([M^\tau_\bk,[M^\tau_\bk,Q]]\sigma_z)\left(\nu\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}+\nu_{z}\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\right), \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\Lambda^{z\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\tr(M^\tau_\bk M^\tau_\bk Q^\tau\sigma_z)\left(\nu\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}+\nu_{z}\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\right), \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\left(\tr m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{A}^{\tau}-\tr m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{B}^{\tau}\right)\Lambda^{z\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\left(\nu\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}+\nu_{z}\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\right), $$

where we decomposed $Q$ into valleys as $Q=\sum_{\tau}Q^{\tau}\frac{1+\tau\tau_{z}}{2}$ . We note that at charge neutrality the ground states have zero sublattice polarization, such that $\nu=\nu_{z}=0$ and the term (52) can be dropped. Furthermore, in more symmetric systems like twisted bilayer graphene $\Lambda^{z}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})=0$ , so that again (52) can be dropped. However, for h-HTG, away from charge neutrality, we must include (52).

We note that due to the presence of $Q_{A}$ and $Q_{B}$ in the traces in the final line, the Hartree contribution to the particle-hole Hamiltonian is not the identity matrix in the space of generators $r^{\mu}$ ; in contrast the Fock Hamiltonian (42), (43) did not depend on $\mu$ . However, we can carefully choose a basis in which the Hartree energy is diagonal in the space of generators such that inversion is still straightforward. To do this, we split the problem into symmetry unrelated cases based on $\frac{1}{2}\tr Q_{A,B}^{\tau}=0,\pm 1$ , which are invariant under the $(U(2))^{4}$ unperturbed symmetry of sublattice and valley resolved spin and charge rotations. We will later merge the final results of this case study with a formula that encompasses all cases.

We begin with the cases $\frac{1}{2}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}=\zeta$ or $\frac{1}{2}\tr Q_{B}^{\tau}=-\zeta$ , where $\zeta=\pm 1$ , such that $Q^{\tau}_{A}=\zeta$ or $Q^{\tau}_{B}=-\zeta$ is proportional to the $2\times 2$ identity matrix in spin-space. We note that $\tr m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{A}^{\tau}=-\tr m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{B}^{\tau}$ , so that we can replace $\tr m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{A}^{\tau}-\tr m^{\tau{\dagger}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}m^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}Q_{B}^{\tau}$ with $2\zeta\tr m^{\dagger}m$ by converting the $Q^{\tau}_{B}$ term to the $Q^{\tau}_{A}$ one if $Q^{\tau}_{A}=\zeta$ , or vice versa if $Q^{\tau}_{B}=-\zeta$ . We note that we have implicitly excluded the case $Q^{\tau}_{A}=Q^{\tau}_{B}=\pm 1$ , but this is because there are no particle-hole excitations in valley $\tau$ in this case: the condition $m=-Q_{A}mQ_{B}$ reduces to $m=-m$ . We will see that this $Q_{A}=Q_{B}$ case is dealt with appropriately in that the superexchange energy will vanish.

The Hartree energy for $Q_{A}=\zeta$ or $Q_{B}=-\zeta$ , for $\zeta=\pm 1$ and in valley $\tau$ , is then

$$ E_{H\tau}[M]=\zeta\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mu}\overline{m}^{\tau}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}R^{\tau}_{H{{\boldsymbol{k}}},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}m^{\tau}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}},\qquad R^{\tau}_{H{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=-\delta_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\frac{2}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\Lambda^{z\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})\left(\nu\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}+\nu_{z}\overline{\rho}^{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\right). $$

To obtain the corresponding superexchange energy associated with valley $\tau$ , we follow the previous subsection with $R^{\tau}_{F}\to R^{\tau}_{F}+\zeta R^{\tau}_{H}$ . We then have

$$ E^{\tau}_{\text{SE}}=\frac{1}{2}J_{\zeta}(\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}Q_{B}^{\tau}-2)=\frac{1}{2}J_{\zeta}(\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}Q_{B}^{\tau}-2)=\frac{1}{2}\zeta J_{\zeta}(\tr Q_{B}^{\tau}-\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}) $$

where

$$ J_{\zeta}=\frac{1}{2N_{M}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\overline{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}(R_{F}^{\tau}+\zeta R_{H}^{\tau})^{-1}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}z_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau} $$

does not depend on $\tau$ due to time reversal symmetry.

We now deal with the other case, where $\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}=\tr Q_{B}^{\tau}=0$ . While the particle-hole Hamiltonian is no longer the identity matrix in the space of generators, we will choose a basis so that it is (block) diagonal. In particular we choose $r^{\mu}$ such that $Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}=-r^{\mu}Q_{B}^{\tau}=\zeta_{\mu}r^{\mu}$ where $\zeta_{\mu}=(+1,-1)$ . Such a basis always exists; to see this we diagonalize $Q^{\tau}_{A}=U^{\tau}_{A}s_{z}U^{\tau{\dagger}}_{A}$ and $Q^{\tau}_{B}=U^{\tau}_{B}(-s_{z})U^{\tau{\dagger}}_{B}$ independently, with two different unitaries $U^{\tau}_{A,B}$ , and define $r^{\mu}=U^{\tau}_{A}\frac{1\pm s_{z}}{2}U^{\dagger}_{B}$ . The Hartree energy is, in this case,

$$ E_{H,\tau}=\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}\mu}\zeta_{\mu}\overline{m}^{\tau}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}R^{\tau}_{H{{\boldsymbol{k}}},{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}m^{\tau}_{\mu{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}, $$

so that the total interacting particle-hole Hamiltonian is diagonal in this basis

$$ R^{\tau\mu\nu}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}=(R^{\tau}_{F{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}+\zeta_{\mu}R^{\tau}_{H{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}})\delta^{\mu\nu} $$

and straightforward to invert in each block separately. The resulting superexchange energy in valley $\tau$ is

$$ E^{\tau}_{\text{SE}}=-\sum_{\mu}J_{\zeta_{\mu}}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}=-J\sum_{\mu}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}-J^{(-)}\sum_{\mu}\zeta_{\mu}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}, $$

where we defined $J^{(\pm)}=\frac{1}{2}(J_{\zeta=+}\pm J_{\zeta=-})$ and $J=J^{(+)}$ . We now use $Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}=\zeta_{\mu}r^{\mu}$ in our choice of basis in one of the traces in the second term to get rid of the $\zeta_{\mu}$ pre-factor which lets us apply the Fierz identity (50) to both terms:

$$ E^{\tau}_{\text{SE}}=-J\sum_{\mu}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}-J^{(-)}\sum_{\mu}\tr r^{\mu}_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}r^{{\dagger}\mu}_{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}J(\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}Q_{B}^{\tau}-2)-\frac{1}{2}J^{(-)}\left(\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}-\tr Q_{B}^{\tau}\right). $$

While the second term above is zero under our assumption of $\tr Q_{A}=\tr Q_{B}=0$ , we note that if we keep it then the above expression also reproduces (54) for $\tr Q_{A}=\zeta$ or $\tr Q_{B}=-\zeta$ . Therefore, (59) actually encompasses both cases, and we can cease our case study. Combining both valleys we have

$$ E^{\tau}_{\text{SE}}=\frac{1}{2}J\tr Q_{A}Q_{B},\qquad J=\frac{2}{N_{M}}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}\overline{z}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\tau}\frac{1}{2}\left((R^{\tau}_{F}+R^{\tau}_{H})^{-1}+(R^{\tau}_{F}-R^{\tau}_{H})^{-1}\right)_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}}z_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\prime}\tau} $$

up to an additive constant that depends on the sublattice polarization $\nu_{z}$ , but doesn’t split the states for a fixed sublattice polarization. We see that we reproduce the answer at charge neutrality, where $R_{H}$ is zero, and away from charge neutrality there is just a quantitative modification to the overall coefficient.

## Appendix B Representative $S_{z}$ conserving states

While generic strong-coupling states need not satisfy spin $S_{z}$ conservation, $[Q,S_{z}]=0$ , we argue here that all ground states are symmetry related to a representative state with conserved $S_{z}$ . To see this, we note that $(J-\lambda)\tr Q_{A}Q_{B}=(J-\lambda)\sum_{\tau}\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}Q_{B}^{\tau}$ where $Q_{A}^{\tau}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that describes the spin occupation and direction associated with sublattice $A$ and valley $\tau$ . If $\tr Q_{A}^{\tau}=\tr Q_{B}^{\tau}=0$ , such that one spin projection in each valley-sublattice sector is filled, then we can write $Q_{\tilde{\sigma}}^{\tau}={\boldsymbol{n}}_{\tilde{\sigma}}^{\tau}\cdot{\boldsymbol{s}}$ where ${\boldsymbol{n}}_{\tilde{\sigma}}^{\tau}$ is the direction of the spin in sublattice $\tilde{\sigma}$ and valley $\tau$ , and ${\boldsymbol{s}}=(s_{x},s_{y},s_{z})$ are spin Pauli matrices. Then, the energetics favor the spin direction of the $A$ sublattice band to be either aligned, for $\lambda>J$ , or antialigned, for $J<\lambda$ , with the $B$ sublattice for each valley $\tau$ , such that both spins lie along the same axis regardless. We can then use the spin rotation symmetry in valley $\tau$ to align this axis with the $z$ axis, such that we arrive at a state with conserved $S_{z}$ as claimed. If one or both sublattices are fully filled or fully empty then the same conclusion straightforwardly holds.

## Appendix C Flavor permutation symmetry

As discussed in the main text, Slater determinant states of h-HTG that are $S^{z}$ and valley conserving have a “flavor permutation symmetry”, which we elaborate on here. We will not assume that $P$ describes a strong coupling state. Using the notation of Appendix A, the Hartree Fock energy is

$$ E[P]=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\langle\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Tr\left([\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},P][P,\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}]\right)+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\langle\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle\langle\delta\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}\rangle $$

The first term is the Fock term and the second term is the Hartree term. We begin with the Fock term. Since the Fock term has a single trace, and both $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ and $P$ are diagonal in flavor, we have

$$ E_{F}[P]=\sum_{\tau s}E_{\tau}[P^{\tau s}],\qquad E_{\tau}[P^{\tau s}]=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{2}\Tr\left([\rho^{\tau s}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}},P^{\tau s}][P^{\tau s},\rho^{\tau s}_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}]\right) $$

where the exchange functional $E_{\tau}$ depends on valley but not spin, because of spin rotation symmetry, and $P^{\tau s}$ and $\rho^{\tau s}$ are the $2N_{M}\times 2N_{M}$ -sized blocks associated with valley $\tau$ and spin $s$ of $P$ and $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ respectively (note that $\rho^{\tau s}$ is $s$ -independent; we kept the label to indicate that its size corresponds to that of a single flavor block). The factor of $2$ in $2N_{M}$ comes from sublattice and $N_{M}$ is the number of moiré cells and the number ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ -points in the mBZ.

We now demonstrate explicitly the flavor permutation symmetry of the Fock term. It is straightforward to see that we can exchange $P^{\tau\uparrow}\leftrightarrow P^{\tau\downarrow}$ , for some fixed $\tau$ , without changing the Fock energy, since the functional $E_{\tau}$ does not depend on $s$ . This processes is simply making use of the spin rotation symmetry $SU(2)_{\tau}$ . More interestingly, we can use TRS to exchange valleys within a single, fixed, spin species. Indeed, time reversal symmetry implies that $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{\tau}=T\overline{\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}^{\tau}}T^{-1}$ , where $T$ takes ${{\boldsymbol{k}}}\to-{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ and $\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{q}}}}=\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{\dagger}$ , so that $E_{\tau}[P^{\tau s}]=E_{{-\tau}}[T\overline{P^{\tau s}}T^{-1}]$ . To understand the flavor permutation symmetry involving opposite valleys that the time reversal relation implies, let us begin with a QSH insulator at neutrality, $P_{\text{QSH}}$ , consisting of filling both sublattices of the flavors $(K,\uparrow)$ , $(\bar{K},\downarrow)$ and leaving the other two flavors empty. By exchanging the flavors $(\bar{K},\downarrow)\leftrightarrow(K,\downarrow)$ , through defining

$$ \displaystyle P_{\text{CI}}^{\tau\uparrow} \displaystyle=P^{(-\tau)\uparrow}_{\text{QSH}} \displaystyle P_{\text{CI}}^{\tau\downarrow} \displaystyle=T\overline{P^{(-\tau)\downarrow}_{\text{QSH}}}T^{-1} $$

we arrive at a valley polarized $C=2$ Chern insulator (CI) with the exact same Fock energy. By combining the action of time reversal on individual spin species and spin flip symmetries within each valley, we can permute the occupations of all flavors without changing the Fock energy.

The Hartree energy is also flavor permutation symmetric, as while the Hartree energy contains a product of traces, from the product of the density expectation values $\langle\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle\langle\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle$ and $\langle\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle=\Tr P\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}-4\overline{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}=\Tr Q\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}$ , each trace on its own decomposes into a sum over flavors that is flavor permutation symmetric. Indeed, TRS implies $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}^{\tau}=T\overline{\rho_{-{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}^{-\tau}}T^{-1}$ where we used that the form factors satisfy $\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{G}}})=\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ in our periodic gauge $c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}=c^{\dagger}_{{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+{{\boldsymbol{G}}}}$ . We therefore have that $\Tr Q^{\tau s}\rho^{\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}=\Tr T\overline{Q^{\tau s}}T^{-1}\rho^{-\tau}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}$ , so that the valleys can be permuted in the same way as in the Fock energy.

## Abstract

Monolayer staggered materials of the graphene family present intrinsic spin-orbit coupling and can be driven through several topological phase transitions using external circularly polarized lasers, and static electric or magnetic fields. We show how topological features arising from photo-induced phase transitions and the quantum Hall effect coexist in these materials, and simultaneously impact their Hall conductivity through their corresponding charge Chern numbers. We also show that the spectral response of the longitudinal conductivity contains signatures about the various phase transition boundaries, that the transverse conductivity encodes information about the topology of the band structure, and that both present resonant peaks which can be unequivocally associated to one of the four inequivalent Dirac cones present in these materials. This complex optoelectronic response can be probed with straightforward Faraday rotation experiments, allowing the study of the crossroads between quantum Hall physics, spintronics, and valleytronics.

## I Introduction

The two dimensional staggered semiconductors [1, 2, 3] silicene [4], germanene [5], stanene [6, 7], and plumbene [8] are monolayer materials made out of Silicon, Germanium, Tin, and Lead atoms, respectively. Together with graphene [9, 10], they make up the group of monolayer honeycomb materials often referred to as the graphene family. However, as opposed to graphene, these materials have an intrinisic spin-orbit coupling that opens a gap in their electronic band structure. They are also non-planar, with their two inequivalent sublattices lying in two distinct parallel planes, and thus respond to the presence of an out-of-plane static electric field [11, 12, 13, 14]. Together with a circularly polarized laser, these external fields allow one to tune the gap for each spin and valley, allowing the materials to be driven through several phase transitions [15, 16, 17, 18]. Many of the achievable phases possess topologically nontrivial features that can be characterized by a topological invariant, namely the charge Chern number. On the other hand, topological states can be also accessed via the quantum Hall (QH) effect [19], where a magnetic field is introduced and the QH Chern number changes depending on the occupation of various Landau levels. The quantum Hall effect has been studied extensively in graphene [20] (where it shows an unconventional odd integer quantization originating from the quantum anomaly of the zeroth Landau level in a relativistic spectrum [21, 22]) and in the other members of the graphene family [23, 24].

Here, we develop a unified and comprehensive study of the interplay between topological features arising from the quantum Hall effect and photo-induced phase transitions in 2D staggered semiconductors. Photo-induced and quantum Hall Chern invariants simultaneously manifest themselves in the DC Hall conductivity, resulting in a complex optoelectronic phase diagram possessing a wealth of phase transitions. We discover that doping the monolayer leads to a shift of the phase diagram, allowing to perfectly replicate all photoinduced topological boundaries without the need of circularly polarized light, a phenomenon that can be traced back to the anomalous nature of the zeroth Landau level. We also demonstrate that the frequency dispersion of the optical conductivity tensor presents several resonances imprinted with signatures of the topologically non-trivial electronic states. Finally, we show that Faraday rotation measurements is a suitable technique to demonstrate the co-existence of Hall effects of distinct origin in the graphene family materials.

## II Optical response of the graphene family

Let us begin with the Hamiltonian for members of the graphene family, found through the use of a tight-binding model and subsequent low energy expansion, including the effects of a circularly polarized laser and electric field [15, 17, 16], $\hat{H}^{\eta}_{s}=v_{F}(\eta p_{x}\hat{\tau}_{x}+p_{y}\hat{\tau}_{y})+\Delta^{\eta}_{s}\hat{\tau}_{z}$ , where $\Delta^{\eta}_{s}=-\eta s\lambda_{\text{SO}}+e\ell E_{z}+\eta\Lambda$ is half the mass gap. Here, $\hat{\tau}_{i}$ are Pauli matrices, $\mathbf{p}=(p_{x},p_{y})$ is the momentum for particles around points $K$ ( $\eta=+1$ ), $K^{\prime}$ ( $\eta=-1$ ) and spin $s=\pm 1$ , $v_{F}=\sqrt{3}dt/2\hbar$ is the Fermi velocity, where $d$ is the lattice constant and $t$ is the nearest neighbor coupling. The Dirac mass $\Delta^{\eta}_{s}$ has contributions from the spin-orbit coupling $\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ , the out-of-plane electric field $E_{z}$ and a circularly polarized laser (see Fig. 1). The spin-orbit couplings for silicene, germanene, stanene and plumbene are $\lambda_{\text{SO}}\approx 3.9,\,43,\,100,\,200\penalty\ \text{meV}$ [15, 17, 16, 8], respectively. Terms originating from Rashba physics are ignored because of their comparitively small effect [15, 16]. The out-of-plane electric field preferences one sublattice over another due to nonzero lattice buckling $2\ell$ ( $\sim 0.46,0.66,0.80,3.00\,\text{\AA}$ , for silicene, germanene, stanene, and plumbene, respectively). The circularly polarized laser of intensity $I_{0}$ and frequency $\omega_{0}$ also modifies the band structure [15, 17, 16]. Its interaction with the monolayer can be well described through the coupling constant $\Lambda=\pm 8\pi\alpha v_{F}^{2}I_{0}/\omega_{0}^{3}$ provided $4\absolutevalue{\Lambda}\hbar\omega_{0}/3t^{2}\ll 1$ (where $\alpha$ is the fine structure constant). The full Hamiltonian is block diagonal for each of the possible values of $\eta,s=\pm 1$ , hence it sufficies to analyze the spectrum of $H^{\eta}_{s}$ . The resulting eigenenergies can be cast as $\varepsilon_{\pm}=\pm\sqrt{v_{\text{F}}^{2}|{\bf p}|^{2}+(\Delta_{s}^{\eta})^{2}}$ . Since the laser opens a gap in the band structure at energies equal to $n\hbar\omega_{0}/2$ , where $n$ is an integer, we shall restrict our discussion to $|\varepsilon_{\pm}|\sim\lambda_{\text{SO}}\ll\hbar\omega_{0}/2$ .

*Figure 1: Schematics of the system considered: a staggered monolayer of the graphene family exposed to out-of-plane static electric and magnetic fields together with a normally incident circularly polarized laser. Optoelectronic properties of the system can be probed with Faraday rotation measurements, where incident linearly polarized light becomes elliptically polarized and undergoes a rotation of the polarization plane after transmission through the monolayer.*

As the material undergoes a quantum phase transition whenever $\Delta^{\eta}_{s}$ vanishes, the tunability of the Dirac mass for each spin and valley allows these materials to exhibit a multitude of different electronic phases, many of which harbor nontrivial topological states [15, 17, 16]. The topology is indexed by the charge Chern number

$$ C=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\eta,s}\eta\;\text{sgn}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s}). $$

The phase diagram for the graphene family is plotted in Fig. 2a. At $E_{z}=\Lambda=0$ , the material is characterized as a quantum spin Hall insulator with $C=0$ . One can verify that non-zero Chern numbers are generated through the time reversal symmetry breaking. If $E_{z}$ and $\Lambda$ are both increased, the material remains in the same state as long as $\absolutevalue{elE_z}+\absolutevalue{\Lambda}<\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ . Along the lines where the previous condition holds as an equality, a single Dirac cone closes giving Chern numbers of $\pm 1/2,\pm 3/2$ . At the points where two of these lines intersect, two cones close and the material reaches either the spin valley polarized semimetal ( $e\ell E_{z}/\lambda_{\text{SO}}=1,\ \Lambda/\lambda_{\text{SO}}=0$ ) or the spin polarized metal ( $e\ell E_{z}/\lambda_{\text{SO}}=0,\ \Lambda/\lambda_{\text{SO}}=1$ ) phase with Chern number $0$ or $\pm 1$ . In the lowermost and uppermost wedges, the monolayer is an anomalous quantum Hall insulator with $C=\pm 2$ , whereas on the leftmost and rightmost wedges, it is a band insulator with $C=0$ . In the regions $\big||\Lambda|-|e\ell E_{z}|\big|<\lambda_{\text{SO}}<|e\ell E_{z}|+|\Lambda|$ the material behaves as a polarized spin quantum Hall insulator with $C=\pm 1$ .

The charge Chern number at the phase transition boundaries (lines and points) is given by the average of the charge Chern numbers of the adjacent regions. The phase diagram remains unchanged in the presence of a static magnetic field provided $\mu=0$ (see text). b) Relevant transitions for the case $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ . For illustration purposes only, we consider a cone for which $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ and choose $\mu<\varepsilon_{0}$ . c) Phase diagram for the static $\sigma_{xy}$ for a dissipationless but doped monolayer with $\mu/\lambda_{\text{SO}}=0.5$ . The magnetic field intensity chosen ( $E_{B}/\absolutevalue{\mu}=100$ ) is such to ensure $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ everywhere in the phase plane and for all Dirac cones. Under these conditions, the plot is independent of the particular value of the magnetic field. The chemical potential has a role similar to $\Lambda$ and therefore shifts the phase diagram vertically.*

In order to investigate the quantum Hall effect in the graphene family, let us now assume that a static magnetic field ${\bf B}=B{\bf\hat{z}}$ is applied perpendicularly to the monolayer (see Fig. 1). The low energy Hamiltonian describing the system is obtained from the above Hamiltonian through a Peierls substitution $\mathbf{p}\to\mathbf{p}+e\mathbf{A}$ , where $\mathbf{A}=-By{\bf\hat{x}}$ is the vector potential in the Landau gauge. Spin splitting due to the Zeeman interaction is ignored owing to its comparatively small effect [23]. Similarly to the case of graphene [20], one can solve the energy spectrum and wavefunctions in terms of those of the harmonic oscillator by introducing creation and annihilation operators. The eigenenergies of the system are $\varepsilon_{n}=\text{sgn}(n)\sqrt{(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})^{2}+\absolutevalue{n}E_{B}^{2}}$ for $n\neq 0$ ( $n$ is an integer), and $\varepsilon_{0}=-\tilde{\eta}\Delta^{\eta}_{s}$ for $n=0$ , where $\tilde{\eta}=\text{sgn}(eB)\eta$ , and $E_{B}=\sqrt{2v_{F}^{2}\hbar\absolutevalue{eB}}$ is the relativistic analogue of the cyclotron energy. We note that the zeroth level is quantum anomalous: its magnitude is independent of the magnetic field and its sign depends on the particular cone (which means it could be occupied either by electrons or holes). We mention that the results we describe in the next sections require $E_{B}\sim\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ , which can be accessed in the graphene family for magnetic fields of the order of a few Teslas. The eigenfunctions associated to the Hamiltonian are $\ket{n}=\left(-\tilde{\eta}\,\text{sgn}(n)A^{+}_{n}\ket{\abs{n}+\frac{1+\tilde{\eta}}{2}}_{\text{HO}},A^{-}_{n}\ket{\abs{n}+\frac{1-\tilde{\eta}}{2}}_{\text{HO}}\right)^{T}$ , where $\ket{n}_{\text{HO}}$ are the harmonic oscillator eigenstates, $A^{\pm}_{n}=\sqrt{[\absolutevalue{\varepsilon_n}\pm\text{sgn}(n)\Delta^{\eta}_{s}]/2\absolutevalue{\varepsilon_n}}$ for $n\neq 0$ , and $A^{\pm}_{0}=(1\mp\tilde{\eta})/2$ .

The optoelectronic response of the monolayer at frequency $\omega$ can be characterized by its conductivity $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$ . For the set of parameters we consider in the rest of the paper, we can neglect effects of spatial dispersion and calculate $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$ using the standard Kubo’s approach in the local regime [25, 26], resulting in

$$ \begin{split}\frac{\sigma_{xx}}{\sigma_{0}}=&\frac{iE_{B}^{2}}{\pi}\sum_{\eta,s}\sum_{n,m}\frac{f_{m}-f_{n}}{\varepsilon_{n}-\varepsilon_{m}}\\
\times&\frac{(A^{+}_{m}A^{-}_{n})^{2}\delta_{\absolutevalue{n},\absolutevalue{m}-\tilde{\eta}}+(A^{-}_{m}A^{+}_{n})^{2}\delta_{\absolutevalue{n},\absolutevalue{m}+\tilde{\eta}}}{\hbar\omega+\varepsilon_{m}-\varepsilon_{n}+i\hbar\Gamma},\end{split} $$

$$ \begin{split}\frac{\sigma_{xy}}{\sigma_{0}}=&-\frac{E_{B}^{2}}{\pi}\sum_{\eta,s}\sum_{n,m}\eta\frac{f_{m}-f_{n}}{\varepsilon_{n}-\varepsilon_{m}}\\
\times&\frac{(A^{+}_{m}A^{-}_{n})^{2}\delta_{\absolutevalue{n},\absolutevalue{m}-\tilde{\eta}}-(A^{-}_{m}A^{+}_{n})^{2}\delta_{\absolutevalue{n},\absolutevalue{m}+\tilde{\eta}}}{\hbar\omega+\varepsilon_{m}-\varepsilon_{n}+i\hbar\Gamma}\,,\end{split} $$

and $\sigma_{yy}=\sigma_{xx}$ , $\sigma_{yx}=-\sigma_{xy}$ . Here, $\sigma_{0}=e^{2}/4\hbar$ is the graphene’s universal conductivity, $f_{n}=[e^{(\varepsilon_{n}-\mu)/k_{\text{B}}T}+1]^{-1}$ denotes the Fermi Dirac distribution, $T$ is the temperature, $\mu$ is the chemical potential, and $\Gamma$ is the dissipation rate. In the next sections we investigate the conductivity tensor for different sets of parameters and show that it contains clear signatures of phase transitions and topology in the graphene family.

## III Interplay between photoinduced topology and quantum Hall effect

In order to better understand the interplay between the quantum Hall effect and topological phase transitions in the graphene family, we start our discussion with the DC conductivity of a lossless 2D staggered monolayer. The results we obtain in this regime are an excellent approximation for the conductivity tensor for low frequency and dissipation ( $\omega,\Gamma\ll E_{B}/\hbar$ ). In this limit, $\sigma_{xx}$ vanishes and $\sigma_{xy}$ is a purely real function. By using that Re $[\sigma_{xy}]$ is symmetric under flipping Landau level indices $n,m$ , we can choose $n>m$ and multiply the sum in Eq. (3) by two. The conductivity can now be interpreted as a sum over transitions $m\to n$ with energy gaps $\varepsilon_{n}-\varepsilon_{m}$ and selection rules $\absolutevalue{n}=\absolutevalue{m}\pm 1$ . We also take the limit of zero temperature, allowing us to replace the Fermi-Dirac distribution with Heaviside functions. As we will show in the next sub-section, the static Hall conductivity can be written as

$$ \sigma_{xy}=\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\sum_{\eta,s}\theta(\varepsilon_{1}-|\mu|)\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}+\theta(|\mu|-\varepsilon_{1})\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}, $$

where $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}=(1/2)\text{sgn}(eB)\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{0}(\Lambda^{\eta}_{s})-\mu)$ is the Chern number per cone associated with the photo-induced topology, and $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}=-(1/2)\text{sgn}(eB\mu)(2N^{\eta}_{s}+1)$ is the Chern number per cone associated with the quantum Hall effect ( $N^{\eta}_{s}$ is the number of filled Landau levels per cone).

### III.1 Calculation of the DC Hall conductivity

To evaluate $\sigma_{xy}$ , we must determine which transitions are allowed according to the selection rules and the value of $\mu$ . When $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ , the zeroth Landau level is involved either in the transition $-1\to 0$ or $0\to 1$ , and there are no intraband transitions. When, on the other hand, $\absolutevalue{\mu}>\varepsilon_{1}$ , the zeroth level no longer contributes, but intraband transitions do. We therefore split the evaluation of $\sigma_{xy}$ into two separate cases, $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ and $\absolutevalue{\mu}>\varepsilon_{1}$ . Note that $\varepsilon_{1}$ depends on the values of $\eta,s,E_{z},$ and $\Lambda$ , and so different transitions are possible depending on the cone and location in the phase diagram.

Let us first consider the case $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ . When this condition holds, the allowed transitions in the calculation of the Hall conductivity are $-1\to 0$ if $\varepsilon_{0}>\mu$ and $0\to 1$ otherwise, as well as the interband transitions $-l\to l+1$ and $-(l+1)\to l$ for all $\l\geq 1$ [see Fig. 2b]. All other transitions are either Pauli-blocked or forbidden by the selection rules. Therefore we can write $\sigma_{xy}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=\sigma_{xy}^{(0)}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})+\sum_{l\geq 1}\sigma_{xy}^{(l)}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})$ , where $\sigma_{xy}^{(0)}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=\sigma_{0}E_{B}^{2}\text{sgn}(eB)\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{0}-\mu)/[\varepsilon_{1}(\varepsilon_{1}+\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{0}-\mu)\varepsilon_{0})]$ is the contribution to the Hall conductivity due to the transition involving the zeroth energy level, and $\sigma_{xy}^{(l)}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=\sigma_{0}E_{B}^{2}\text{sgn}(eB)\,\varepsilon_{0}/[\varepsilon_{l}\varepsilon_{l+1}(\varepsilon_{l}+\varepsilon_{l+1})]$ is the corresponding contribution due to the $l$ and $l+1$ Landau levels. The sum over $l$ can be evaluated analytically by noting that $(\varepsilon_{l}+\varepsilon_{l+1})^{-1}=(\varepsilon_{l+1}-\varepsilon_{l})/E_{B}^{2}$ and concluding that it telescopes, resulting in $\sum_{l\geq 1}\sigma_{xy}^{(l)}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=\text{sgn}(eB)\varepsilon_{0}/\pi\varepsilon_{1}$ . The final result for the Hall conductivity for a given cone that satisfies the condition $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ is

$$ \sigma_{xy}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\text{sgn}(eB)\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{0}-\mu)\equiv\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}, $$

where $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}$ is the photo-induced Chern number per cone introduced in Eq.(4), which is independent of the magnitude of the magnetic field. A possible way to understand this result is by means of a quantum field theory approach, in which the conductivity can be computed as a sum over filled Landau levels, where negative energy levels are treated as positive ones that can be occupied by holes [21]. From this perspective, it is clear that only the zeroth Landau level contributes to the conductivity for $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ . This is a more physical reason why in the previous approach the sum over transitions telescopes and leaves only the zeroth level contribution.

When the stronger condition $\absolutevalue{\mu}<E_{B}$ is satisfied, then $\absolutevalue{\mu}<\varepsilon_{1}$ for all Dirac cones and everywhere in the phase diagram. In this case the total conductivity is given by

$$ \sigma_{xy}=\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\sum_{\eta,s}\frac{\text{sgn}(eB)\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{0}(\Lambda)-\mu)}{2}\equiv\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\tilde{C}_{\rm ph}, $$

where in the last equality we have used that the DC Hall conductivity can always be written in terms of a topological invariant [19] and defined a global photo-induced Chern number $\tilde{C}_{\rm ph}$ for our problem with the magnetic field. We note that when the monolayer is neutral ( $\mu=0$ ), using the expression for $\varepsilon_{0}$ it follows that the photo-induced generalized Chern number $\tilde{C}_{\rm ph}$ is identical to that defined before in the absence of magnetic field Eq.(1), $\tilde{C}_{\rm ph}=C$ , and hence we recover the same phase diagram for the Hall conductivity as in the case $B=0$ [15, 16, 17] (see Fig. 2a). This result holds for any magnetic field as long as $\mu=0$ , since $\varepsilon_{0}$ is independent of the magnitude of $B$ in a relativistic spectrum, as already mentioned.

For $\mu\neq 0$ , one can verify that $\varepsilon_{0}(\Lambda)-\mu=\varepsilon_{0}(\Lambda+\text{sgn}(eB)\mu)$ . Therefore, as long as $\absolutevalue{\mu}<E_{B}$ so that Eq.(6) holds, doping the monolayer shifts all phase boundaries vertically, as depicted in Fig. 2c. As a result, we can conclude that the chemical potential has a similar effect to that of the circularly polarized laser, allowing us to replicate all photoinduced phase transition boundaries even for $\Lambda=0$ . Thus, in this regime, the chemical potential can serve as an alternative to the high frequency external laser, which is experimentally very difficult to implement since the intensities needed to probe the various topological phase transitions are too large. For example, for a green laser impinging on a silicene monolayer (in this case the condition $\hbar\omega_{0}\gg 2\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ for the validity of the Hamiltonian is well satisfied), one would need a laser intensity as high as $2.3\times 10^{14}\,\text{W}/\text{m}^{2}$ in order to probe regions of the phase diagram with $\Lambda=\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ . Such high laser intensities would quickly heat up the sample to $k_{B}T>\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ , blurring the topological phases altogether (see, e.g., [17]). The above results then show that a non-zero chemical potential in addition to a weak magnetic field such that $\absolutevalue{\mu}<E_{B}$ , (e.g. $\mu=0.5\lambda_{\text{SO}}$ and $B\sim 0.1\,\text{T}$ suffices for silicene) would allow experimentalists to probe the different topological phases of these materials [15, 16, 17], which was until now unrealistic.

Let us now consider the situation when $|\mu|>\varepsilon_{1}$ , where the allowed transitions depend on the last filled Landau level per cone $N^{\eta}_{s}=\Theta(\mu^{2}-(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})^{2})\,{\rm Floor}\left[(\mu^{2}-(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})^{2})/E_{B}^{2}\right]$ . Note that $N^{\eta}_{s}>0$ as we assume $\absolutevalue{\mu}>\varepsilon_{1}$ . In order to ease notation, in the following we will drop the indexes $\eta$ and $s$ from $N^{\eta}_{s}$ , but the reader should remember that $N$ depends on cone and on the location in phase space. The allowed transitions for $\mu>0$ are the interband transition $-N\to(N+1)$ , the interband transitions $-l\to l+1$ and $-(l+1)\to l$ for all $\l\geq N+1$ , and the intraband transition $N\to(N+1)$ [see Fig. 3a]. For $\mu<0$ the sign of the level index and the direction of the transition are both flipped, in accordance with Pauli blocking and selection rules. The inter- and intra-band transitions can be computed following similar techniques as above, resulting in the full DC Hall conductivity tensor per cone when $|\mu|>\varepsilon_{1}$ holds, namely

$$ \sigma_{xy}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=-\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\text{sgn}(eB\mu)(2N+1)\equiv\frac{2\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}, $$

where $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}$ is the quantum Hall Chern number per cone introduced in Eq.(4). Summing over spin and valley, this result reproduces the relativistic Hall effect in gapless graphene ( $\Delta^{\eta}_{s}\to 0$ ), for which the Chern number is $C_{\rm QH}=-\text{sgn}(eB\mu)(4N+2)$ [21].

Finally, we combine the results of case $|\mu|<\varepsilon_{1}$ (for which $N=0$ ) with those of case $|\mu|>\varepsilon_{1}$ (for which $N\geq 1$ ), and write a simple expression for the full DC Hall conductivity per cone in the presence of a static electric field, a circularly polarized laser, and a magnetic field, namely

$$ \sigma_{xy}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})=-\frac{\sigma_{0}}{\pi}\text{sgn}(eB\mu)\left\{2N-\text{sgn}(\mu)\text{sgn}[\varepsilon_{0}(\Delta^{\eta}_{s})-\mu]\right\}. $$

This result is identical to Eq.(4) after summing over spin and valley indices. We also see that this fits our physical picture of electrons (holes) occupying positive energy Landau levels, where the zeroth level has half the degeneracy and an anomalous sign.

### III.2 Co-existence of Hall effects in the graphene family

We now discuss how $\sigma_{xy}$ depends on the location in the $(E_{z},\Lambda)$ phase plane at nonzero chemical potential and magnetic field. When $\mu^{2}/E_{B}^{2}<1$ , we have that $N=0$ everywhere in the phase plane, and then $\pi\sigma_{xy}/2\sigma_{0}$ is simply equal to $\tilde{C}_{\rm ph}$ with a vertical shift along the $\Lambda$ axis of magnitude $\absolutevalue{\mu}$ , as discussed before and shown Fig. 2c. If, however, $\mu^{2}/E_{B}^{2}>1$ , then sufficiently close to the unshifted boundaries (where the gap goes to zero for a particular cone) $N>0$ contributions arise, and $\pi\sigma_{xy}/2\sigma_{0}$ is a weighted combination of $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}$ and $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}$ as in Eq.(4). This results in a multitude of phase transitions arising from the usual quantum Hall effect ( $N\geq 1$ ) and the photo-induced topological phases ( $N=0$ ), see Fig. 3b. For the chosen parameters in the figure, regions between adjacent dashes lines correspond to situations in which at least one Dirac cone has $N=2$ , while those between adjacent parallel solid and dashes lines to situations in which at least one Dirac cone has $N=1$ . Squared regions bounded by two solid and two dashed lines correspond to cases in which, out of the four Dirac cones, one has $N=2$ , another $N=1$ , and the remaining two have $N=0$ . Note that the shifted boundaries due to the photo-induced phase transitions also appear in the figure. Furthermore, in some regions of phase space the Hall conductivity vanishes due to a cancellation between $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm ph}$ of some cones and $\tilde{C}^{\eta,s}_{\rm QH}$ of other ones.
