## Appendix A Continuum Models, Magnetic Translations, and Hartree-Fock

This Appendix provides a self-contained formalism for working with continuum models with and without magnetic field on an equal footing, allowing us to work with the Bistritzer-MacDonald model and its finite field extensions. [77, 78, 79, 17] on equal footing. The crux of our approach is that all model-dependent information is reduced to three operators $\hat{\lambda},\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ , and $\hat{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}$ , whose matrix elements must be computed. We start by reviewing some salient facts about the magnetic translation algebra. Then we describe continuum models the single-particle level to establish definitions, and consider the Coulomb interaction in second quantization. Finally re-derive the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian as a partial trace operation that will be used to integrate out the remote bands in App. C.

### A.1 Magnetic Translation Algebra

This section will briefly review the magnetic translation algebra [119, 120, 121, 17]. A standard model for electrons in a solid is $\hat{H}=\hat{p}^{2}/(2m)+\hat{V}(\boldsymbol{r})$ , where $\hat{V}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})=\hat{V}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is periodic under lattice translations $\boldsymbol{R}\in\Lambda$ . The corresponding discrete translation operators $\hat{T}(\boldsymbol{R}):=e^{i\boldsymbol{R}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}}$ commute both with the Hamiltonian and each other. That is, $[\hat{H},\hat{T}(\boldsymbol{R})]=[\hat{T}(\boldsymbol{R}),\hat{T}(\boldsymbol{R}^{\prime})]=0$ , which is the assumption needed for Bloch’s theorem.

In a magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r})=B(\boldsymbol{r})\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}={\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\times{\boldsymbol{A}}$ (we restrict to the 2d case and with a periodic or flat magnetic field so that $B(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})=B(\boldsymbol{R})$ ), the canonical momentum becomes $\boldsymbol{\pi}=\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\hat{H}_{B}=\hat{\pi}^{2}/(2m)+\hat{V}(\boldsymbol{r})$ , which fails to commute with ordinary translation operators. To rectify this, we define magnetic translation operators

$$ \hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R}):=e^{-i\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})}T(\boldsymbol{R}) $$

. The magnetic twists $\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}$ are chosen to satisfy $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})-\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r})=\boldsymbol{\nabla}\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})$ . One can check that $[\hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}},\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R})]=0$ , so $[\hat{H}_{B},\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R})]=0$ . However, Eq. (25) is a projective representation of the group of lattice translations, and commutators are modified by phase factors relative to the normal case. In particular, if $\boldsymbol{R}_{1}$ and $\boldsymbol{R}_{2}$ are the primitive vectors,

$$ \hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R}_{1})\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R}_{2})=\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R}_{2})\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{R}_{1})\zeta,\text{ where }\zeta:=e^{i2\pi\phi},\quad\phi:=\frac{BA}{h/e}, $$

where $A=\hat{z}\cdot(\boldsymbol{R}_{1}\times\boldsymbol{R}_{2})$ is the (signed) area of the unit cell and $\phi$ is the flux in units of the flux quantum.

To apply Bloch’s theorem, the translation operators must mutually commute. If the flux is a rational number

$$ \phi=\frac{BA}{h/e}=\frac{p}{q}\in\mathbb{Q}, $$

then we may enlarge the unit cell by a factor of $q$ , with new primitive vectors $\tilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}=r\boldsymbol{R}_{1}$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}=s\boldsymbol{R}_{2}$ where $rs=q$ . Since $\zeta^{rs}=e^{i2\pi(p/q)q}=1$ , one has $[\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}),\hat{\mathcal{M}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2})]=0$ . We may then employ a (generalized) Bloch’s theorem for the expanded magnetic unit cell. We note that the resulting Bloch wavefunctions have differ from the non-magnetic ones by their boundary conditions, which will be important below.

Henceforth, we assume that the unit cell has always been properly expanded so that the (magnetic) translation operators commute.

### A.2 First Quantization

Suppose we have a sample geometry $M$ with a finite area (IR cutoff) $A_{s}\gg 1$ . Suppose we have a lattice $\Lambda=\left\{n\boldsymbol{R}_{1}+m\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\right\}$ with reciprocal lattice $\Lambda^{*}=\left\{n\boldsymbol{G}_{1}+m\boldsymbol{G}_{2}\right\}$ . Let $A=A_{s}/N$ be the area of a (possibly magnetic) unit cell. Let $\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{R})$ be the magnetic translations operators described above, which mutually commute (after expanding the unit cell if necessary)[120, 119]. The Bloch states are simultaneous eigenstates of the Hamiltonian and the translation algebra

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}_{0}\ket{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}} \displaystyle=\epsilon_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}\ket{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}} \displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{R})\ket{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}} \displaystyle=e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}}\ket{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}} $$

where $\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}$ , $n$ labels bands, $\mu$ labels flavors such as spin and valley, and $a=(\gamma,\sigma,\ldots)=(\text{layer},\text{sublattice},\dots)$ runs over internal degrees of freedom. For convenience, we group $\alpha=(\mu,n)$ , and suppress internal (“ $a$ ”) indices whenever possible.

The Bloch states $\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}^{a}(\boldsymbol{r}):=\braket{\boldsymbol{r},a|\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}}$ comprise a unitary transformation between the $(\boldsymbol{r},a,\mu)$ and $(\boldsymbol{k},n,\mu)$ bases:88 8 Due to the finite sample area, the $\boldsymbol{k}$ -points are discrete.

$$ \braket{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}|\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}}=\int_{M}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;\overline{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{\boldsymbol{k}\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha\beta};\hskip 20.00003pt\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\overline{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})=\delta(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}). $$

Bloch waves, defined by $u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}):=N^{1/2}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})$ , are the eigenvectors of $\hat{H}_{0}(\boldsymbol{k}):=e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\hat{H}_{0}e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}$ , and are normalized on a single unit cell as $\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}|u_{\boldsymbol{k}\beta}}=\int_{uc}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;\overline{u}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})u_{\boldsymbol{k}\beta}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ .

The magnetic field imposes twisted boundary conditions on the real-space unit cell. Translation acts as $\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{R})\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})=e^{-i\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})}\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})$ , so

$$ \phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})=e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}+i\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})}\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})\implies u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})=e^{i\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})}u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}). $$

For any $\boldsymbol{k}$ , we define $\boldsymbol{k}=[\boldsymbol{k}]+\boldsymbol{G}$ where $[\boldsymbol{k}]$ is in the first Brillouin zone and $\boldsymbol{G}\in\Lambda^{*}$ . In this section we impose a periodic gauge by defining

$$ \ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}}:=\hat{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})\ket{u_{[\boldsymbol{k}]\alpha}};\quad\hat{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k}):=e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}. $$

for $\boldsymbol{k}$ outside the first Brillouin zone. One can check that $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}}$ is an eigenstate of $\hat{H}(\boldsymbol{k})=\hat{H}([\boldsymbol{k}]+\boldsymbol{G})$ .

We define form factors as matrices

$$ [\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\beta}:=\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}|u_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q},\beta}}, $$

for any $\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}$ . They obey the relation $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})^{\dagger}=\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q})$ and, due to the periodic gauge, $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})^{\dagger}=\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ .

To work with a continuum Hamiltonian in practice, one must choose a computational basis $v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}(\boldsymbol{r})=\braket{r|v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}}$ where the internal index $I$ indexes a function space on the (magnetic) Brillouin zone. By performing the unitary transformation

$$ \ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}}=\sum_{I}\ket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}}U^{I}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}, $$

(28) is equivalent to

$$ [\hat{H}_{0}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{J}^{I}U_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}^{J}=\epsilon_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}U_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}^{I} $$

where $[\hat{H}_{0}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{J}^{I}=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}|\hat{H}_{0}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}J}}$ and the $U$ ’s are often found numerically in practice.

The drawback of this representation is that quantities that are natural in real space have non-trivial matrix elements in the computational basis. We now define three of the most common matrix elements for moire systems, which must be computed analytically once a basis is chosen. Let $\boldsymbol{k}$ be in the first Brillouin zone, let $\boldsymbol{G}=r\boldsymbol{G}_{1}+s\boldsymbol{G}_{2}$ be a reciprocal lattice vector, and let $\boldsymbol{q}$ be an unconstrained momentum. Define:

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I} \displaystyle:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I^{\prime}}|e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}} \displaystyle(\text{tunneling matrix element}) \displaystyle[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I} \displaystyle:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I^{\prime}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q},I}} \displaystyle(\text{computational basis form factor}) \displaystyle[\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I} \displaystyle:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G},I^{\prime}}|e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k},I}} \displaystyle(\text{reciprocal lattice translation}) $$

The $\mathcal{\mathcal{T}}$ ’s appear as tunnelling terms in TBG. Form factors are matrices in the band basis $[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{\alpha}_{\beta}~=~\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}|u_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q},\beta}}$ , and may be computed in the computational basis as

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})=\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}|u_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}}}=U^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}}}U_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}}=U_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q})U_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]}, $$

for any $\boldsymbol{k}$ in the first Brillouin zone. In terms of these, the Berry curvature may be computed from an infinitesimal Wilson loop

$$ \mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{k})=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\operatorname{Im}\log[\Lambda_{\delta\boldsymbol{q}_{x}}\Lambda_{\delta\boldsymbol{q}_{y}}\Lambda_{-\delta\boldsymbol{q}_{x}}\Lambda_{-\delta\boldsymbol{q}_{y}}] $$

and similarly the quantum metric can be computed in terms of $\Lambda_{\delta\boldsymbol{q}}\Lambda_{-\delta\boldsymbol{q}}$ with $\delta\boldsymbol{q}$ along the first, second, or diagonal axes respectively. These definitions are gauge invariant and numerically stable. Finally, the periodic gauge choice (32) implies the relation $U_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G},\alpha}^{I}=[\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I}_{J}U_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}$ . So, thanks to our choice of a periodic gauge, all physical quantities can be computed from the solutions to Eq. (35) within the first Brillouin zone alone — a result which applies in either the magnetic or non-magnetic cases.

### A.3 Second Quantization

Suppose we have a microscopic creation operator $\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r})$ that obeys the standard anti-commutation relations $\{\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r}),\hat{\psi}_{\nu b}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\}=\delta_{\mu\nu}\delta_{ab}\delta(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})$ . For $\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}$ , i.e. only inside the first Brillouin zone, define band creation operators

$$ \hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}:=\sum_{a}\int_{M}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}^{a}(\boldsymbol{r})\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r}). $$

Employing the unitarity condition Eq. (30), we have anti-commutation relations $\{\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha},\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}$ and the inverse transform

$$ \hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum_{n}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu}^{\dagger}\overline{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{k}n\mu a}(\boldsymbol{r}). $$

Our goal is to express the Coulomb interaction in this basis. The key ingredient we need is an expression for the density operator at finite wavevector. Charge density operators are defined as

$$ \hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q}):=\sum_{\mu}\sum_{a}\int_{M}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r})\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}(\boldsymbol{r}). $$

Transforming to the band operators and splitting $\int_{M}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}\in\Lambda}\int_{uc}$ yields

$$ \hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{\alpha\beta}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}\in\Lambda}\int_{uc}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})}\overline{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R})\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}. $$

Using Eq. (31), we translate to the fundamental unit cell (the magnetic twists cancel),

$$ \hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{\alpha\beta}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\int_{uc}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}\in\Lambda}e^{-i(\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q})\cdot\boldsymbol{R}}e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\right)\overline{\phi}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}(\boldsymbol{r})e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\beta}. $$

Using Poisson summation on the lattice sum (parentheses above) gives $N\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}\in\Lambda^{*}}\delta(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{k}-q+\boldsymbol{G})$ . For a fixed $\boldsymbol{k}$ , there is unique non-zero term $N\delta(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}-[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}])$ in this sum where $\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}=[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]+\boldsymbol{G}$ . Eliminating the $\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}$ sum and switching to the Bloch waves gives

$$ \hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}\left(\sum_{\alpha\beta}\int_{uc}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\;\overline{u}_{\boldsymbol{k}\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}e^{i[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}u_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}],\beta}\right)\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]\beta}. $$

As $e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}e^{i[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}=e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}=\hat{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ , the term in parentheses is $\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}|\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})|u_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]}}=\braket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}|u_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}}}=\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ . So, altogether,

$$ \hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]}, $$

where the operators and form factors are vectors and matrices in the band-flavor space respectively.

Coulomb and other density-density interactions are defined as

$$ \hat{V}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu\nu}\sum_{a,b}\int_{M}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\,d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}\;V(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r})\hat{\psi}_{\nu b}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}_{\nu b}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}_{\mu a}(\boldsymbol{r}). $$

The potential can be written as $V(\boldsymbol{r})=\frac{1}{A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in M^{*}}V(\boldsymbol{q})e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}$ , where the sum runs over all of reciprocal space $M^{*}$ . Hence

$$ \hat{V}=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\;V(\boldsymbol{q})\hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})\hat{\rho}(-\boldsymbol{q})-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\;V(\boldsymbol{0})\hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{0}):=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\;V(\boldsymbol{q}):\hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{q})\hat{\rho}(-\boldsymbol{q}):, $$

where the normal ordering is defined relative to the vacuum. The second term $V(\boldsymbol{0})\hat{\rho}(\boldsymbol{0})$ is a chemical potential. Note that Eq. (47) takes the same form in magnetic and non-magnetic systems. Therefore the interaction is entirely specified by the Bloch waves $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ in the first Brillouin zone, together with the operators $\hat{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ .

### A.4 Derivation of Hartree-Fock

This section will derive Hartree-Fock using a partial-trace approach, wherein only some of the bands are integrated out at mean-field level. Standard Hartree-Fock is the case where all bands are integrated out. However, the partial version will prove useful below when integrating out the remote bands of the BM model.

Consider the four-body interaction

$$ \hat{V}:=V:\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\,[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}],\gamma}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}],\delta} $$

where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ run over all species (i.e. bands and flavors). Suppose the species are partitioned into active species $\mathcal{A}$ and remote species $\mathcal{R}$ . Physically, one normally considers the eight flat bands of TBG to be active, and the rest remote. In Step 5 of App. C and the main text, we take the more restrictive perspective of a single active band.

Our goal is to integrate out the remote bands, which is a partial trace

$$ \hat{V}\mapsto\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{V}]. $$

Here $\rho_{\mathcal{R}}$ is a density matrix for the remote bands, not a charge density operator. We treat remote bands at mean-field level such that $\rho_{\mathcal{R}}$ is quadratic, and any quadratic density matrix is fully characterized by its correlation matrix $\tr[\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{R}}\;\hat{c}_{\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\beta}]=(P_{\mathcal{R}})_{\beta\alpha}$ . For convenience, define $\braket{\mathcal{O}}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}~:=~\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\mathcal{O}]$ , which is an operator on the Hilbert space of the active bands. For brevity we drop the subscript $\mathcal{R}$ on $\rho$ when the $P_{\mathcal{R}}$ dependence is made explicit.

Integrating out the remote bands of $\hat{V}$ — an operation that changes the Hilbert space — requires us to evaluate terms of the form

$$ \tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]. $$

There are six cases depending on which fermions are remote [41]: 1. $A,B,C,D\in\mathcal{R}$ , 2. $B,D\in\mathcal{R}$ , 3. $B,C\in\mathcal{R}$ , 4. $A,D\in\mathcal{R}$ , 5. $A,C\in\mathcal{R}$ , 6. All in $\mathcal{A}$ . These may all be evaluated straightforwardly from Wick’s theorem, and the fact that one can pull fermions in $\mathcal{A}$ outside the partial trace, which yields:

- 1. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=\phantom{-}\text{constant}$

- 2. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=-\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{D}}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{C}$

- 3. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=\phantom{-}\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{D}$

- 4. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=\phantom{-}\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{D}}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}$

- 5. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=-\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{C}}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{D}$

- 6. $\tr_{\mathcal{R}}[\hat{\rho}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}]=\phantom{-}\braket{I}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{B}\hat{c}_{C}\hat{c}_{D}$ .

We now restore momentum indices. We will find 3 & 4 combine to give the Hartree Hamiltonian, while 2 & 5 give the Fock term. For term 4, $\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{D}}_{P}=\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}],\delta}}_{P}=[P(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\delta\alpha}\delta(\boldsymbol{k}-[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{q}])$ , so

$$ \hat{V}_{4}=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\,[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}P(\boldsymbol{k})\delta(\boldsymbol{k}-[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{q}])\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}],\gamma} $$

The $\delta$ -function is only satisfied if $\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{G}$ for some $\boldsymbol{G}$ in the reciprocal lattice, so

$$ \hat{V}_{4}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\left[\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V(\boldsymbol{G})[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\beta\gamma}\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}[P(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}\right)\right]\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\gamma}. $$

Due to the periodic gauge, $\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})=\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})^{\dagger}$ , which means $\hat{V}_{4}$ is half the Hartree term (and $\hat{V}_{3}$ is the other half).

Meanwhile, term 5 involves the expectation $\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{A}\hat{c}_{C}}_{P}=\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}],\gamma}}_{P}=[P(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\gamma\alpha}\delta(\boldsymbol{k}-[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}])$ , giving

$$ \hat{V}_{5}=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\,[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}[P(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\gamma\alpha}\delta(\boldsymbol{k}-[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}])\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}],\delta} $$

The $\delta$ -function implies $\boldsymbol{k}=\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}+\boldsymbol{G}$ for some reciprocal lattice vector $\boldsymbol{G}$ , so

$$ \hat{V}_{5}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\left[-\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}[P(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q})]_{\alpha\gamma}[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q})]_{\alpha\delta}\right]\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\delta} $$

Using the relation $\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q})=\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})^{\dagger}$ , we recognize this as half the Fock contribution.

Combining all these, we have

$$ \displaystyle\tr[\hat{\rho}[P]\hat{V}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i}\hat{V}_{i}=\hat{H}_{H}[P]+\hat{H}_{F}[P]+\hat{V}_{\mathcal{A}}+\text{ const} \displaystyle\hat{H}_{H}[P] \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\left[\frac{1}{A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V(\boldsymbol{G})\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})\Tr[P^{T}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}^{\dagger}]\right]\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle\hat{H}_{F}[P] \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\left[-\frac{1}{A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})P(\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q})^{T}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})^{\dagger}]\right]\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle\hat{V}_{\mathcal{A}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\,[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}],\gamma}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}],\delta} $$

Here and below we use a convenient matrix notation for the form factors and correlation matrices (which runs over all bands of both $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ ), $\Tr$ gives the trace over both $\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}$ and all bands, and the fermions $\hat{c}^{\dagger},\hat{c}$ run over active bands $\mathcal{A}$ . Note that the last term is the restriction of $\hat{V}$ to the active bands.

If $\mathcal{R}$ runs over all bands, then $\hat{H}_{HF}$ is a quadratic operator on all the bands, and $E_{HF}=\Tr\big[\hat{\rho}[P]\hat{H}_{HF}[P]\big]$ is simply a number. In this case, one can use this as a procedure for finding the “best quadratic representation” of an operator with respect to a given correlation matrix:

$$ \hat{V}\to\hat{V}\big|_{MF,P}:=\hat{H}_{HF}[P]. $$

This formula is used below to implement the Hartree-Fock subtraction procedure to account for the background charge density of remote bands in TBG.

This Appendix has now defined all the notation and Hamiltonian-independent formalism we shall use to consider the problem TBG at finite field. We again highlight that the only model-specific information needed are the single particle energies and wavefunctions within the first Brillouin zone, and the matrix elements from Eq. (36).

## Appendix B TBG in Magnetic Field

In this section we review the construction of a model for MATBG at finite field and derive the form of Hartree-Fock interactions at finite field.

This Appendix will construct a model for TBG at finite field. We start by recalling the BM model, then discuss its modifications from a magnetic field and compute the needed matrix elements. We then describe how the remote bands should be integrated out and the details of a “Hartree-Fock subtraction” procedure employed to prevent double-counting various interaction effects. We conclude by discussing the Hamiltonian for the spin- and valley-polarized $\nu=3$ state, and the proper way to split it into a dispersion and interaction.

### B.1 BM Model

To start, let us review the standard Bistritzer-MacDonald model. The moiré unit cell and Brillouin zone are spanned by primitive and reciprocal lattice vectors

$$ \boldsymbol{a}_{1,2}=\frac{4\pi}{3k_{\theta}}(\pm\sqrt{3}/2,1/2);\quad\boldsymbol{b}_{1,2}=k_{\theta}(\pm\sqrt{3}/2,3/2) $$

so $\boldsymbol{a}_{i}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}_{j}=2\pi\delta_{ij}$ . Here $k_{\theta}=\frac{8\pi}{3\sqrt{3}a}\sin\theta/2$ , where $\theta$ is the twist angle and $a\approx$1.36\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolAngstrom}$$ is the carbon-carbon bond length of graphene. Let $A_{0}$ the unit cell area.

The BM model is defined as a real-space continuum model with four species: two layers and two sublattices, labeled by Pauli matrices $\gamma^{\mu}$ and $\sigma^{\mu}$ respectively. The Hamiltonian in the $K$ valley consists of two Dirac ones, one for each layer, and an interlayer tunneling term

$$ H^{K}_{BM}(\boldsymbol{r})=\begin{pmatrix}h^{+}&T(\boldsymbol{r})\\
T(\boldsymbol{r})^{\dagger}&h^{-}\end{pmatrix},\quad h^{\pm}=-i\hbar v_{F}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\pm\theta/2}\cdot\left[\boldsymbol{\nabla}\mp\frac{i}{2}\boldsymbol{q}_{1}\right],\quad T(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum_{s=0}^{2}T_{s}e^{-i\boldsymbol{b}_{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}},\quad T_{s}=\begin{pmatrix}w_{0}&\zeta^{s}w_{1}\\
\zeta^{-s}w_{1}&w_{0}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta/2}=e^{-i\theta\sigma_{z}/4}\boldsymbol{\sigma}e^{i\theta\sigma_{z}/4}$ , $\zeta=e^{i2\pi/3}$ , $\boldsymbol{b}_{0}=0$ , $\boldsymbol{q}_{1}=k_{\theta}(0,-1)$ is the offset of the Dirac point, and $v_{F}$ is the Fermi velocity of graphene. The moire Brillouin zone (mBZ) is shown in Fig. 9.

The other valley may be obtained under time-reversal symmetry, and we express it here for convenience. For simplicity, let us make the approximation $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\theta/2}\approx\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ , which has the effect of making the model particle-hole symmetric. Let $\tau\in\left\{K,K^{\prime}\right\}$ index the valley. Then

$$ H_{BM}(\boldsymbol{r})=\begin{pmatrix}h_{t}&T(\boldsymbol{r})\\
T(\boldsymbol{r})^{\dagger}&h_{b}\end{pmatrix},\quad h(\boldsymbol{r})=-v_{F}[\tau_{z}\sigma_{x}p_{x}+\sigma_{y}p_{y}]-v_{F}[\tau_{z}\sigma_{x}K_{x}-\tau_{z}\gamma_{z}\sigma_{y}K_{y}], $$

where $p_{\alpha}=-i\partial_{\alpha}$ and $K_{\alpha}$ are the coordinates of $K^{t}=R(\theta/2)K_{\text{graphene}}$ . The tunneling term is unchanged.

We take a computational basis of Fourier series in the real-space unit cell

$$ \braket{\boldsymbol{r}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}}=v_{\boldsymbol{k},\gamma,\sigma,\tau,\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{r})=A_{0}^{-1/2}e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\gamma,\sigma,\tau} $$

where $\boldsymbol{G}$ runs over reciprocal lattice vectors and $I=(\gamma,\sigma,\tau,\boldsymbol{G})$ is a multi-index. The matrix elements from Eq. (36) are then relatively simple:

$$ [\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{G^{\prime\prime}}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\gamma\sigma\boldsymbol{G}}^{\gamma^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}\boldsymbol{G}^{\prime}}=[\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{G^{\prime\prime}}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\gamma\sigma\boldsymbol{G}}^{\gamma^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}\boldsymbol{G}^{\prime}}=\delta_{\gamma^{\prime}\gamma}\delta_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{G}-\boldsymbol{G}^{\prime\prime},\boldsymbol{G}^{\prime}},\quad[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I}_{J}=\delta^{I}_{J}. $$

In particular, the form factor in the computational basis, $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ , is trivial. This will not be the case at finite field.

### B.2 Magnetic BM Model

At finite field we adopt a rectangular magnetic Brillouin with sides lengths $Q_{x}=(\sqrt{3}/2)k_{\theta}$ and $Q_{y}/q=(3/2)k_{\theta}/q$ , shown in Fig. 9. As $2Q_{x}Q_{y}=A_{\rm{mBZ}}=(2\pi)^{2}/A_{\rm{UC}}$ is the area of the moiré Brillouin zone in terms of the area of the moiré unit cell $A_{\rm UC}$ , the commensurability condition is

$$ \phi:=\frac{BA_{\rm{UC}}}{\Phi_{0}}=\frac{p}{2q}\text{ or }Q_{x}Q_{y}\ell^{2}=2\pi\frac{q}{p} $$

where $\Phi_{0}=h/e$ , $\ell=(\hbar/eB)^{1/2}$ . In real space the magnetic unit cell is twice as wide and $q$ times as tall as the moiré unit cell.

We adopt Landau gauge $\boldsymbol{A}=(-By,0)$ so that $\boldsymbol{\pi}=\boldsymbol{p}+e\boldsymbol{A}=(p_{x}-eBy,p_{y})$ where $p_{\alpha}=-i\hbar\partial_{\alpha}$ as usual. Solving for the twists $\xi_{\boldsymbol{R}}(\boldsymbol{r})$ gives boundary conditions

$$ \displaystyle u(x+a_{x},y)=u(x,y) \displaystyle a_{x} \displaystyle=2\pi/Q_{x} \displaystyle u(x,y+a_{y})=e^{ixa_{y}\ell^{2}}u(x,y) \displaystyle a_{y} \displaystyle=2\pi/(Q_{y}/q). $$

For numerical convenience, we now adopt a basis of offset superpositions of Landau levels so that (i) the kinetic term is simple (2) the tunnelling terms are easily computable and (3) the boundary condition Eq. (64) are manifestly satisfied. To this end, we work with eigenstates of the free magnetic Hamiltonian $H_{f}(B)=\pi^{2}/(2m)$ . Define Landau level operators

$$ \hat{a}^{\pm}:=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}\hbar}(\hat{\pi}_{x}\pm i\hat{\pi}_{y}) $$

and select a guiding center coordinate $\hat{Y}:=\hat{y}+\frac{\ell^{2}}{\hbar}\hat{\pi}_{x}=\frac{\ell^{2}}{\hbar}\hat{p}_{x}$ where $[\hat{a}^{\pm},\hat{Y}]=0$ . The eigenstates of $\hat{Y}$ are plane waves $e^{ik_{x}x}$ and, in the position basis, the raising and lowering operators act along $y$

$$ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\hbar\ell}\hat{a}=-\partial_{y}-[y-Y]/\ell^{2} $$

for each $Y$ . The wavefunctions of the free magnetic Hamiltonian are therefore planewaves along $x$ and harmonic oscillators along $y$ :

$$ \displaystyle\braket{x,y|n,Y}=\ell^{-1/2}e^{iYx}\phi_{n}([y-Y]/\ell),\quad\phi_{n}(y)=(2^{n}n!\sqrt{\pi})^{-1/2}H_{n}(y)e^{-y^{2}/2}, $$

where $H_{n}$ are the Hermite polynomials and $n$ is the Landau level index. Whenever possible we will switch to dimensionless quantities $\tilde{y}=[y-Y]/\ell$ , $\tilde{p}_{y}=-i\partial_{\tilde{y}}$ , and $\tilde{a}=-2^{-1/2}[\tilde{y}+i\tilde{p}_{y}]$ .

We define our computational basis in terms of these as a discrete Fourier transform in $Y$ in steps of $Q_{x}\ell^{2}$ . Let $\gamma$ and $\sigma$ label layer and sublattice. Then define

$$ \displaystyle Y_{M,j,k_{x}} \displaystyle:=k_{x}\ell^{2}+(Mp+j)Q_{x}\ell^{2},\qquad M\in\mathbb{Z},j\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, \displaystyle\ket{\gamma,\sigma,n,j,k_{x},k_{y}} \displaystyle:=a_{x}^{-1/2}\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{ik_{y}(Mp+j)Q_{x}\ell^{2}}\ket{\gamma,\sigma}\otimes\ket{n,Y_{M,j,k_{x}}}, \displaystyle v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}(\boldsymbol{r})=v_{\boldsymbol{k},\gamma,\sigma,n,j} \displaystyle:=\braket{\boldsymbol{r}|e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}|\gamma,\sigma,n,j,\boldsymbol{k}}=(a_{x}\ell)^{-1/2}\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-ik_{y}[y-(Mp+j)Q_{x}\ell^{2}]}e^{ix(Mp+j)Q_{x}}\phi_{n}([y-Y_{M,j,k_{x}}]/\ell), $$

where $I=(\gamma,\sigma,n,j)$ is a multi-index. The $v$ ’s are the Bloch waves of the free electron in a magnetic field. They obey boundary conditions (64) with standard normalization $\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}J}}=\int_{uc}d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\,\overline{v}_{\boldsymbol{k}I}(\boldsymbol{r})v_{\boldsymbol{k}J}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{IJ}$ over the magnetic unit cell. We consider the eigenproblem in this computational basis with a UV cutoff of a few hundred Landau levels.

As discussed in the main text, three types of matrix elements suffice to describe the Hamiltonian and all other quantities of interest to us. We merely quote their formulas here, and delay their derivation to Sec. B.3 below. Let $\boldsymbol{G}=r\boldsymbol{G}_{x}+s\boldsymbol{G}_{y}=(rQ_{x},sQ_{y}/q)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I}:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I^{\prime}}|e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}I}} \displaystyle=\left[e^{ir\frac{k_{y}}{G_{2}}2\pi/p}e^{-i\frac{k_{x}}{G_{1}}s2\pi q/p}\right]e^{-i(sj-rs/2)2\pi q/p} \displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\times\delta_{\gamma^{\prime}\gamma}\delta_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-r}D_{n^{\prime}n}(\overline{z}_{\boldsymbol{G}}),\quad(\text{assuming }q|s) \displaystyle[\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I}:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I^{\prime}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q},I}} \displaystyle=\left[e^{-i\frac{k_{x}}{G_{1}}\frac{q_{y}}{G_{2}}2\pi/p}\right]\times e^{-i\frac{q_{x}}{G_{1}}\frac{q_{y}}{G_{2}}2\pi/p}\delta_{\gamma^{\prime}\gamma}\delta_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}\delta_{j^{\prime}j}D_{n^{\prime}n}(\overline{z}_{\boldsymbol{q}}), \displaystyle[\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{I^{\prime}}_{I}:=\braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G},I^{\prime}}|e^{-i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}|v_{\boldsymbol{k},I}} \displaystyle=\left[e^{ir\frac{k_{y}}{G_{2}}2\pi/p}\right]\times e^{-isj^{\prime}2\pi/p}\delta_{\gamma^{\prime}\gamma}\delta_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-r}\delta_{n^{\prime}n}, $$

where $\overline{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}:=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}(k_{x}-ik_{y})$ is a complexified momentum, $G_{1}=Q_{x}$ and $G_{2}=Q_{y}/q$ are the dimensions of the magnetic Brillouin zone, and

$$ \hat{D}(z):=e^{za^{\dagger}-z^{*}a} $$

is the standard displacement operator for the harmonic oscillator, whose matrix elements may be expressed in terms of the associated Laguerre polynomials $L_{n}^{\alpha}(x)$ as

$$ D_{mn}(z)=\braket{m|e^{za^{\dagger}-z^{*}a}|n}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{\frac{n!}{m!}}(z)^{m-n}L_{n}^{m-n}(\left|z\right|^{2})e^{-\left|z\right|^{2}/2}&\text{ if }m\geq n\\
\sqrt{\frac{m!}{n!}}(-z^{*})^{n-m}L_{m}^{n-m}(\left|z\right|^{2})e^{-\left|z\right|^{2}/2}&\text{ if }m<n.\end{cases} $$

We now resolve the Hamiltonian in this basis. The kinetic energy for the $K$ valley can be written in terms of the Landau level lowering operator as

$$ (\hat{h}_{0})^{K}_{\pm}=v_{F}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\pm\theta/2}\cdot\left[\hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\mp\frac{\hbar}{2}\boldsymbol{q}_{0}\right]=\hbar v_{F}\sigma^{+}e^{\pm i\theta/2}\left[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\ell}\hat{a}\mp\frac{ik_{\theta}}{2}\right]+\text{ h.c.} $$

where the second equality follows from (66). For both valley, this takes the form

$$ \hat{h}_{0}=-\frac{v_{f}\sqrt{2}\hbar}{\ell}\left\{[\hat{a}\sigma^{+}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}\sigma^{-}]\gamma^{z}\frac{\tau_{0}+\tau_{z}}{2}+[-\hat{a}^{\dagger}\sigma^{+}-\hat{a}\sigma^{-}]\gamma^{z}\frac{\tau_{0}-\tau_{z}}{2}\right\} $$

where the matrices are in sublattice space and the combinations of $\tau$ ’s give projectors to the $K$ and $K^{\prime}$ valleys respectively. The tunneling matrix elements take the form

$$ \braket{v_{\boldsymbol{k}I^{\prime}}|T(\boldsymbol{r})|v_{\boldsymbol{k}J}}=\sum_{i=0}^{2}(\gamma^{+})^{\gamma^{\prime}}_{\gamma^{\prime\prime}}(T_{i})^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}[\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{b}_{i}}(\boldsymbol{k})]^{\gamma^{\prime\prime}\sigma^{\prime\prime}j^{\prime}n^{\prime}}_{\gamma\sigma jn}+h.c. $$

where the reciprocal translations are $\boldsymbol{b}_{0,1,2}=r\boldsymbol{G}_{x}+s\boldsymbol{G}_{y}$ with $(r,s)=(0,0),(1,q),(-1,q)$ in terms of the magnetic lattice.

### B.3 Magnetic Matrix Elements

This technical section derives the magnetic matrix elements in Eq. (71). Let $\boldsymbol{G}=(G_{x},G_{y})=(rQ_{x},sQ_{y}/q)$ and $\boldsymbol{q}=(q_{x},q_{y})$ . For concision, let $\Delta=Q_{x}\ell^{2}$ . We will often use the fact that $Q_{x}Q_{y}\ell^{2}=2\pi q/p$ or $G_{1}G_{2}\ell^{2}=2\pi/p$ . We also recall a fact about the Harmonic oscillator matrix eigenstates $\phi_{n}(y)$

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}dy\,\varphi_{n^{\prime}}(y)e^{-iq_{y}y}e^{-iq_{x}\ell p_{y}}\varphi_{n}(y)=e^{-iq_{x}q_{y}\ell^{2}/2}D_{n^{\prime}n}(\overline{z}_{q});\quad\overline{z}_{q}:=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}(q_{x}-iq_{y}), $$

which follows from Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff and the definition of the displacement operator.

Form factors of the basis vectors

## Appendix C Hartree-Fock Subtraction

This Appendix defines the Hamiltonian and — crucially — the bandwidth of the $\nu=3$ state of TBG we consider as a parent state for fractional Chern insulators. In the presence of interactions, the bandwidth is not uniquely defined, as there are many ways to group terms between the dispersion and interaction. Four common options, suitable for different purposes, are

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{A} \displaystyle=\hat{h}_{A}+V\;\rho\rho \displaystyle=\hat{H}_{B} \displaystyle=\hat{h}_{B}+V:\rho\rho: \displaystyle=\hat{H}_{C} \displaystyle=\hat{h}_{C}+V\;\delta\rho\delta\rho \displaystyle=\hat{H}_{D} \displaystyle=\hat{h}_{D}+V:\delta\rho\delta\rho: $$

where $:\hat{\mathcal{O}}:$ denotes normal ordering and $\widehat{\delta\rho}=\hat{\rho}-\braket{\hat{\rho}}$ is the charge density with respect to a reference state. We note that option D has the form employed by psuedopotential arguments. Physically, $\hat{h}_{D}$ gives the exact 1-electron excitation spectrum above the normal-ordering reference state— in our case, the $\nu=3$ spin- and valley-polarized state. This assumes the restriction to the space of active bands alone. Therefore splitting D is the physically relevant choice for studying FCIs and their indicators. The total dispersion used in the main text is defined as $\hat{h}_{T}:=\hat{h}_{D}$ .

In Steps 1-4 below we consider eight active bands, as is standard in TBG. We restrict only in Step 5 to a single active band.

We now proceed to construct $\hat{H}_{D}$ for the $\nu=3$ state of TBG using the so-called ‘Hartree-Fock subtraction’ procedure to account for the effect of the remote bands at mean-field level. Our main tool is the partial trace with respect to a quadratic density matrix. Suppose we have a Hamiltonian $V:\rho\rho:$ defined for many species of fermions, and suppose the species are partitioned into active species $\mathcal{A}$ and remote species $\mathcal{R}$ . Suppose $P_{\mathcal{R}}(k)=\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hat{c}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ is a quadratic density matrix for the remote bands.

We may then integrate out the remote bands at mean-field level via a partial trace. The result, derived in Eq. (55a) below, is

$$ \braket{V:\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:}_{P_{\mathcal{R}}}=\hat{H}_{H}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]+\hat{H}_{F}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]+V:\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}:+\,\text{constant} $$

where $\hat{H}_{H}[P]$ and $\hat{H}_{F}[P]$ are the Hartree and Fock contributions respectively, and the last term is the residual interaction for any species that have not been traced out. We use this repeatedly below.

We provide a detailed construction, following [43, 41, 122]. We first derive the standard Hamiltonian for the active bands of TBG in Steps 1-4, then specialize to the case of $\nu=3$ .

- 1. Microscopic Definition We take the total Hamiltonian to be

$$ \hat{H}:=\hat{h}_{B}+V:\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:=\hat{h}_{B}+\frac{1}{2A_{s}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{BZ}}V(\boldsymbol{q})\,[\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k})]_{\alpha\delta}[\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime})]_{\beta\gamma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},\beta}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{q}],\gamma}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}],\delta} $$

(96) where the first equality defines an abbreviated notation for concision, $A_{s}$ is the sample area, and $[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{G}$ lies in the first Brillouin zone. The quadratic term $\hat{h}_{T}$ is the total dispersion of bilayer graphene, and the Fermions $\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}$ are vectors running over all bands (not just the flat bands) and all species.

- 2. Reference Density The dispersion $\hat{h}_{B}$ is unknown. Why? Consider the simpler situation of graphene. The standard tight-binding model $H=\sum t\hat{c}^{\dagger}\hat{c}$ is defined in terms of single hopping parameter $t\approx$2.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ . However, this is not the bare electron hopping $t_{B}$ , but rather a renormalized hopping that gives the best one parameter tight-binding model in the presence of electron-electron interactions. Schematically, $\sum t_{B}\hat{c}^{\dagger}\hat{c}~+~\hat{V}\big|_{MF}=\sum t\hat{c}^{\dagger}\hat{c}$ . For twisted bilayer graphene, the same logic should apply. Let us assume that a Bistritzer-MacDonald model is the best quadratic model of TBG. We then have

$$ \hat{H}_{BM}=\hat{h}_{0}+\hat{V}\big|_{MF,P_{0}} $$

(97) where $\hat{V}\big|_{MF,P_{0}}$ , defined in Eq. (56), is the interaction at mean-field level with respect to a “reference” density matrix $P_{0}$ at charge neutrality. The reference density matrix is non-unique, and three common choices in the literature are: (a) Decoupled subtraction: take $P_{0}$ to be the density matrix of two layers of twisted graphene without tunneling between them at charge neutrality and without an hBN mass. (b) BM Subtraction: take $P_{0}$ to be the density matrix of the BM model at charge neutrality without an hBN mass. (c) Infinite-temperature subtraction: take $P_{\mathcal{A}}=\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}$ for the active bands, then remote bands filled at negative energy. We will see below that this choice implies $\hat{h}_{C}=\hat{H}_{BM}$ . This choice is physical, and effects the final Hamiltonian at the level of a few $\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ . With whatever choice we make for the reference density matrix, we may solve for the dispersion as

$$ \hat{h}_{B}=\hat{H}_{BM}-\left[\hat{V}:\rho\rho:\right]_{MF,P_{0}}=\hat{H}_{BM}-\hat{H}_{HF}[P_{0}] $$

(98) where we have used Eq. (95) and (56). One should think of this as a renormalization procedure: we seek a dispersion so that, after adding interactions, integrating out high energy modes, and reducing to mean-field level, we match IR observations from DFT and/or experiments.99 9 See [64] for a careful treatment from a similar perspective. Under this philosophy, the reference density aims to reduce double-counting related to the high-energy physics and should not be sensitive to the details of the reference state at low energy. In practice, however, the dispersion is extremely sensitive to the IR details of the reference state within the flat bands. For instance, choosing a reference density without $C_{2}$ symmetry in the flat bands can cancel out the Fock contribution in some situations. To evade these subtleties insofar as possible, we pick the simplest possible density matrix at half-filling: $P_{0}=I_{\mathcal{A}}/2$ , option (c). Ideally, one would like to select $P_{0}$ so as to reproduce a set of experimental observations.

- 3. Integrate out Remote Bands Next we integrate out the remote bands at mean-field level. Let

$$ [P_{\mathcal{R}}]_{\alpha\beta}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\begin{cases}1&\text{ $n$ remote and below charge neutrality}\\ 0&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases} $$

(99) be a density matrix for the occupied remote bands. Using Eq. (95), we have

$$ \tr_{\mathcal{R}}\left[\rho[P_{\mathcal{R}}]\left(\hat{h}_{B}+V:\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:\right)\right]=\left.\hat{h}_{B}\right|_{\mathcal{A}}+\hat{H}_{H}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]+\hat{H}_{F}[P_{\mathcal{R}}]+V:\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}:+\,\text{constant} $$

(100) where $\big|_{\mathcal{A}}$ is the restriction to the active bands. Using the linearity of Hartree-Fock, we have

$$ \hat{H}\big|_{\mathcal{A}}=\hat{h}_{B}\big|_{\mathcal{A}}+V:\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}}:,\quad\hat{h}_{B}\big|_{\mathcal{A}}:=\hat{H}_{BM}\big|_{\mathcal{A}}+\hat{H}_{HF}[P_{\mathcal{R}}-P_{0}]. $$

(101) We now restrict ourselves to the Hilbert space of the active bands. In a slight abuse of notation, we drop all $\big|_{\mathcal{A}}$ ’s. Note, however, that the quadratic density matrices are still defined over all bands. For practical numerics, one usually keeps $M\approx 3-5$ bands below and above the active bands in $P_{\mathcal{R}}$ and $P_{0}$ .1010 10 Depending on the form of $P_{0}$ , $\hat{h}_{B}$ may contain a logarithmic divergence with $M$ , which is non-physical. We have now arrived at the form $\hat{H}_{B}$ of the Hamiltonian.

- 4. Regroup to ‘Standard Form’ We now transform between the various forms of the Hamiltonian to arrive at the standard form for analytics, $\hat{H}_{C}$ . First, we remove the normal ordering. By Fermion anticommutation, $\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\gamma}\hat{c}_{\delta}\hat{c}_{\beta}=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\hat{c}_{\beta}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\gamma}\hat{c}_{\delta}+\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\hat{c}_{\delta}\delta_{\gamma\beta}$ , so

$$ :\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:=[\Lambda]_{\alpha\beta}[\Lambda]_{\gamma\delta}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\gamma}\hat{c}_{\delta}\hat{c}_{\beta}=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}[\Lambda]_{\alpha\beta}\hat{c}_{\beta}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\gamma}[\Lambda]_{\gamma\delta}\hat{c}_{\delta}-\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\left([\Lambda]_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\beta\gamma}[\Lambda]_{\gamma\delta}\right)\hat{c}_{\delta}=\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}+\hat{H}_{F}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}] $$

(102) where we have used the definition of the Fock Hamiltonian (55c). Therefore

$$ \hat{H}_{B}=\hat{h}_{B}+V:\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}:=\hat{h}_{B}+\hat{H}_{F}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]+V\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}=\hat{h}_{A}+V\hat{\rho}\hat{\rho}=\hat{H}_{A}\implies\hat{h}_{A}=\hat{h}_{B}+\hat{H}_{F}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]. $$

(103) Until now, we have worked with $\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ , which measures the electron density relative to the vacuum (i.e. $\nu=-4$ after integrating out the remote bands). This is unwieldy in the current context, where most of the density comes from completely filled bands which provide only a background charge density. To rectify this, we switch to measuring charge density relative to a reference state, characterized by a third density matrix $P_{C}$ . We then define the relative charge density by

$$ \widehat{\delta\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}:=\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}-\braket{\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}}_{P_{C}}. $$

(104) Rewriting the interaction with respect to $\widehat{\delta\rho}$ amounts to a quadratic shift:

$$ V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\widehat{\delta\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\widehat{\delta\rho}_{-\boldsymbol{q}}=V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{\rho}_{-\boldsymbol{q}}-V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left(\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\braket{\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}}+\braket{\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}\right)+V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\braket{\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}}\braket{\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}}. $$

(105) The expectation value may be written in terms of the form factor as

$$ \braket{\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}}_{P_{C}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\braket{\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{q}]}}_{P_{c}}=\delta(\boldsymbol{k}-[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}])\Tr[P_{c}\Lambda_{-\boldsymbol{q}}]=\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{G}}\Tr[P_{C}\Lambda_{G}^{\dagger}] $$

(106) where the sum is over the reciprocal lattice and comes from the fact that $P_{C}$ is defined only on the Brillouin zone and is $\boldsymbol{k}$ -diagonal. Hence

$$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left(\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}\braket{\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}}+\braket{\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rho_{-\boldsymbol{q}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{BZ}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\left(\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{G}}\Tr[P_{C}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}^{\dagger}]\right)\hat{c}_{[\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{q}]}+(\boldsymbol{q}\leftrightarrow-\boldsymbol{q})=\hat{H}_{H}[P_{C}]. $$

(107) Most commonly, one takes $P_{C}$ as the density matrix of the BM model at half filling. Writing $P_{C}=\tfrac{1}{2}[I_{\mathcal{A}}+Q]$ one can show [43] that the symmetries $U(2)\times U(2)$ , $\mathcal{C}_{2}\mathcal{T}$ , and particle-hole symmetry together imply that $\Tr[Q\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}]=0$ , so that $\hat{H}_{H}[P_{C}]=\hat{H}_{H}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]$ . Therefore $V\widehat{\delta\rho}\widehat{\delta\rho}+\hat{H}_{H}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]=V\rho\rho$ . Altogether, we have

$$ \hat{H}=\hat{h}_{C}+V\widehat{\delta\rho}\widehat{\delta\rho};\quad\hat{h}_{C}=\hat{h}_{A}+\hat{H}_{H}[\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]=\hat{H}_{BM}+\hat{H}_{HF}[P_{\mathcal{R}}-P_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathcal{A}}]. $$

(108) One can immediately see why the choice of $P_{0}$ in the “infinite temperature” subtraction scheme gives $\hat{h}_{C}=\hat{H}_{BM}$ .

- 5. The Top Band We now consider the case of $\nu=3$ where a single spin- and valley-polarized band is unoccupied. We can partition the active bands as $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\cup\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ , where $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ is the “top” unoccupied band. Our goal is to express the Hamiltonian in this band after integrating out the other bands at mean-field level. The most straightforward method is to consider the $\mathcal{B}$ bands as (occupied) remote bands: $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}=\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{B}$ . As we do not use any properties of the active bands themselves, the same logic that led to Eq. (101) now gives

$$ \hat{H}^{(\nu=3)}=\hat{h}_{B}^{(\nu=3)}+V:\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}:,\quad\hat{h}_{B}^{(\nu=3)}=\hat{H}_{BM}^{(\nu=3)}+\hat{H}_{HF}[P_{\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{B}}-P_{0}]. $$

(109) Note that this is normal-ordered with respect to the $\nu=3$ state (which is also the vacuum, after reducing the Hilbert space) where $7$ out of the $8$ active bands are filled. Furthermore, since we have dropped constant terms from the partial trace, $\rho$ is measuring deviations in density from the same state. That is, $\rho_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}=\delta\rho^{(\nu=3)}$ . Therefore we have $h_{B}^{(\nu=3)}=h_{D}^{(\nu=3)}$ , which is the form we sought. Using properties of the active bands allows us to simplify further. In the infinite-temperature subtraction scheme

$$ P^{\nu=3}=P_{\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{B}}-P_{0}=\operatorname{diag}\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2&1/2&1/2;&1/2&1/2&1/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}, $$

(110) where the semicolon separates the active bands below and above the CNP. In the case of hBN-alignment, all four bands above the CNP have different spin/valley quantum numbers. Since the form-factors are flavor-diagonal, the Fock contribution to the 8th band come only from the 4th and 8th band, giving $\hat{h}_{F}$ . Furthermore, with particle-hole symmetry, the Hartree contribution is only weakly band- and valley-dependent, so the contributions from all bands are essentially the same. If we let $\hat{h}_{H}$ be the Hartree potential of a single band, then we have $H_{H}[P^{(\nu=3)}]\approx\frac{7-1}{2}H_{H}=\nu H_{H}$ . Altogther,

$$ \hat{h}_{D}^{(\nu)}=\hat{H}_{BM}^{(\nu)}+\hat{H}_{HF}[P^{(\nu)}]\approx\hat{H}_{BM}^{(\nu)}+\nu\hat{h}_{H}+\hat{h}_{F}, $$

(111) where the approximation is good at zero field. In fact, if we fill $\nu\in\left\{0,1,2,3\right\}$ spin- and valley-polarized bands above the CNP, then $\hat{h}_{D}^{(\nu)}$ is the Hamiltonian for the next polarized band. This concludes our detailed construction of the Hamiltonian Eq. (1) used in the main text.

## Appendix D Numerical Details of DMRG Calculations

This Appendix gives additional numerical details on the DMRG simulations employed. We follow the methods developed in [65, 50, 45] and perform DMRG calculations using the open-source TeNPy library [123], developed by one of us.

To apply DMRG to the 2d problem of TBG, we employ an infinite cylinder geometry with real-space along the cylinder and $L_{y}$ discrete $k_{y}$ momenta around the cylinder. We take $L_{y}=8$ cuts through the Brillouin zone at $k_{y}=-\pi+2\pi n/L_{y}$ and Fourier transform along $x$ to produce maximally localized Wannier-Qi states[70]. Explicitly, we define creation operators for the Wannier orbital in the $n$ th unit cell along the $x$ direction

$$ \hat{d}^{\dagger}_{n,k_{y}}:=\int\frac{dk_{x}}{\sqrt{Q_{x}}}e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}_{n}}e^{i\theta(k_{x})}\hat{c}_{k_{x},k_{y}} $$

where $\boldsymbol{R}_{n}=n\boldsymbol{a}_{1}$ and $\theta(k_{x})$ is chosen to give maximally localized 1d Wannier orbitals along the cylinder. We may then project the Hamiltonian Eq. (1) into these degrees of freedom, whereupon it becomes a quasi-1D model with long-range interactions. To perform DMRG, this Hamiltonian must be encoded as an matrix product operator (MPO). A naive encoding of the Hamiltonian results in an MPO with bond dimension $\chi_{\text{MPO}}\sim 10^{6}$ ; typical DMRG problems have Hamiltonians with $\chi_{\text{MPO}}\sim 10^{1}$ . Ref. [50] developed a method, which we apply here, to compress the MPO down to $\chi_{\text{MPO}}\approx 500$ , while retaining an accuracy of $10^{-3}$ $\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ .

We then perform DMRG over a range of $\lambda$ and $\kappa$ values at bond dimension $\chi=256$ , shown in Fig. 10 and in the main text. (Recall that $\lambda$ directly scales the dispersion.) As there are only $8$ sites per unit cell, and the FCI phase is well-described by a small bond dimension, this is sufficient to capture the essential physics. Each of the observables shown in Fig. 10 separately suggests a phase transition out of the FCI phase found at smaller $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ . In particular, the translation order parameter along the $\boldsymbol{a}_{1}$ direction is large both at large $\kappa$ and at large $\lambda$ , suggesting that the competing phase breaks translation symmetry strongly. Near $(\kappa,\lambda)=(3/4,1)$ , i.e. in the upper-right hand corner, DMRG converges to ‘cat’ states, whose transfer matrix has a largest eigenvalue with an 8-fold degeneracy. (Dan) Note $L_{y}=8$ . This suggests the ground state may break translation symmetry, but in a direction that is not along the cylinder and hence cannot be captured in this geometry. Fig. 10c shows that the 1-electron correlation length is large and growing with $\chi$ in this region, which suggests the possibility of a subdominant metallic character to the state. (if there is a Fermi surface, then it diverges with $\chi$ .) A Hartree-Fock calculation suggests that a gapped state which breaks translation symmetry along $\boldsymbol{a}_{1}$ is lower energy than a metallic state at this filling, but this may not be the true ground state.

To ensure these observations are not artifacts of low bond dimension, we have performed higher bond dimension calculations, and show four special points in Fig. 11. The entanglement spectrum in panels abcd clearly shows a different character inside and outside of the FCI phase. As remarked in the main text, the FCI phase (Laughlin state) is easily distinguished by a chiral entanglement spectrum whose low-lying states have counts of the corresponding chiral CFT partition function. Though we have chosen a point deep in the FCI phase, the entanglement spectrum pattern is also clear even near the boundary. We note that even an ideal Laughlin state on a cylinder has a small amount of translation breaking, and relatively large translation-breaking can coexist with the FCI phase. This makes it difficult to identify the precise phase boundary and the nature of any phase transition out of the FCI phase; we see no clear signs of a continuous transition. Panels efg) of Fig. 11 show how various quantities scale with the MPS bond dimension. It is clear that the FCI is well-converged by $\chi=256$ or $\chi=512$ , and has a low translation-breaking, entanglement entropy, and 1-electron correlation length. For the other points, $\langle O_{T}\rangle$ decreases with $\chi$ but asymptotes to a finite value. As remarked above, $\xi_{1e}$ may diverge with $\chi$ for the points as $\kappa=3/4$ , but it is difficult to determine this precisely as most of the state’s “entanglement budget” is used to make cat states.

Despite these subtleties, we may draw two conclusions. First, the extent of the FCI phase may be clearly determined by the entanglement spectra and, less certainly, from the quantities shown in Fig. 10. Second, although the precise nature of the competing phase (or phases) is elusive, they exhibit large translation-breaking and thus have CDW order. We note that the same analysis was performed on the $(\theta,\kappa)$ plane, with similar conclusions that were summarized in Fig. 8 of the main text.

## Appendix E Constant Berry curvature and the GMP algebra

In this section we show that if $\sigma[\mathcal{F}]=T[\eta]=0$ , i.e. if the Berry curvature is uniform and the trace condition holds

$$ \mathcal{F}=2\pi C\,\textrm{Id}_{N}\quad\&\quad\Tr[\tr g]=\Tr[\mathcal{F}], $$

then the (multiband) projected density operators satisfy the GMP algebra [124]. This was first proven in Ref. 9, and elegantly reformulated and applied by Ref. 21. Our proof is a direct generalization of the latter work. For concreteness, we take $\zeta=+1$ and accordingly $\mathcal{F}_{0}>0$ (the $\zeta=-1$ case is identical mutatis mutandis). Along the way we show that $T[\eta]=\Tr[\tr g]-\Tr[\mathcal{F}]\geq 0$ .

Consider $N$ bands (separated by a gap), and define the single particle projector

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\psi}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\sum_{a=1}^{N}\ket{\psi^{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\bra{\psi^{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}. $$

Note that this is different from the band projector $P(\boldsymbol{k})=1-Q(\boldsymbol{k})=\sum_{a}\ket{u^{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\bra{u^{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ used in the definitions of the band geometry. This distinction is necessary because the projected density operators and, and hence the GMP algebra, are naturally expressed in terms of the single particle wavefunctions $\psi(r)$ , rather than the Bloch states. The single particle projected density operator is defined as

$$ \hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\mathcal{P}_{\psi}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}\mathcal{P}_{\psi}. $$

Our goal is to show that Eq. (113) implies that the density operators obey the GMP algebra [75]

$$ [\hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}},\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}]=2i\sin\left(\frac{\mathcal{F}_{0}{\boldsymbol{q}}\times{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}{2}\right)e^{\mathcal{F}_{0}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}/2}\hat{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}. $$

We show this by first translating our knowledge of the trace condition on the level of the $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}$ to the single-particle $\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}$ ’s, where holomorphicity places a crucial role. The GMP algebra will then follow by direct computation.

Differentiating $\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{k}$ and rearranging gives

$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}-e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}}i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

(We note that the action of the position operator can be quite subtle in $k$ -space [125].) Acting with $\mathcal{Q}_{\psi}=1-\mathcal{P}_{\psi}$ annihilates the first term entirely and allows us to replace $\mathcal{Q}_{\psi}$ with $Q(\boldsymbol{k})$ in the second term, since translation symmetry gives a $\delta$ -function in $k$ -space:

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\psi}\boldsymbol{r}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=-ie^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}}Q({\boldsymbol{k}}){\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

Taking complex coordinates $z=x+iy$ in real space, we therefore have

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\psi}\hat{z}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0\iff Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0. $$

The right hand side holds if and only if the (multiband) trace condition is satisfied — which it is, by hypothesis. To see this, for each $a$ , $\boldsymbol{k}$ , we directly compute

$$ \tr g^{aa}(\boldsymbol{k})-\zeta\mathcal{F}^{aa}(\boldsymbol{k})=\bra{\partial_{\zeta}u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}Q(\boldsymbol{k})\ket{\partial_{\zeta}u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}\geq 0 $$

from the definition of the quantum metric. The trace condition holds if and only if the summed inequality $\Tr\tr g\geq\Tr\mathcal{F}$ is saturated which shows that $T[\eta]\geq 0$ as we claimed in the main text. Additionally, the sum of inequalities is saturated if and only if each summand is saturated, which means $\tr g^{aa}(\boldsymbol{k})-\zeta\mathcal{F}^{aa}(\boldsymbol{k})=0$ for all $a$ and $\boldsymbol{k}$ . Since $Q=Q^{2}=Q^{\dagger}$ is positive semidefinite we must have $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0$ as we claimed above.

Eq. (119) implies $\mathcal{Q}_{\psi}\hat{z}\mathcal{P}_{\psi}=0$ or $\hat{z}\mathcal{P}_{\psi}=\mathcal{P}_{\psi}\hat{z}\mathcal{P}_{\psi}$ . Then using Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff and the fact that $[\mathcal{P}_{\psi}\hat{x}\mathcal{P}_{\psi},\mathcal{P}_{\psi}\hat{y}\mathcal{P}_{\psi}]=-i\mathcal{F}=-i\mathcal{F}_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ is a constant by (113), we compute

$$ \hat{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}=P_{\psi}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}}P_{\psi}=P_{\psi}e^{\frac{i}{2}q\overline{z}}e^{\frac{i}{2}\overline{q}z}P_{\psi}=e^{\frac{i}{2}qP_{\psi}\overline{z}P_{\psi}}e^{\frac{i}{2}\overline{q}P_{\psi}\hat{z}P_{\psi}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot P\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}P}e^{-\mathcal{F}_{0}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}/4}. $$

The GMP algebra (116) then follows by direct computation of the commutator, again using Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff.

This result highlights how the trace condition, a fact about ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ space geometry, tells us about real space holomorphicity. Namely, multiplying by the holomorphic coordinate $z$ , and applying any power series in $z$ (i.e. any holomorphic function), keeps the wavefunction within the bands of interest.

We also note that $[P_{\psi}\hat{x}P_{\psi},P_{\psi}\hat{y}P_{\psi}]=-i\mathcal{F}_{0}$ means that the electrons feel a uniform effective magnetic field, just as in the lowest Landau level. Furthermore, the GMP algebra allows Bloch states to be “boosted” to any other momentum, which implies that the total bandwidth of the $N$ bands together must vanish.
