## IV Interacting Hamiltonian, Exact $T=0$ ferromagnets

*Figure 3: Panels (a,b): Hartree dispersion $h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and Fock dispersion $h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ for different values of the parameter $s$ . Both Hartree and Fock dispersions have dips at the $\Gamma$ point of width $\sim s$ . Panel (c): Energy of the Goldstone branch of particle-hole excitations. The overall bandwidth of the branch decreases with $s$ , while the stiffness of the Goldstone mode itself remains $s$ independent due to the generation of a long length scale $s^{-1}$ .*

In this section we will review the exact zero-temperature ferromagnetic eigenstates in the strong coupling limit, in the context of our model wavefunctions (5). This section will also serve to set notation for subsequent sections, which will focus on $T>0$ . The full Hamiltonian is

$$ \mathcal{H}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}h_{\rm{BM}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}} $$

where the bare BM dispersion $h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , possibly renormalized by integrating out remote bands [96], is small sufficiently close to the magic angle and will be neglected in this section and the next. We will reintroduce it in the final section of the manuscript. $A=NA_{\mathrm{UC}}$ is the area of the sample in terms of the number of unit cells $N$ and the area of the unit cell $A_{\mathrm{UC}}$ . We use the densities $\delta\rho$ which are measured relative to the charge neutrality density,

$$ \displaystyle\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle=\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}-4N\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{G}}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}} \displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\qquad\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}), $$

consistent with particle-hole symmetry. Here and throughout, we will use variables ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , ${\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}$ , $\dots$ to denotes BZ momenta, ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ , ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ , $\dots$ to denote unrestricted momenta associated with the interaction $V_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{G}}$ , ${\boldsymbol{G}}^{\prime}$ , $\dots$ to denote reciprocal lattice vectors. The form factor is an $8\times 8$ matrix in the space of flat bands given by

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})I_{4\times 4}&0\\
0&\overline{\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})}I_{4\times 4}\end{pmatrix} $$

indicating four bands with $C=+1$ and four bands with $C=-1$ . Here, we used $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ to relate the form factors in opposite Chern sectors, such that $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{-}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\overline{\lambda^{+}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})}$ where $\pm$ labels the Chern sector and $\lambda:=\lambda^{+}$ . $\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ is a scalar whose value for ${\boldsymbol{q}}={\boldsymbol{G}}$ is equal to the Fourier components of the density of a fully filled band in either sector: time reversal relates the Chern sectors as $\lambda^{+}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\overline{\lambda^{-}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-{\boldsymbol{k}})}=\lambda^{-}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}})$ , which implies $\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{+}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\lambda^{-}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . $c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ represents an eight-dimensional vector that is composed of electron creation operators corresponding to the four $C=+1$ and four $C=-1$ bands.

For $h_{\mathrm{BM}}=0$ , it is straightforward to reproduce the exact $T=0$ generalized ferromagnets at integer filling $\nu\in[-4,4]$ originally obtained in the strong coupling limit for the BM model [3, 95, 27, 122, 123]. Consider a many-body state $\ket{\Psi}$ which fully fills some subset of the four Chern $1$ bands, and some subset of the four Chern $-1$ bands, described by a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent projector $P_{\alpha\beta}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\beta}c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\alpha}\rangle$ that is diagonal in Chern sector. The state $\ket{\Psi}$ is then an exact eigenstate of $\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}$ , and thus $\mathcal{H}$ , because $\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ cannot scatter an electron within the same band due to Pauli blocking and there are no matrix elements between different bands due to the $\rm{U}(4)\times\rm{U}(4)$ symmetry of the form factors (10). Furthermore, single particle excitations on top of $\mathcal{H}$ are also exact eigenstates with energy bands $E_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\pm h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})+\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , where $+$ corresponds to the conduction band and $-$ corresponds to the valence band [124, 125]. Here $h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and $h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ are the Hartree and Fock energies calculable from the form factors (see App A).

$$ \displaystyle h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{UC}}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}} \displaystyle=2U\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}+2(U-U_{\Gamma})\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}, \displaystyle h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle=U\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}+U_{\Gamma}\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle U \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}e^{-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}V({\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime})\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}}\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}} $$

is the on-site potential associated with two exponentially localized Gaussian orbitals with width $\delta$ , and

$$ \displaystyle U_{\Gamma} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}e^{-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}}, $$

is an interaction scale of order $U$ associated with scattering between the $\Gamma$ point electrons and the electrons away from $\Gamma$ . For the Coulomb potential $V_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\varepsilon\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert}$ we have

$$ U=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4}\frac{e^{2}}{\varepsilon\delta},\qquad U_{\Gamma}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{16}\frac{e^{2}}{\varepsilon\delta}=\frac{U}{4}. $$

From (11), we see explicitly that charged excitations in this model have a characteristic energy scale of $U\sim e^{2}/\varepsilon\delta$ . The Hartree and Fock dispersions are plotted in Fig. 3a,b, reproducing analytically the dip at the $\Gamma$ point [27, 44, 3, 124, 125]. Note that in our model, the minimum at $\Gamma$ is controlled by the scale $U_{\Gamma}$ which is of the same order as the Hubbard scale, yielding $\sim U$ gaps for the correlated insulators. Similar expressions have been obtained in the projected limit of the Song-Bernevig model [60].

In anticipation of the discussion of scales for spin and charge ordering in the next sections, we will now comment on the energy scale associated with particle-hole excitations on top of the generalized quantum Hall ferromagnets. Practically, the spectrum of these excitations can be solved for exactly by diagonalizing a particle-hole Hamiltonian $H_{\boldsymbol{Q}}$ acting on the space of excitations $\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\phi_{\boldsymbol{Q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{Q}}}$ for each total-momentum ${\boldsymbol{Q}}\in\rm{BZ}$ [6, 124]. Due to the ${\rm U}(4)\times{\rm U}(4)$ symmetry, excitations are split into two types: those in which the particle and hole are in the same Chern sector (intra-Chern) and those in which the particle and hole are in opposite Chern sectors (inter-Chern). Both spectra are split into some low-energy and high energy branches with the latter corresponding to far-separated particle hole pairs with energy of the order $2U$ . The low energy branch of the intra-Chern modes corresponds to Goldstone modes of the broken ${\rm U}(4)\times{\rm U}(4)$ , which generalize spin waves of conventional ferromagnets [6]. At small ${\boldsymbol{Q}}$ this particle-hole band has the ferromagnetic Goldstone mode dispersion $E=\frac{1}{\pi}\rho_{s}|\ell{\boldsymbol{Q}}|^{2}$ , where we have reinstated $\ell$ temporarily to clarify that $\rho_{s}$ has the dimensions of energy. We find that the stiffness $\rho_{s}\sim U$ , such that low ${\boldsymbol{Q}}$ spin-wave excitations also seem to have an energy scale $\sim U$ , see Fig. 3c. In particular, $\rho_{s}$ is independent of the concentration scale (other than through the implicit dependence $U=U(\delta))$ . Thus, the low lying excitations on top of the ferromagnet appear to be characterized by a single energy scale $U$ .

However, in Fig. 3c we see that the Goldstone energy begins to flatten at a small momentum scale $|{\boldsymbol{Q}}|\sim s$ , so that the top of the Goldstone energy band has energy decreasing with $s$ . We will see in upcoming section that this is representative of a ferromagnetic exchange energy scale $J\sim Us^{2}\ll U$ albeit over a long characteristic length scale $s^{-1}$ . This state of affairs will lead to the conclusion that moments are mostly decoupled, though at very low temperatures the relevant spin-waves, that exist in a small area of phase space $|{\boldsymbol{Q}}|\sim s$ , are described by a large stiffness $U\gg Us^{2}$ . The parametric separation of the stiffness and exchange scales stands in stark contrast to lattice models with short-range interactions, e.g. Heisenberg model, where both are controlled by the same scale $J$ .

## V Nearly Decoupled nonlocal Moments

*Figure 4: The Chern band Wannier states and their decoupled nonlocal moments. In panels (a) and (b) we plot the Wannier state centered at the origin in linear and log scale respectively, where each peak is an AA site. We use $s=0.05$ to better depict the multi-scale nature of the Wannier state. The central peak has almost all the weight of the state (note the $y$ -axis discontinuity in panel (a)). Correspondingly, the long-distace tail, which cannot be suppressed at asymptotic distances, has its onset pushed to a long length scale $s^{-1}$ . In panel (c), we show the hierarchy of scales associated with the Wannier states. The on-site scale $U$ originates from the large repulsion associated with having two central peaks at the same site, whereas exchange is suppressed by $s^{2}$ , since there is only $\sim s^{2}$ weight outside the central peak. Panel (d) plots the zero strain entropy of the decoupled moments, $S_{0}$ . For $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ , charge fluctuations are mostly frozen and the moments are mostly decoupled, up to order $s^{2}$ corrections, such that the total entropy $S\approx S_{0}$ . This is consistent with the rigorous lower bound that we proved at integer fillings (dotted entropy values), $S\geq S_{0}-NJ_{*}/T$ , where $J_{*}\sim Us^{2}$ at small $s$ .*

In the previous section, we have described the ferromagnetic ground state at charge neutrality and nearby integers. However, the treatment in the previous section is agnostic regarding nearby states, activated by $T>0$ , consisting of fluctuating nonlocal moments. In this section we will describe such states and show that they have ground state energies $\sim Us^{2}$ above the ground state ferromagnets. This leads to an intermediate temperature regime $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ where the entropy is expected to be that of free decoupled moments. We will prove a rigorous lower bound on the entropy that demonstrates this fact, including when the ground state is not a ferromagnet due to strain, sufficiently large integer filling $\nu$ , or both.

### V.1 Wannier functions

To describe the fluctuating moment state, we need to construct a basis of orthogonal orbitals associated with different lattice sites22 2 An exponentially localized but overcomplete and non-orthogonal basis of “coherent states” [13, 126] can also be used to study direct exchange in Chern bands [126].. In a trivial band, this can be chosen to be a basis of exponentially localized Wannier orbitals, and the resulting moments will be local. Here, due to band topology, Wannier functions have a power law tail, but we can still use them to define decoupled nonlocal moments as follows. Consider the Wannier states defined via

$$ w_{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}})e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}, $$

where $\gamma=\pm$ labels the Chern sector. Due to band topology , the Wannier functions will be power law delocalized with infinite localization length. Their asymptotics depend only on the gauge singularity, whose existence is dictated by topology, and the normalized Bloch state at the singularity as shown in Ref. [13]:

$$ \displaystyle w_{{\boldsymbol{R}}=0}^{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}}\to\infty) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{i\gamma\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\psi^{\gamma}_{\Gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=-\frac{e^{-i\gamma\theta_{\boldsymbol{r}}}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}\sqrt{N}\psi^{\gamma}_{\Gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}}) $$

Importantly, this power law tail cannot be made small. However, this universal power-law tail does not preclude parametrically small overlap between different Wannier states since the latter also depends on the length scale at which the tail set in. In fact, we find that in the gauge (5), this overlap is parametrically small and leads to an exchange energy $Us^{2}$ , as shown below.33 3 We note that Bloch gauge transformations generally mix classical Wannier density-density and exchange terms; indeed, we choose the gauge (5) to minimize the exchange terms relative to the density-density terms.

To understand how nonlocal Wannier states can nonetheless be nearly non-overlapping, we note that for most ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ in the BZ, other than an order $s$ region surrounding the $\Gamma$ point, the wavefunctions (5) are approximately ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent. As a result, almost all the weight of the Wannier state is concentrated in its central Gaussian peak, a fact which was noticed numerically in the BM model [90]. Indeed, we may directly calculate the weight of the Wannier function for ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ in the first unit cell (UC)

$$ \displaystyle w_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}}\in\mathrm{UC}) \displaystyle\approx(1-2s^{2}\log s^{-1})\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{4s^{2}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}, $$

such that there is only $O(s^{2})$ weight left for the peaks centered at other unit cells. For a detailed derivation of the asymptotic form of the Wannier states, see App. C.

At first sight the form of the Wannier state is surprising, because (16) appears to have order one weight when integrated. However, such tail only sets in when ${\boldsymbol{R}}\gg 1/s$ is sufficiently large that $e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}$ probes momenta in the vicinity of the $\Gamma$ -point, ${\boldsymbol{k}}\ll s$ . Thus, as $s$ is decreased towards zero, the onset of the tail (16) gets pushed to longer length scales, reducing the weight in the tail and concentrating it in the central peak. The Wannier states are plotted in Fig. 4(a)-(b) for a small $s=0.05$ to emphasize the aspects described above. Schematically speaking, $s^{-1}$ is the length scale at which the nontrivial band topology can be detected in the system. The emergence a long length scale $s^{-1}$ from a short length scale $\delta\sim s$ can be understood a consequence of UV/IR mixing, a generic feature topological bands due to the non-commutative geometry necessary for a nonzero Chern number, $C=2\pi i\Tr[X,Y]$ . Here $\Tr$ is a suitably regularized trace per unit volume and $X,Y$ are projected position operators [127, 128, 129].

### V.2 Rigorous bound on the entropy

We will now derive a rigorous bound on the entropy which, when combined with the properties of the Wannier functions constructed and the hierarchy of energy scales in the model, implies the existence of temperature window $Us^{2}\ll T\ll U$ where the entropy is $O(1)k_{B}$ per unit cell, reflecting the presence of decoupled moments. Our approach to establish the bound is to split the Hamiltonian for the density-density interaction in two pieces, $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}+\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ . The first part corresponds to the classical interaction energy associated with the local density operators constructed from the power-law localized Wannier functions whereas the second part contains the non-classical part of the interaction. We identify an exponentially degenerate manifold of ground states for $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ . This space is spanned by $e^{S_{0}}$ states at an energy $E_{\rm cl}$ equal to that of the exact ferromagnetic eigenstate of $\mathcal{H}$ , where $S_{0}=N\log\begin{pmatrix}8\\ \nu+4\end{pmatrix}$ is the entropy of decopuled moments.

We show that $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ (i) lifts the average energy of the $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ ground states by an amount $NJ_{\rm ex}$ and (ii) cannot lower the ground state energy below $E_{\rm cl}$ by more than $NJ_{\rm h}$ ; both terms are of order $Us^{2}$ and are computed explicitly below. Points (i) and (ii) together imply that the total average energy $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ in the degenerate set of trial states differs from the ground state energy by at most $NJ_{*}$ , where $J_{*}=J_{\rm ex}+J_{\rm h}$ . This fact is sufficient to rigorously bound the entropy by $S/N\geq S_{0}/N-\frac{J_{*}}{T}$ . The bound holds without any assumptions on the hierarchy of scales but is only non-trivial in the small $s$ limit where we can show that $J_{*}\sim Us^{2}$ . The $\sim s^{2}$ dependence comes from the fact that $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ acts nontrivially (and non-perturbatively) only on an $\sim s^{2}$ area of phase space. As a result, for $Us^{2}\ll T\ll U$ , this bound implies an entropy at least of order 1 per site confirming the existence of decoupled moments despite the power law tails of the associated Wannier functions. The hierarchy of scales and entropy bound are depicted in Fig. 4(c)-(d).

We begin by expanding the projected density operator $\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ in terms of the operators $c_{{\boldsymbol{R}},\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime},\alpha}$ where $c_{{\boldsymbol{R}},\alpha}$ is the annihilation operator for the power-law localized Wannier function at site ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ for band $\alpha$ . Splitting the density in the parts with ${\boldsymbol{R}}={\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}$ and ${\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}$ , we note that the first part yields a classical Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ written purely in terms of the Wannier density operators $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}=\sum_{\alpha}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\alpha}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\alpha}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm{cl}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}},{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})(n_{\boldsymbol{R}}-4)(n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}-4), \displaystyle U({\boldsymbol{R}})=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}})}. $$

Since the Wannier orbitals are orthogonal, $[n_{\boldsymbol{R}},n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}]=0$ for ${\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}$ , we can consider many-body states which are simultaneous eigenstates of all $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}$ . These are states with definite occupation number at each lattice site. This allows us to divide the many-body Hilbert space into sectors described by the occupations $\{n_{\boldsymbol{R}}\}$ . At any integer filling $\nu$ , $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ is minimized for states with $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}=4+\nu$ at every ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ . There are $\binom{8}{4+\nu}^{N}$ such states whose classical energy is $E_{\rm cl}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}},{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})\nu^{2}$ . Deviations from $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}=4+\nu$ typically cost an energy of order $U$ and play the role of double occupancies in the Hubbard model.

We begin with step (i). Projecting the remaining part of the Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\mathcal{H}-\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ onto the ground state manifold of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ yields an effective exchange Hamiltonian given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}{\boldsymbol{R}}}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}} \displaystyle\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\langle w_{\boldsymbol{R}}|e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}|w_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\frac{e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}}) $$

Note that while $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ generally contains various correlated hopping terms, these vanish upon projected to a space with fixed occupation $\{n_{\boldsymbol{R}}\}$ leading to $\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}$ . The exchange Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}$ splits the degeneracy of the exponentially many states which minimize $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ by favoring ferromagnets, which are the only states with vanishing expectation value under $\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}$ . Let $\rho_{0}$ be the equal-weight density matrix of ground states of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ . Then in App. D we compute

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\Tr\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rho_{0}=\Tr\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rho_{0} \displaystyle=(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}|\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}|^{2}, \displaystyle\approx 2U_{\Gamma}s^{2}(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\log s^{-1} $$

where we recall $\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is the average form factor and $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is the form factor for one of the $C=1$ bands. The first two lines are exact whereas in the third line we used $s\ll 1$ .

We now briefly describe step (ii). For integer filling away from charge neutrality the exact ferromagnetic eigenstate may not be the ground state; in this case it is not sufficient to evaluate $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ in the ground state subspace of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ . In App. D we prove

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm GS} \displaystyle\geq E_{\rm cl}-J_{H} \displaystyle J_{H} \displaystyle=4\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}|h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{H}^{\rm avg}|, \displaystyle\approx 16\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert U_{\Gamma}s^{2}\log s^{-1} $$

where $h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is the Hartree dispersion (11).

We are now ready to discuss the entropy bound. We will lower bound the entropy through the Bogoliubov inequality $F[\rho_{\rm trial}]\geq F[\rho]$ , where $\rho_{\rm trial}$ is any trial density matrix, $\rho\propto e^{-\beta\mathcal{H}}$ is the exact thermal density matrix, and $F[\rho]=\Tr\mathcal{H}\rho-TS[\rho]$ is the free energy functional. We will take $\rho_{\rm trial}=\rho_{0}$ , the density matrix we used in step (i). This immediately translates to a lower bound on the exact thermal entropy,

$$ S[\rho]\geq S_{0}-\frac{\Tr\mathcal{H}\rho_{0}-\Tr\mathcal{H}\rho}{T}. $$

where $S_{0}=N\log\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 4+\nu\end{pmatrix}$ . Step (i) implies $\Tr\mathcal{H}\rho_{0}=E_{\rm cl}+NJ_{\rm ex}$ , while step (ii) implies $\Tr\mathcal{H}\rho\geq E_{\rm GS}\geq E_{\rm cl}-J_{H}$ . We therefore obtain

$$ \frac{S[\rho]}{N}\geq\log\begin{pmatrix}8\\
4+\nu\end{pmatrix}-\frac{J_{*}}{T},\quad J_{*}=J_{\rm ex}+J_{\rm H}. $$

We conclude that the bound (23) holds with $J_{*}=O(Us^{2})$ . We emphasize that no approximations were needed for this bound, with the sole exception of the concrete evaluation of the momentum-sums. In particular, while the bound is most useful and directly applicable for $T\gg Us^{2}$ , in which it implies $S/N\gtrsim\log\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 4+\nu\end{pmatrix}$ , we did not use such a hierarchy to prove (23). In fact, (23) implies a meaningful lower bound even when $T\sim Us^{2}$ , and only becomes useless when $T\ll Us^{2}$ . While the result above is only a bound, we can also argue that as long as $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ , $S\approx S_{0}$ up to order $s^{2}$ corrections. We now briefly discuss this argument, which will be made more precise in the subsequent section.

Stepping back, an upshot of the above calculation is that even though the bands of twisted bilayer graphene are topological, with nonlocal Wannier states, the thermal entropy is similar to that of the trivial classical model (18), which arises from formally setting $s=0$ and ignoring the $\Gamma$ point, provided $T\gg Us^{2}$ . While for many quantities, such as Hall conductance and transport more generally, the $\Gamma$ point region is crucially important, for bulk thermodynamic quantities at not-too-small temperatures, small regions of phase space play a correspondingly small role. This intuition will be made more precise in the final technical section of the paper, where we will argue both diagrammatically and non-perturbatively that 1PI correlation functions with external legs away from $\Gamma$ mimic those of the classical model (18), provided $T\gg Us^{2}$ . Bulk thermodynamic quantities such as free energy, internal energy, entropy, and (generalized) magnetization, can all be broken down into such correlation functions to leading order in $s^{2}$ , while transport quantities and the spectral function $A({\boldsymbol{k}}\approx\Gamma,\omega)$ are dominated by correlation functions with external momenta near the $\Gamma$ point and differ nonperturbatively from the classical model. The latter quantities must be computed carefully. However, we will show appropriately that the spectral function is analytically tractable through integrating out the momenta away from $\Gamma$ , which serve as a classical bath.

Away from integer fillings, the classical Hamiltonian is minimized by states where $N(\lceil\nu\rceil-\nu)$ sites has filling $4+\lfloor\nu\rfloor$ and $N(\nu-\lfloor\nu\rfloor)$ sites has filling $4+\lceil\nu\rceil$ . We therefore conclude that the entropy at non-integer filling will be equal to that of the classical model for $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ . We note that in the Hubbard approximation $U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})=U\delta_{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}$ the classical model (18) has a significant configurational charge entropy at non-integer $\nu$ : here however we will assume that further-neighbor interactions (suppressed by a single power of $\delta$ ) are strong enough to quench the additional configurational entropy in practice. The classical entropy, for $T\ll U\delta$ , is then equal to the sum of the flavor entropies at each site, such that $S_{0}(\nu)$ linearly interpolates between the nearest integers,

$$ S\approx S_{0}=(\lceil\nu\rceil-\nu)S_{0}(\lfloor\nu\rfloor)+(\nu-\lfloor\nu\rfloor)S_{0}(\lceil\nu\rceil), $$

where we recall $S_{0}(\nu\in\mathbb{Z})=N\log\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 4+\nu\end{pmatrix}$ .

Likewise, again for $T\gg Us^{2}$ , and for an applied (generalized) Zeeman field coupling to the $\mathrm{SU}(8)$ moments, we obtain generalized Curie laws for the magnetization. For example, consider an in-plane magnetic field in twisted trilayer graphene (for twisted bilayer graphene, there is an orbital coupling of the same order that should also be included [111, 114, 112, 113]; we neglect it here for simplicity) leads to the Zeeman coupling $-\mu_{B}B_{||}S_{x}$ , where $S_{x}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}s_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}$ is written in terms of the spin Pauli matrix $s_{x}=\pm 1$ . The spin operator receives only an $O(s^{2})$ contribution from the $\Gamma$ point electrons, such that we can compute its expectation value from the trivial classical model (18). At an integer filling $\nu$ , we can specialize to an single site partition function

$$ Z=\sum_{l=0}^{4+\nu}\binom{4}{l}\binom{4}{4+\nu-l}e^{(2l-m)\beta\mu_{B}B_{||}} $$

where we used that there are four states with each spin and $4+\nu$ electrons on the site; $l$ labels the number of $+x$ spins occupied. The full magnetization then follows from $\langle S_{x}\rangle=N\frac{\partial}{\partial(\beta\mu_{B}B_{||})}\log Z$ , generalizing the usual Curie law $\tanh\frac{\mu_{B}B}{T}$ to our eight component on-site space.

Above we have argued $S\approx S_{0}$ within the hierarchy $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ . Let us briefly comment on corrections to this result. First, we expect negative corrections to $S$ of the order $Us^{2}/T$ due to exchange interactions. While we have not computed these explicitly, our rigorous entropy bound functions to upper bound their magnitude at integer filling. We can also have positive corrections to $S$ due to charged excitations. While in typical Mott insulators charge fluctuations are exponentially suppressed at $T\ll U$ , we will find in Sec. VI that the charge neutrality state is a Mott semimetal, with low energy charge excitations in an $\sim s^{2}$ region of the $\Gamma$ point. We therefore expect a power law positive correction to $S$ , of the order $T^{2}s^{2}/U^{2}$ .

### V.3 Entropy with Strain

In this section we lower bound the entropy in the presence of strain, specifically uniaxial heterostrain which is the most important form of strain in TBG [97, 99]. This rigorous lower bound is most relevant for $E_{\rm str}\gg T$ , so that only the spin and valley moments present in the lower bound remain. As in the previous section, we will also report on a parametrically controlled entropy calculation within the hierarchy of scales $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ ; here the strain energy scale can be of the same order as $T$ , and we will find close agreement with the curves in [49]. Finally, we will briefly discuss the ground state at charge neutrality in the presence of strain (the nematic semimetal), which is favored at parametrically small $E_{\rm str}\gtrsim Us^{2}$ .

In App. B.2 we compute the projection of the strain part of the BM Hamiltonian on the wavefunctions (5). We obtain a dispersion of the form

$$ \displaystyle H_{\rm{str}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}},\,\,\,\,h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})=E_{\rm str}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}, $$

where $E_{\rm str}$ is the energy scale associated with the projected strain dispersion.

We use a similar technique as in the strain-free case to lower bound the entropy. We split the Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}+\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ , only now

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl} \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}|_{E_{\rm{str}}=0}-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av}\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}} \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{\prime} \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{\prime}|_{E_{\rm{str}}=0}-\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}(h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av})c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}. $$

We see that the average value of the strain dispersion, $h_{\rm str}^{\rm av}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , acts as a classical ${\rm U}(8)$ Zeeman field along the $\gamma_{x}$ “inter-Chern” direction. This leads to a single classical ground state at $\nu=0$ , defined by $c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}=4$ for all ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ . For $\nu>0$ ( $\nu<0$ ), the four states per site with $\gamma_{x}=+1$ $(-1)$ are fractionally filled, leading again to exponentially many classical ground states. As before we define $\rho_{0}$ to be the equal-weight density matrix of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ ground states. The entropy of $\rho_{0}$ is $N\log\binom{4}{\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert}$ , equal to the classical thermal entropy $S_{0}$ at temperatures $T\ll E_{\rm str},U$ .

We now carry out steps (i) and (ii) as before, beginning with the evaluation $\Tr\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rho_{0}$ . The strain dependent term $\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}(h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h^{\rm av}_{\rm str})\langle c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}$ vanishes. Indeed, the ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ -independence of $\langle c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}$ implies the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independence of $\langle c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}$ . It suffices to evaluate the expectation value of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}$ in $\rho_{0}$ , which is carried out in App. D. The result is

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\Tr\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{N}\Tr\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rho_{0} \displaystyle=4(J_{s}-\tilde{J}_{s})+2\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\tilde{J}_{s}-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4}(J_{s}+\tilde{J}_{s}) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle J_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle\approx 2U_{\Gamma}s^{2}\log s^{-1} \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\Re(\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}})^{2} \displaystyle\approx(\log(4)-1)Us^{2} $$

are two exchange scales. The scale $J$ characterizes exchange between intra-Chern moments, while the scale $\tilde{J}<J$ couples inter-chern moments. These scales differ due to the ${\rm U}(8)$ anisotropy in (10); the form factors in the two Chern sectors are necessarily distinct $\lambda\neq\overline{\lambda}$ . Step (ii) is modified by the second term in $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ , which we must bound. We obtain (App D):

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm GS} \displaystyle\geq E_{\rm cl}-NJ_{H}-NJ_{\rm str} \displaystyle J_{\rm str} \displaystyle=\frac{4}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}|h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av}| \displaystyle\approx 8E_{\rm str}s^{2}\log s^{-1} $$

We therefore have the bound

$$ \displaystyle\frac{S[\rho]}{N}\geq\log\begin{pmatrix}4\\
\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\end{pmatrix}-\frac{J_{*}}{T} $$

where

$$ J_{*}=J_{\rm ex}^{\rm str}+J_{\rm{H}}+J_{\rm str}\sim Us^{2},E_{\rm str}s^{2}. $$

We emphasize that the ground state could be a nematic semimetal, intervalley kekule spiral, or even a metal with a Fermi surface. The bound (31) still proves that the entropy will be bounded by that of decoupled moments as long as $T\gg Us^{2},E_{\rm str}s^{2}$ .

As discussed at the end of the previous subsection, we can also use the hierarchy of scales $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ to argue that the entropy of $\mathcal{H}$ is equivalent to that of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ . This reasoning enables us to compute $S\approx S_{0}$ away from the integers, as in the previous section. It also enables us to compute $S$ at temperatures $T\sim E_{\rm str}$ , where the entropy crosses over between the strain-free and strainful limits. The entropy curves are plotted in Fig. 5 at a variety of temperatures, relative to a strain scale $E_{\rm str}=55$ K. With this single fit parameter, we closely reproduce the curves in Ref. [49].

Let us briefly comment on the ground state at charge neutrality with strain. As mentioned above, there is a non-degenerate ground state of $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ at this filling, $\ket{\Psi_{\nu=0}}$ , defined by $c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}=4$ for all ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ . Under the Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{\rm cl}$ , the state $\ket{\Psi_{\nu=0}}$ describes a generalized ferromagnet in an “inter-Chern” direction $\gamma_{x}$ with a gap of $U+E_{\rm{str}}$ to charge excitations. However, under the full topological Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}$ , an inter-Chern order parameter must have a $4\pi$ Berry phase winding around the BZ. The Berry phase winding implies that there are two vortices where the order parameter vanishes [104, 130, 131, 132]. Indeed, the state $\ket{\Psi_{\nu=0}}$ describes the nematic semimetal (NSM) state, which has numerically been shown to be the ground state of the strained interacting BM model at charge neutrality[107, 105]. The NSM Fock dispersion renormalizes the strain dispersion $h_{\rm str}$ via $E_{\rm{str}}\to E_{\rm{str}}+U$ , which has its two vortices at the $\Gamma$ point quadratic band touching. For most of the BZ, the classical spectral gap of $U+E_{\rm{str}}$ survives.

The NSM becomes the ground state at parametrically small values of strain, $E_{\rm{str}}\gtrsim Us^{2}$ . Indeed, the NSM has energy $-4E_{\rm{str}}+N^{-1}\langle\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\rangle=-4E_{\rm{str}}+4(J-\tilde{J})$ per site, where we used (28) at $\nu=0$ . This energy should be compared to $E_{\rm FM}=0$ , where $E_{\rm FM}$ is the ground state energy of the intra-Chern ferromagnets. We again see that $s>0$ can qualitatively alter excitations with $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert\sim s$ while having limited influence on bulk quantities such as ground state energy.

## VI Mott Semimetal and Insulators

In this section, we study the properties of the fluctuating moment phase obtained at intermediate temperature $Us^{2}\ll T\ll U$ . At this temperature range, the moments are disordered and the entropy is large, as shown in the previous section. However, we will show that the spectral function of this phase still encodes non-trivial information about the topology of the underlying bands leading to an interesting “Mott semimetal” at charge neutrality where the spectral gap closes near the $\Gamma$ point. Away from neutrality, we obtain an interesting class of ”spectrally imbalanced” Mott states where the spectral weight continuously shifts between the lower and upper bands as we approach the $\Gamma$ point. These Mott spectra are calculable because the small parameter $s$ , while non-perturbative, allows us to simplify the evaluation of all diagrams that contribute to the self-energy. The simplification arises due to phase space considerations. This allows us to obtain the leading part of the spectral function in $s$ exactly.

Let us briefly discuss the model in a context and notation that will be useful for the spectral function calculation. A key observation is that all quantities of interest, including the form factors, Hartree, Fock, and strain dispersions, simplify to be essentially independent of the Bloch momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ as long as ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ is not close to the $\Gamma$ point. We will use the symbol $``*"$ to indicate any BZ momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ that we can assume is “not near the $\Gamma$ point.” Then we have, from (11) and (68)

$$ h_{F}(*)=U,\,\,h_{H}(*)=2U,\,\,\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(*)=\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}. $$

These simplifications extend to the strain dispersion, which when evaluated away from $\Gamma$ has the generalized Zeeman form that we discused in the previous section, $h_{\rm str}(*)=-E_{\rm str}\gamma_{x}$ .

Furthermore, these “starred quantities” are exactly what one would compute in the classical model (18). For these concrete computations, these simplifications are not too surprising: after all, the wavefunctions (5) look like Bloch states of the classical model as long as ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ is not near the $\Gamma$ point.

We can also reintroduce the bare BM flat-band dispersion dispersion, $h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , in this context. Note that $h_{\rm BM}$ nearly vanishes at the magic angle $\theta_{M}$ and increases linearly with small $(\theta-\theta_{M})$ . We will therefore capture its effect by expanding the full BM Hamiltonian $H_{\rm{BM}}^{\theta}$ around $\theta_{M}$ and projecting the term proportional to $(\theta-\theta_{M})$ onto the wavefunctions (5). We obtain (App. B.1)

$$ h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})=E_{\rm BM}\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}0&e^{-2i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\\
e^{2i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}}&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $E_{\rm BM}\propto(\theta-\theta_{M})$ and $k_{x}+ik_{y}=\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert e^{i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ . Note that $h_{\rm BM}$ appears singular around ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ , but this is simply because we chose a gauge that has its singularity at $\Gamma$ . The Fourier transform of $h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ can be interpreted as a long-range hopping between the non-local Wannier states; it decays as $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{-2}$ due the gauge singularity (matching the Wannier tail amplitude). We have $h_{\rm BM}(*)=0$ in this case, which is consistent with the fact that the Dirac points at $K$ and $K^{\prime}$ have negligible velocity near the magic angle.

### VI.1 Diagram set up

To set up the diagrammatic calculation for the Green’s function and self-energy, we shift to a Lagrangian path integral formulation. We start by rewriting the Hamiltonian as

$$ \mathcal{H}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}h_{T}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}:\delta^{\nu}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta^{\nu}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}: $$

where

$$ \delta^{\nu}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}-(4+\nu)N\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{G}}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}} $$

is the density relative to the average density at integer filling $\nu$ , and we have normal ordered the interaction with respect to the fully empty $\nu=-4$ state. The rewriting of the interaction induces a shift in the two body term $h_{\rm BM}\to h_{T}$ . In particular, the shift in average density leads to a two-body Hartree term, while the normal ordering produces a Fock term:

$$ h_{T}({\boldsymbol{k}})=h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})+h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})+\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

It is important to note that all terms contributing to $h_{T}$ are nearly ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent for most of the BZ, away from an $O(s^{2})$ region of the $\Gamma$ point (see Eqs. (34),(11) and the discussion surrounding (33)). The associated Green’s function

$$ G_{0}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=(i\omega_{n}+\mu-h_{T}({\boldsymbol{k}}))^{-1} $$

then satisfies $G(*,i\omega_{n})=1/(i\omega_{n}+\mu+(1+\nu)U)$ for ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to*$ (away from $\Gamma$ ). Here $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is a fermionic Matsubara frequency.

We emphasize that $G_{0}$ is not the physical Green’s function in any physical limit, but it will play the role of the “non-interacting” Green’s function in the diagrammatics associated with (35). We also emphasize that the analysis of individual diagrams in the next section are not for the purpose of a perturbative calculation; rather, their purpose is to gain intuition for how diagrammatics simplify for small $s^{2}$ . We will eventually consider all diagrams by computing suitable correlation functions.

Introducing a Hubbard-Stratonovich field to decouple the interactions, our path integral formulation is expressed as follows

$$ \displaystyle Z \displaystyle=\int D\overline{\psi}D\psi D\phi e^{-S[\overline{\psi},\psi,\phi]} \displaystyle S \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}+\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n,m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\delta^{\nu}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n}V^{-1}({\boldsymbol{q}})\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}},-n} \displaystyle\delta^{\nu}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},m+n}-(4+\nu)\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}],0}\delta_{m,0}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}} $$

We can write the full Green’s function as

$$ \displaystyle G^{-1}=G_{0}^{-1}-\tilde{\Sigma}=-i\omega_{n}-h_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\Sigma \displaystyle\Sigma=\tilde{\Sigma}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})+\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})+h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}) $$

We note that $\tilde{\Sigma}$ should be understood as the self energy relative to $h_{T}$ and the associated $G_{0}^{-1}$ , and differs by some counter terms from total interaction-induced dispersion $\Sigma$ . Indeed, $G_{0}^{-1}$ already contains the full Hartree self energy as well as a Fock counterterm associated with normal ordering with respect to $\nu=-4$ . The physical self energy should be regarded as $\Sigma$ , but our diagrammatics associated with (39) will compute $\tilde{\Sigma}$ .

We have dropped the Matsubara frequency labels on the internal Green’s functions; they may be read off from the momenta.

The essential approximation is that internal lines within 1PI diagrams mostly have momenta away from the $\Gamma$ point. Indeed one sees explicitly that the momenta of all internal lines in $D_{1}$ vary over the BZ as ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ are summed over. For most ${\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ , these momenta do not lie in the $O(s^{2})$ region around the $\Gamma$ point with nontrivial ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependence. Furthermore, any potential divergences associated with the region around the $\Gamma$ point are regulated by $T>0$ . We may therefore replace the internal vertices and Green’s functions by $\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ and $G_{0,*}$ , which are their respective values away from $\Gamma$ (c.f. Eq. 33). Due to this great simplification, the momentum dependence may be extracted since it lies only in the external vertices:

$$ \displaystyle D_{1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\beta^{2}A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}} \displaystyle\times\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}mm^{\prime}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\left[G_{0,*}\xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}G_{0,*}\xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}G_{0,*}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\right\rvert^{2}}{\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}}D(*,i\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})}{U}D(*,i\omega_{n}). $$

where we have identified the Fock dispersion (11).

Furthermore, 1PI diagrams with external momenta far from the $\Gamma$ point, such as $D_{1}(*,i\omega_{n})$ , may as well have been evaluated in the effective classical model (18) with ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent form factors $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}(*)=\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ . While our model of interest differs non-perturbatively from this trivial model, these distinctions lie in the external vertices where the momenta either not summed, or contracted with e.g. a current operator that has strong ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependence near $\Gamma$ . Indeed, even in the diagram $D_{1}$ , the limit $s\to 0$ is singular due to the strong ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ dependence of $h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ .

We again obtain a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependent prefactor, which depends on $s$ non-perturbatively, multiplied by the value of the diagram in a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent model with form factors $\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ . The prefactor may be evaluated similarly to the Fock dispersion below (68). We obtain

$$ D_{2}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}D(*,i\omega_{n}). $$

The fact that $D_{2}\to 0$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ may be understood by noting that the form factor $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ has a Berry phase of $2\pi$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ encircles the $\Gamma$ point, for generic ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ . In the diagram $D_{2}$ , the average over ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ are uncorrelated such that the scattering amplitude away from the $\Gamma$ point and the scattering amplitude into it separately vanish due to destructive interference as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ . In contrast, in diagram $D_{1}$ , the momentum transfers at the two external vertices are the same and the Berry phases cancel each other for each ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ . These scattering processes, with the external vertex processes highlighted as pink arrows, are depicted in Fig. 6.

### VI.3 All diagrams

We are now ready to explain the general calculation. We begin by deriving it diagrammatically, but we will later describe a corresponding non-perturbative Schwinger-Dyson calculation that yields the same result. We note that every diagram has the form depicted Fig. 6, where the rectangular block $\Xi$ consists of all 1PI diagrams with the depicted external legs. This is nothing but the 1PI four point function, which is related to the usual four-point function by subtracting off the non-1PI part consisting of two connected three-point functions,

$$ \displaystyle\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=-\langle\mathcal{T}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle_{\rm{1PI}} \displaystyle=-\langle\mathcal{T}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle \displaystyle+\langle\mathcal{T}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle G^{-1}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\langle\mathcal{T}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle. $$

Note that the disconnected contributions to $\Xi$ , which correspond to self-energy diagrams with no vertex corrections, are regarded as 1PI here. We then have (see Fig. 6)

$$ \tilde{\Sigma}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=-\frac{1}{\beta^{2}A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

The relationship (46) is exact, with no approximations. Indeed, it can be derived as a Schwinger-Dyson equation for the self energy, where $\Xi$ is expressed in terms of third and fourth order 1PI vertices in the effective action (App. E).

We now use techniques equivalent to those used in the evaluation of $D_{1,2}$ to evaluate $\Xi$ at $T\gg Us^{2}$ . From the diagrammatic viewpoint, because $\Xi$ is 1PI, any vertical cut through the diagram will intersect at least two lines which the momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ must be split between. Thus for most values of loop momenta, no internal line within $\Xi$ will have momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}\approx\Gamma$ , and $\Xi$ may be evaluated within the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent classical model (18). From the non-perturbative Schwinger-Dyson viewpoint (App. E), $\Xi$ may be evaluated in terms of irreducible vertex functions $\Gamma^{(3)}(*),\Gamma^{(4)}(*),\ldots$ with ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ arguments away from $\Gamma$ . These irreducible vertex functions are related to each other self-consistently, with corrections from ${\boldsymbol{k}}\approx\Gamma$ suppressed by $s^{2}$ . A self-consistent solution to this set of Schwinger-Dyson equations is computable from the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent classical model. From either perspective, we arrive at the conclusion that, for $T\gg Us^{2}$ , we can replace $\Xi({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\Xi(*)$ in (46) and evaluate $\Xi(*)$ in the classical model (18).

We pause to emphasize that the same logic implies that any 1PI correlation function with external momenta away from $\Gamma$ may be calculated through the classical model. Many physical quantities, at $T\gg Us^{2}$ , break down into such correlation functions and can be directly read off from the classical model. Entropy, as well as flavor magnetization and susceptibility, all take the values associated with the classical model, as we claimed at the end of Sec VB. For these quantities, the small area of phase space near $\Gamma$ cannot compete with or reduce the large bulk contribution from the rest of the BZ. In contrast, quantities which either probe the $\Gamma$ point region directly, such as $G_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}$ where $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert\sim s$ , or transport quantities, which involve ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space derivatives that effectively magnify the $\Gamma$ region, often differ non-perturbatively from those of the classical model. For these quantities, the larger trivial region of the BZ serves as a bath for the active electrons near the $\Gamma$ point.

The quantity $\Xi(*)$ is most readily evaluated in real space in terms of the original fermionic variables $c_{{\boldsymbol{R}},\alpha}$ . Thus it can be written explicitly by integrating out the Hubbard-Stratonovich field and Fourier transforming to real space as

$$ \displaystyle\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}(*,i\omega_{n})=\beta V({\boldsymbol{q}})G_{*,n-m}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\delta_{m,m^{\prime}} \displaystyle-\frac{V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}}{N}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}},{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2})}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1})}\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{R}}), \displaystyle\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{R}})=-\langle\mathcal{T}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}n-m^{\prime}}\delta^{\nu}n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}m^{\prime}}\delta^{\nu}n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}-m}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}n-m}\rangle \displaystyle+\langle\mathcal{T}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}n-m^{\prime}}\delta^{\nu}n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}m^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}n}\rangle G_{*,n}^{-1}\langle\mathcal{T}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}},n}\delta^{\nu}n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}-m}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}n-m}\rangle $$

where $\mathcal{T}$ denotes imaginary time ordering and $\delta^{\nu}n_{\boldsymbol{R}}=n_{\boldsymbol{R}}-(\nu+4)$ is the occupation of site ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ relative to its average at arbitrary filling $\nu$ .

We have thus established a concrete, tractable, procedure to calculate the self energy in the TBG model, provided $T\gg Us^{2}$ . One finds the classical ground state, evaluates (47), and plugs into (46).

In this paper, we will restrict our attention to integer fillings where we can benefit from some convenient simplifications, but this restriction is not necessary. At integer fillings and $U\gg T$ , the densities $\delta^{\nu}n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1,2}}$ annihilate the classical ground states. Thus, the densities must be evaluated at the same position as the fermion operators, ${\boldsymbol{R}}={\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}={\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}$ , sit between them in the time ordering, and have sign $\pm 1$ depending on whether the excitation is electron-like ( $c$ has larger $\tau$ ) or hole-like ( $c^{\dagger}$ has larger $\tau$ ). We obtain44 4 The Matsubara sum over $m$ , $m^{\prime}$ sets the time of each density equal to the corresponding fermion, leading to an ambiguity in time-ordering. One symmetric prescription for alleviating this ambiguity is $\mathcal{T}[c_{\tau}\delta n_{\tau}]\to\frac{1}{2}\{c_{\tau},\delta n_{\tau}\}$ , which can be separately justified through deriving the equation in a Hamiltonian picture without normal ordering. Because the path integral is derived through normal ordering the fermions, it also makes sense to normal order in the presence of this ambiguity; $\mathcal{T}[c_{\tau}\delta n_{\tau}]\to:c_{\tau}\delta n_{\tau}:$ . Both of these prescriptions ultimately lead to the same result for $\Xi(i\omega_{n})$ . We thank Qingchen Li for a useful discussion on this point.

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\sum_{mm^{\prime}} \displaystyle\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{R}})=\frac{1}{4}\Xi(i\omega_{n})\delta_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{R}}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{R}}_{2},{\boldsymbol{R}}}, \displaystyle\Xi(i\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=G_{*,n}-(G_{*,n}^{+}-G_{*,n}^{-})G_{*,n}^{-1}(G_{*,n}^{+}-G_{*,n}^{-}), \displaystyle=2\left(G_{*,n}^{-}G_{*,n}^{-1}G_{*,n}^{+}+G_{*,n}^{+}G_{*,n}^{-1}G_{*,n}^{-}\right). $$

where $G_{*,n}^{\pm}=-\int_{-\beta/2}^{\beta/2}d\tau e^{i\omega_{n}\tau}\Theta(\pm\tau)\langle\mathcal{T}c_{\tau}c^{\dagger}_{0}\rangle$ are the electron-like and hole-like parts of the Green’s function $G_{*,n}=G^{+}_{*,n}+G^{-}_{*,n}$ .

The self-energy (46) splits into two parts when (47) is inserted. The first part combines with the Fock counter term in $G_{0}^{-1}$ , see (37),(38) after using $\beta^{-1}\sum_{m}G_{*,n-m}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}\rangle=P_{*}$ , which is a projector for a Slater determinant state but not otherwise. In the second term, the sums over ${\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ reproduce those of (43),(44).

We then have, for the full self-energy,

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma \displaystyle=\tilde{\Sigma}+h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})+\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q_{*}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}U^{2}\Xi(i\omega_{n})+\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}}) $$

where $P_{*}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q_{*})$ .

The first part can be traced to diagrams of the form (42) where the momenta ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ in Fig. 6 are set to be equal. These are diagrams where vertex corrections are not included. If the state is a Slater determinant with $Q^{2}=1$ , this part simply reduces to the Fock exchange energy. The second term includes non-trivial vertex corrections and corresponds to diagrams of the form (43),(44) where ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ in Fig. 6 are independent. This term vanishes for a Slater determinant since $G^{+}=PG^{+}P$ , where $P$ projects onto occupied orbitals, while $G^{-}=(1-P)G^{-}(1-P)$ , leading to $\Xi(i\omega_{n})=0$ .

In contrast, for the symmetric state where the moments are disordered, the second term in (49) is crucial: it opens the Mott gap away from the $\Gamma$ point. Indeed, a symmetric state at filling $\nu$ has $Q_{*}=\nu/4$ , proportional to the identity matrix, so the first term gives a frequency and band independent dispersion that cannot open a Mott gap anywhere in the BZ. The second term should be computed from the Green’s function of the classical model, which can be solved as a single site problem at integer filling:

$$ G_{*,n}=G^{+}_{*,n}+G^{-}_{*,n},\quad G^{\pm}_{*,n}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\mp\frac{\nu}{8}}{i\omega_{n}+\mu_{\nu}\mp U}. $$

Here $\mu_{\nu}=\mu-2\nu U$ is the chemical potential relative to the Hartree offset $h_{H}(*)=2\nu U$ . We should have $\left\lvert\mu_{\nu}\right\rvert<U$ in order to be consistent with integer filling $\nu+O(s^{2})$ . The function (50) leads to a nonzero, and ultimately self-consistent, expression for $\Xi(i\omega_{n})$ as we now discuss.

### VI.4 Mott Semimetal at Charge Neutrality

*Figure 7: Mott states at charge neutrality ( $\nu=0$ ). A broadening term $\Sigma\to\Sigma-iUs^{2}$ is added to all spectral functions to model theoretical uncertainty. (a) Mott semimetal at charge neutrality with a single Dirac cone per spin per valley, described by the self energy (52). (b) Mott semimetal gapped by particle-hole breaking dispersion $E_{\rm ph}=U/2$ , with $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}\sim|{\boldsymbol{k}}|^{2}$ in the doublon band for ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ . The eight-fold at the Mott semimetal touching point is preserved, but it is inherited entirely by the holon band. (c) Mott semimetal with BM dispersion $E_{\rm BM}=0.3U$ . There is an exotic quadratic band touching at $\omega=0$ , with $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}\sim|{\boldsymbol{k}}|^{2}$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ ; the latter makes the touching difficult to identify without analytical insight.(d) Curie-gapped Mott semimetal with in-plane Zeeman field $\mu_{B}B_{||}/T=1$ .*

We begin with the self energy and spectral function for the symmetric Mott state at charge neutrality. Using (50), with $\mu=\nu=0$ , we obtain

$$ \Xi(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}} $$

such that

$$ \Sigma({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}. $$

We see that the self energy is equal to the self energy of the usual Hubbard model except modulated by a factor

$$ W_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}} $$

The fact that $W_{\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ quadratically with ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ is reminiscent of a quadratic band touching and the $4\pi$ Berry phase typical in symmetric TBG band structures; Indeed, as we discussed in the example diagram $D_{2}$ , the vanishing as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ , arises from the Berry phase of the external form factors $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ when averaged over scattering directions ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ . Remarkably, however, we obtain a linear dispersion in the spectral function. Indeed, for zero bare dispersion, a partial fraction decomposition leads to

$$ \displaystyle G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}-\Sigma({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})} \displaystyle=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{i\omega_{n}-\sqrt{W_{\boldsymbol{k}}}U}+\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{i\omega_{n}+\sqrt{W_{\boldsymbol{k}}}U} $$

The spectral function associated to (54) (Fig. 7a) looks like a single Dirac cone per spin and valley flavor near ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ . Crucial to this apparent halving is the Mott-type $1/(i\omega_{n})$ dependence of $\Sigma$ , which leads to a square root of the Berry-phase induced prefactor of $\Sigma$ . For ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to*$ we reproduce $G_{*}$ as required by self-consistency. The Mott semimetal state we obtain is consistent with quantum Monte Carlo simulations at intermediate temperatures at charge neutrality [67, 133].

The Mott semimetal is qualitatively distinct from all other TBG semimetals that we know of. The non-interacting or renormalized “BM semimetal” has Dirac points at $K$ and $K^{\prime}$ rather than $\Gamma$ , as does the “symmetric Kondo state” [63, 134]. The nematic semimetal breaks $C_{3}$ and has either a quadratic band touching at $\Gamma$ or two Dirac cones in the vicinity of $\Gamma$ . Another state was discussed in Ref. [135] from the THF perspective and also dubbed Mott semimetal. This state appears to be describable by two decoupled systems, consisting of a traditional Mott insulator and eight Dirac bands, where the Dirac dispersion comes from the bare Hamiltonian. Our Mott semimetal possesses a few qualitative differences: (i) the semimetallic dispersion comes entirely from interactions; (ii) we have half the Dirac cone degeneracy, a fact which is enabled by the Mott-like self energy $\propto\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}/\omega$ ; and (iii) our Mott semimetal responds to perturbations in a manner distinct from any non-interacting or mean-field system as we discuss below.

We now discuss how a variety of different perturbations affect the Mott semimetal(54) (we will use this abbreviated phrase to refer to the Mott semimetal): particle-hole breaking terms, BM dispersion, and Zeeman fields. We begin with the particle-hole breaking terms. We note that while such terms likely exist at some level microscopically, we are primarily discussing them here for conceptual purposes and as a simpler version of $\nu\neq 0$ . We take

$$ h_{\rm ph}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-E_{\rm ph}\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}=-E_{\rm ph}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}), $$

for some scale $E_{\rm ph}$ , which we choose to be positive for concreteness. Note that (55) has the same form as the non-constant part of the Hartree dispersion (11). Any particle-hole breaking potential term $\Delta({\boldsymbol{r}})$ projected to the wavefunctions (5) produces a term of the form (55), up to a constant that can be absorbed into the chemical potential. Since $h_{\rm ph}(*)=0$ , the self energy (52) is unchanged. We have

$$ G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+E_{\rm ph}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}})-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}}. $$

The eight-fold degeneracy ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ is preserved and shifted to the energy $-E_{\rm ph}$ . Despite this, we still open up a gap equal to $E_{\rm ph}$ . To see this, we analytically continue $i\omega_{n}\to\omega$ and note that the denominator diverges when $\omega(\omega+E_{\rm ph}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}))-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U^{2}=0$ . This leads to the doublon ( $+$ ) and holon ( $-$ ) branches

$$ \omega_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-\frac{E_{\rm ph}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}})}{2}\pm\sqrt{E_{\rm ph}^{2}+W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U^{2}}, $$

with quasiparticle residues

$$ Z_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\frac{|\omega_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})|}{\omega_{+}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\omega_{-}({\boldsymbol{k}})}. $$

The holon branch has $\omega_{-}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to-E_{\rm ph}$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ . The doublon branch has $\omega_{+}(0)=0$ , and is separated by a gap $\geq E_{\rm ph}$ at all ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . Both $\omega_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ are quadratic in ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ in the vicinity of ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ , with effective mass $\propto E_{\rm ph}^{-1}$ . Note that $Z_{-}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to 1$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ for each of the eight bands. The holon band thus has the full spectral weight at the $\Gamma$ point. The doublon branch correspondingly has $Z_{+}({\boldsymbol{k}})\propto\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ . As ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to*$ , we have $\omega_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\pm U$ and $Z_{\pm}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\frac{1}{2}$ , as required by self consistency. The corresponding spectral function is shown in Fig. 7b. 55 5 It may seem like the filling has deviated from $\nu=0$ by an order $s^{2}$ amount, since spectral weight has shifted from the doublon to the holon band at $\Gamma$ . However we are not including order $s^{2}$ corrections to the Green’s function $G(*,i\omega_{n})$ , which describes the rest of the Brillouin Zone. As a result, the filling of (56) is only controlled up to order $s^{2}$ corrections. Order $s^{2}$ corrections away from $\Gamma$ that shift spectral weight in the opposite direction, from the holon band to the doublon band, likely exist. We also expect an order $s^{2}$ broadening of the Mott bands which could lead to order $s^{2}$ weight at the Fermi level; we therefore do not claim that our Mott states with a spectral gap, which we define as the separation between peaks in the spectral function, are insulators. We conclude that the particle hole breaking term (55) preserves the eight fold degeneracy of the Mott semimetal but still manages to open up a gap through making the $\Gamma$ point maximally spectrally imbalanced between the holon and doublon bands.

We now show that the BM dispersion leads to a quadratic touching at $\omega={\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ with $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}\propto\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}$ . Since $h_{\mathrm{BM}}(*)=0$ , we may again use the self energy (52). We will also work in the BM energy band basis, which is straightforward since $\Sigma$ is a scalar. In this basis we have $h_{\mathrm{BM}}=\diag(h^{+}_{\mathrm{BM}}I_{4\times 4},h^{-}_{\mathrm{BM}}I_{4\times 4})$ , where

$$ h^{\pm}_{\mathrm{BM}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\pm E_{\rm BM}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

We relatedly have $G^{\pm}=\diag(G^{+},I_{4\times 4},G^{-}I_{4\times 4})$ with

$$ G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})^{\pm}=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}\mp E_{\rm BM}(1-W_{\boldsymbol{k}})-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}}. $$

We see that in the $\mp$ BM-band we reproduce (56) with $E_{\rm ph}=\pm E_{\rm BM}$ . Thus, the doublon branch in the $-$ BM band and the holon branch in the $+$ BM band remain at $\omega=0$ at ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ . These branches touch quadratically as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ with quasiparticle residue $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}\propto\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}$ (Fig. 7c).

Next we discuss the inclusion of a Zeeman field $-\mu_{B}B_{||}S_{x}$ . The Zeeman field affects states uniformly across the BZ, and we therefore need to obtain $G_{*}$ and $\Xi$ as a function of the field. In particular, we must use a nonzero $Q_{*\alpha\beta}=2\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\beta}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\alpha}\rangle-1$ in (48) to capture the magnetization of the system. The Hermitian matrix $Q_{*}$ has eigenvalues $\in[-1,1]$ , and in the diagonalized basis corresponds to a quarter of the filling of each diagonal component. The Green’s function away from $\Gamma$ can still be computed in real space as a single site problem. For simplicity we will take $B_{||}\ll U$ since the most interesting effects come from comparing $B_{||}$ with $T$ . Then, the holon and doublon band persist at $\pm U$ but become increasingly spin polarized:

$$ G(*,i\omega_{n})=\frac{P_{*}}{i\omega_{n}-U}+\frac{1-P_{*}}{i\omega_{n}+U}. $$

If $P_{*}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q_{*})$ is a projector, the above Green’s function reduces to the Slater determinant form $\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+Q_{*}U}$ as expected. From (61) we obtain

$$ \Xi(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1-Q_{*}^{2}}{i\omega_{n}-Q_{*}U}, $$

which vanishes when the state is a Slater determinant, due to $Q_{*}^{2}=1$ . From (49),

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=-Q_{*}h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})+W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U^{2}\frac{1-Q_{*}^{2}}{\omega-Q_{*}U} \displaystyle G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\omega+Q_{*}h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})-W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U^{2}\frac{1-Q_{*}^{2}}{\omega-Q_{*}U}} $$

where we used $[\Lambda,Q_{*}]=0$ to simplify the first term in $\Sigma$ . The calculation of the spectral function then proceeds in two steps: first we calculate the magnetiation through the single site partition function (25) to obtain $Q_{*}=ms_{x}/4$ , where $m=\langle S_{x}\rangle/N\in[-4,4]$ is the magnetization per site. Then we compute the poles and residues associated with (63). The resulting spectral function is shown in Fig. 7d. At ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ the Mott term drops and we obtain two poles from $\omega=-Q_{*}h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}=0)$ , one for each eigenvalue of $Q_{*}$ , with quasiparticle residue $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}=1$ . For $Q_{*}\neq 0,1$ there are also two other poles that have vanishing residue as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ , with energy $\omega({\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0)=Q_{*}U$ , coming from the denominator of the second term in the self energy (63). We see that all four poles have energy proportional to $Q_{*}$ as ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ ; a nonzero magnetization gaps the Mott semimetal.

### VI.5 Spectrally Imbalanced Mott states

*Figure 8: Mott states near fillings $\nu=1,2,3$ (top, middle, and bottom rows) in response to, from the left column to the right column, no extra dispersion, BM dispersion $E_{\mathrm{BM}}=0.3U$ , large Zeeman magnetic field $B_{||}\gg T$ , and large strain $E_{\rm str}\gg T$ . All Mott states have large gaps $\gtrsim U$ in the absence of additional terms, larger than those of the zero temperature exact ferromagnets. The Zeeman magnetic field reduces the spectrally-imbalanced $\Gamma$ point gap, especially at $\nu=1$ where the gap is reduced to $\approx U/8$ , rather than opening it as it does at $\nu=0$ . At intermediate temperatures $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ , the Mott states on the leftmost column occupy all the $\Gamma$ point states available, reducing the quasiparticle weight $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ at the $\Gamma$ point of the doublon band.*

We now discuss fillings away from neutrality. Here, the Hartree and Fock potentials break particle-hole symmetry and have a similar effect to the particle hole breaking dispersion considered earlier, Eq. (55). They gap the Mott semimetal and lead to spectrally imbalanced Mott states.

The influence of symmetry breaking terms have a distinct effect, however. For example, at charge neutrality a large in-plane magnetic field is sufficient to turn the Mott state into a mean-field ferromagnet; the four Chern and valley states are in singlet representations at each site. But away from charge neutrality, spin polarization is not enough to quench the entropy; fluctuating Chern and valley moments with definite spin persist.

The calculation of the spectral function is along the same lines as the previous section, with only a few differences. Now $Q_{*}=(\nu+ms_{x})/4$ , and $\left\lvert m\right\rvert\leq 1-\frac{\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert}{4}$ . We also have a nonzero chemical potential $\mu\approx 2\nu U$ , and there is a Hartree dispersion $\nu h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . We have

$$ G_{*}=\frac{P_{*}}{i\omega_{n}+\mu_{\nu}+U}+\frac{1-P_{*}}{i\omega_{n}+\mu_{\nu}-U} $$

such that the self energy and full Green’s function are given by

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma({\boldsymbol{k}})=\nu h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})-Q_{*}h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})+W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U^{2}\frac{1-Q_{*}^{2}}{i\omega_{n}+\mu_{\nu}-Q_{*}U} \displaystyle G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\mu-\Sigma({\boldsymbol{k}})}. $$

We can verify self-consistency, $G({\boldsymbol{k}}\to*)=G_{*}$ , after recalling $h_{H}(*)=2U$ and $\mu_{\nu}=\mu-2\nu U$ .

We can also study the influence of strain in a similar manner to the in-plane Zeeman field; let us briefly discuss the modification necessary. Strain induces $Q_{*}$ to have a $\gamma_{x}$ component instead of a $s_{x}$ component. The first term in (49) then evaluates to the nematic semimetal form $\frac{1}{2A}Q_{*}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}(\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}}))^{2}=Q_{*}W_{\boldsymbol{k}}U$ instead.

In Fig. 8 we plot Mott spectra at fillings $\nu=1,2,3$ in response to no extra dispersion, BM dispersion, large Zeeman field relative to temperature, and large strain relative to temperature. The Mott states with nothing added, left column of Fig. 8 have large gaps $\gtrsim U$ : even larger than those of the $\nu>0$ exact ferromagnets. If one starts with a zero temperature generalized ferromagnetic ground state, the spectral gap will increase by an amount $\sim U$ when temperature is raised from zero to $\gtrsim Us^{2}$ . The essential reason for the increased gap of the Mott states is their ability to have a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependent spectral imbalance between the holon and doublon bands. This enables the Mott states to entirely occupy the “Hartree dip” at the $\Gamma$ point for $\nu>0$ and lower the bandwidth of the conduction band. In contrast, the conduction band Hartree dip pierces the gap of the ferromagnet and rapidly lowers the gap as $\nu$ increases. We note that this points to an interesting connection to the intervalley Kekulé spiral state [103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 131, 132], which fully occupies the $\Gamma$ point electrons albeit through breaking translation symmetry[107, 108]. The spectrally imbalanced Mott states we obtain thus seem similar in spirit to thermally disordered intervalley Kekulé spirals.

In the Mott regime, $Us^{2}\ll T\ll U$ , the spectral function only depends on the ratio $T/E_{\rm str}$ . We see that while the gap increases with temperature for all fillings $\nu=1,2,3$ , the increase for $\nu=1$ is especially drastic. Furthermore, both $B_{||}/T$ and $E_{\rm str}/T$ decrease the $\Gamma$ point Mott gap.
