Of course for transport measurements it is difficult to disentangle the increase in the spectral gap from the temperature dependence of scattering off of activated moment fluctuations, though one may expect that the latter would not show a dramatic difference between $\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert=1$ and other integers. Measurements of the spectral gap as a function of temperature, through e.g. STM or Dirac cone spectroscopy in trilayer [92, 93], should be able to test directly if the $\nu=-1$ spectral gap itself exhibits a Pomeranchuk effect.

## VII Discussion

We conclude by discussing the hierarchy of scales in TBG samples, the relevance of our results to TBG experiment, our relationship to other approaches, and promising future directions.

Studying TBG by projecting into the flat band subspace is, in our view, harmonious with the most exciting and unique aspect of the system: its realization of strongly interacting topology in a time-reversal invariant and beyond Landau level context. We also believe it is justified in reality, given the hierarchy of energy scales as we discuss now. To justify a projective treatment, we have taken the interaction scale $U$ to be much smaller than the gap to the remote bands $\Delta$ . Whereas $\Delta$ is a band structure property, $U$ is sensitive to the dielectric environment which receives contributions both from the hBN substrate and the remote bands. The scale $U$ is thus difficult to determine precisely from first principles. On the other hand, since $U$ is the largest interacting scale in the problem, it should be possible to reliably extract it from experiment. There are several ways to do this. One is to identify the separation of the main peaks of the density of states at charge neutrality with $2U$ . This is justified close to the magic angle and for not-too-large strain; for larger strain the separation is $2(U+E_{\rm str})$ , which still yields an upper bound on $U$ . This estimate does not depend on symmetry breaking except through subleading anisotropies. The separation seen in various experiments [41, 136, 103, 137, 102, 138] is consistently between 30 and 40 meV, leading to an estimate of $U\approx 15-20$ meV. Another estimate is obtained by the requirement to reproduce [34] the measured change in chemical potential between $\nu=0$ and $4$ [139, 50] which leads to $U\approx 20$ meV (assuming our parameters). A third independent estimate can be obtained from recent nanoSQUID quantum oscillations in alternating twist trilayer graphene [93]. The Fock scale and $K_{M}$ -point gap scale obtained in that work are both $\sim 20$ meV. Taking into account that all scales in trilayer are enhanced by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ [140], this gives a value $U\approx 15$ meV. Thus, rather remarkably, all these experiments across different devices yield a consistent estimate of $U\approx 15-20$ meV.

Phenomenologically determining the gap to the remote bands, $\Delta$ , is more tricky. However, since $\Delta$ does not feature explicitly in our approach, we only need to justify the hierarchy $U\ll\Delta$ on phenomenological grounds. This can be addressed by noting that it is very difficult to reconcile $U\gtrsim\Delta/2$ with an insulating gap at full filling. To see this, we note that the last flat band electron added before $\nu=4$ will be away from $\Gamma$ and feel a strong repulsion $2\nu U=8U$ . While half the remote bands are also AA localized and will feel the same repulsion, the other half have wavefunctions similar to the $\Gamma$ point flat bands [56] which are not AA-localized; the latter feel a reduced repulsion. The reduction in repulsion is exactly the $\nu=4$ Hartree bandwidth, and can be estimated as $8U-2\nu(U-U_{\Gamma})\approx 2U$ for Coulomb interactions using Eq. (14). The non-interacting gap of $\Delta$ is therefore reduced by $\approx 2U$ at full filling which means that the gap is eliminated entirely if $U\gtrsim\Delta/2$ . Taking a $\nu=4$ gap of 15 meV from SET measurements [139] yields $\Delta\approx 40-55$ meV, consistent with our hierarchy of scales $U\lesssim\Delta$ .

Although we derived the parameters of our model in Sec. III by fitting to the BM model, one of the advantages of our minimal approach is that it depends only on a few phenomenological parameters that can be extracted from experiments. In fact, once the hierarchy of scales $h_{b}\ll U\ll\Delta$ is established, we only need to determine the parameters $\delta$ , $s$ , $U$ , in addition to the strain scale to explain most of the intermediate temperature physics. The interaction scale $U$ can be estimated from experiment as explained above. The AA-localization scale $\delta$ can be extracted by fitting the width of the charge distribution extracted from STM data [38, 40, 32, 41, 136, 30, 103]. The strain scale, if present, can be extracted by identifying the temperature at which entropy gets quenched at charge neutrality. The parameter $s$ is more difficult to estimate at present, but will be obtainable once momentum-resolved probes like ARPES [141, 142, 143] and the quantum twisting microscope [91] are sufficiently developed.

It is worth comparing and contrasting our approach to the topological heavy fermion (THF) approach [56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66]. In this approach, the system is described using two flavors of fermions: the localized $f$ electrons that support local moments and are described by Hubbard physics, and the mobile $c$ electrons that are introduced through mixing with dispersing remote bands and support topology. We note that while the THF model can be studied in the projected limit, $U\ll\Delta$ [60], it has been predominantly motivated by and studied in the opposite limit $U\gg\Delta$ [56] where local moment states exist in the low-energy Hilbert space. However, as we have shown here, explicit local moments are not required to explain the extensive entropy seen in experiment. Furthermore, calculations done in the limit $U\gg\Delta$ do not yield a gapped band insulator at $\nu=-4$ [59], consistent with the arguments given above.66 6 Note that our definition of $U$ is smaller by a factor of $2$ compared to that of the THF papers; in our convention they quote $U\approx 30$ meV [56]. In our convention, $U$ is half the Mott gap and $\Delta$ is half the hybridization gap, while in the THF papers $U$ is the full Mott gap.We note that our argument does not preclude a gap at intermediate values $U\sim\Delta$ , which can only be determined using unbiased numerics. Finally, while both approaches are motivated by concentration of topology at the $\Gamma$ point, our approach formalizes this notion by introducing a small parameter $s$ and demonstrating that controlled analytic calculations of many-body observables can be achieved using phase space arguments.

In particular, our approach has enabled the analytical calculation of electron spectral functions in TBG as reported here. Our analytic calculation for the spectral function explains some of the features observed numerically in DMFT for the THF model. For example, Fig. 1a of Ref. [66] looks qualitatively similar to our charge neutrality Mott semimetal with BM dispersion (Fig. 7c), and is generally consistent with our claim of a quadratic band touching at zero energy with vanishing residue; Figs. 1b,c of the same reference appear similar to our Fig. 8 at finite doping with BM dispersion by a particle-hole transformation. Furthermore, our spectral function for the Mott semimetal at neutrality agrees qualitatively with results obtained with QMC in the band-projected limit [67, 133]. A quantitative comparison between our theory and numerical calculations would be valuable and is left to future work. It is also worth noting that some of the insights from our calculations may help uncover an analytically tractable regime of the THF model. In the THF model language, our $s\ll 1$ projected limit amounts to taking large $c$ -electron Fermi velocity $v_{F}k_{\theta}\gg U,\Delta$ in the projected limit $U\ll\Delta$ . We anticipate large $v_{F}$ , with $v_{F}k_{\theta}\gg U,\Delta$ , will also yield analytical progress for the THF hierarchy of scales $U\gg\Delta$ . This ensures that the $c$ -electron phase space is parametrically small and one can use small phase space approximations similar to those that we have developed here. These approximations could be used to control the strength of RKKY interactions that couple the local $f$ moments [59], for example. We also anticipate $U/\Delta$ corrections to the projected limit to be tractable within $s\ll 1$ . Such corrections could capture effects beyond any projected model, such as filling dependence of the active low-energy states.

We reiterate that our projected-limit spectral functions do not admit an interpretation in terms of local moments weakly coupled to a bath of conduction electrons. The presence of local moments imply a nearly ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent branch of the spectral function; this is inconsistent with the lack of spectral weight at $({\boldsymbol{k}}=\Gamma,\omega=\pm U)$ in almost all of the spectra we obtain. Similarly, a weakly interacting bath of conduction electrons cannot explain the dispersion of our spectra near $\Gamma$ nor their response to perturbations.

We now discuss an outlook towards future experiments. A direct observation of the spectral function of the Mott semimetal and the spectrally imbalanced Mott state is a clear goal. This is in principle possible with momentum-resolved techniques under active development [141, 142, 143, 91]. We have also predicted a Pomeranchuk effect for the spectral gap, especially at $\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert=1$ when strain $E_{\rm str}\ll U$ is not too large. Further measurements on entropy over a wide temperature range as a function of in-plane field direction would would provide a further test of our results. Indeed, because the in-plane field couples orbitally in TBG with a strength that is comparable to the Zeeman splitting, we expect the residual degeneracy to depend on whether the in-plane field is parallel or perpendicular to the axis of strain. Trilayer entropy measurements as a function of in-plane field would also be useful, since here the orbital effect can be neglected [111, 114, 112, 113].

There are also a number of theoretical calculations that now appear within reach. For example, the intervalley Kekulé spiral (IKS) state [103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 131, 132] first obtained within Hartree-Fock [107] and later verified in DMRG [108], has thus far evaded strong coupling arguments that would analytically establish it as the ground state in the presence of strain. We are optimistic that our $s^{2}\ll 1$ phase space approximations will both enable such a treatment and shed light on some puzzling features of the state, including the nearly flat landscape of spiral wavevectors. We also speculate that a theory of superconducting pairing could be analytically controlled with $s\ll 1$ . Initial steps could be to calculate the Drude weight for the $T\gg Us^{2}$ normal state, or the total flat-band optical spectral weight[70]; the latter is an upper bound for the superconducting stiffness [69, 68, 71].

More broadly, we propose that our techniques lay the groundwork for a new analytical approach towards low-temperature TBG. We have worked in the hierarchy of scales $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}\sim 1$ meV. There are several other effects we have neglected such as asymmetric form factors, dispersion-induced superexchange, and phonons; all are on the $1$ meV scale. While the zero temperature symmetry breaking pattern depends sensitively on these anisotropies [3, 144], for us their effect is suppressed by temperature. Beginning with the symmetric state and incorporating the various $\sim 1$ meV effects perturbatively relative to temperature will of course lead to more accurate $T>0$ spectral functions (e.g. through incorporating nonzero broadening, or splitting from asymmetric form factors[130]). However, the process of initially ignoring them, and then gradually incorporating them perturbatively relative to temperature, could also yield a more universal perspective on the doped state that is obscured by doping a very particular zero temperature insulator.

Furthermore our findings invite some deeper conceptual questions. In this work, we have described thermal Mott states where charge is mostly frozen but the nonlocal moments are disordered. A natural conceptual question is to ask about states where nonlocal moments are quantum disordered at zero temperature. For the $\nu\neq 0$ states, it seems likely that the state will be a gapped spin-liquid, and that the main signature of the non-interacting topology will be the $Z_{\boldsymbol{k}}\to 0$ imbalance in the spectral function. For $\nu=0$ , however, the situation is more interesting. Let us consider a simpler case of a single $C=1$ spinful band for concreteness and a chiral symmetry that pins the filling at zero (which can be regarded as a combination of particle-hole and time reversal). Then the system may be regarded as the surface of a three-dimensional class AIII topological insulator at level $k=2$ . It was shown that $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ symmetric surface states in this class do not admit gapped ground states, even in the presence of topological order [145]. A quantum disordered version of our Mott semimetal, with a spectral function equivalent to a single Dirac cone, then seems like a natural possibility. Note that it has half the spectral weight of the minimal non-interacting surface state.

In closing, we point out potential generalizations of the model we have presented here beyond the $|C|=1$ bands relevant to twisted bilayer graphene. For example, what types of Chern bands host decoupled nonlocal moments when $|C|>1$ ? We anticipate that the concentration of topology will still be an essential feature, but for $|C|>1$ we anticipate a wider range of possibilities with distinct physics and Mott spectra. Finally, an exciting question raised by recent experiments [146] which observed enhanced entropy and isospin fluctuations in rhombohedral graphene, is whether the concepts presented here can be extended to flat band systems even in the absence of a moiré lattice.

## Appendix A Form factors and Hartree Fock Dispersion

In this section we compute the form factors $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and Hartree Fock dispersion. It suffices to calculate the form factor associated with the $C=+1$ bands, $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , because the form factors, as well as the Hartree and Fock dispersions, are diagonal in Chern sector with the two Chern sectors related by $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ . For notational simplicity we will drop the Chern sector label $\gamma=+$ throughout this section. Using that we are in a periodic gauge $\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}}$ , such that the periodic wavefunction satisfies $u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}u_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\braket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}}=\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{u_{[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}]}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\boldsymbol{k}}N_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\int_{\mathrm{UC}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\left(1+i\frac{\overline{z}/\delta}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1-i\frac{z/\delta}{[k+q]/s}\right) \displaystyle\times e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}} $$

where

$$ N_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}} $$

is a normalization factor. We have used the notation $[k+q]$ to denote the part of $k+q=[k+q]+G$ in the first BZ, and also take $k=[k]$ and $z$ in the first unit cell. Since the integral is dominated by $\left\lvert z\right\rvert\sim\delta$ , we can remove the integration bound restriction to the first unit cell and integrate over the whole plane, as is standard in saddle point approximations. Furthermore we can replace $e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\approx e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}$ : the difference ${\boldsymbol{q}}-{\boldsymbol{G}}$ is BZ scale and exponential $e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}$ is only sensitive to momenta $\sim\delta^{-1}$ much larger than the BZ scale. The resulting Gaussian integral can be explicitly evaluated, though the calculation is made slighlty easier with the trick of replacing factors of $z$ and $\overline{z}$ with derivatives with respect to $\overline{q}$ and $q$ respectively:

$$ \displaystyle\braket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}\int_{\mathrm{UC}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\left(1+i\frac{\overline{z}/\delta}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1-i\frac{z/\delta}{[k+q]/s}\right)e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}\left(1-\frac{2\delta^{-1}\partial_{q}}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1+\frac{2\delta^{-1}\partial_{\overline{q}}}{[k+q]/s}\right)\int_{\mathrm{UC}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}e^{-\frac{i}{2}(\overline{q}z+q\overline{z})}\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert z\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}\left(1-\frac{2\delta^{-1}\partial_{q}}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1+\frac{2\delta^{-1}\partial_{\overline{q}}}{[k+q]/s}\right)e^{-q^{2}\delta^{2}/2} \displaystyle=\frac{\left(1+\frac{\overline{q}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1-\frac{q\delta}{[k+q]/s}\right)+\frac{2s^{2}}{\overline{k}[k+q]}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}/2} $$

The Fock dispersion is given by

$$ \displaystyle h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\frac{1+\frac{\overline{q}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}}}\right\rvert^{2}e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} $$

where we used that while ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ may be near $\Gamma$ , for most of the ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ -integral $\left\lvert[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}]\right\rvert\gg s$ . Expanding out the suare and dropping terms that vanish after the ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ integral by circular symmetry, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle h_{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=U\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}+U_{\Gamma}\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}} $$

where

$$ U=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}e^{-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle U_{\Gamma} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}e^{-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}}. $$

The Hartree dispersion is

$$ \displaystyle h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{UC}}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\xi_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{UC}}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\frac{\left(1+\frac{\overline{G}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}\right)\left(1-\frac{G\delta}{k/s}\right)+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}e^{-\left\lvert G\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{q}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}s^{2}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}+2s^{2}}e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=2U\frac{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}+2s^{2}}+2(U-U_{\Gamma})\frac{2s^{2}}{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}+2s^{2}} $$

where we used the fact that the characteristic scale of the summand is ${\boldsymbol{G}}\sim\delta^{-1}\gg\ell^{-1}$ , such that we can replace the sum by an integral (and relabel ${\boldsymbol{G}}\to{\boldsymbol{q}}$ ).

## Appendix B Single particle terms

In addition to the form factors and Hartree and Fock dispersions derived in the previous section, in the main text we have occasionally referenced the non-interacting BM dispersion as well as the strain dispersion. In this section we derive these expressions. We note that in this section, since we will be interfacing with the microscopic Hamiltonian, we will not adopt the $\ell=1$ units in which $A_{\mathrm{UC}}=(2\pi)^{2}/A_{\mathrm{BZ}}=2\pi\ell^{2}\to 2\pi$ until the end. The model parameters $\delta$ and $s=\beta^{-1}\ell^{-2}\delta$ then have units of length and inverse length respectively.

### B.1 BM dispersion

We begin with the BM dispersion. We note that the BM Hamiltonian has very small bare bandwidth at the magic angle, even away from the chiral limit. However, the bandwidth increases quickly upon deviating slightly from the magic angle, such that $h_{\rm BM}\propto(\theta-\theta_{M})$ , where $\theta_{M}$ is the magic angle. We will therefore approximate the BM dispersion through this linearization in the vicinity of the magic angle. The BM Hamiltonian in the $K$ valley of graphene is given by

$$ H_{\mathrm{BM}}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}-iv{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}&T({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})&-iv{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where we neglected the twist angle dependence of the kinetic terms (their effect goes as $\theta^{2}\ll\theta$ ). The Hamiltonian in the $K^{\prime}$ graphene valley is related by time reversal. The $\theta$ dependence enters in the moiré scale modulation of the tunneling terms through the wavevector $k_{\theta}=2k_{D}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\approx k_{D}\theta$ where $k_{D}$ is the distance between the grpahene $K$ -points (side length of the graphene BZ hexagon). Explicitly we have

$$ T({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})=w_{\rm AB}\begin{pmatrix}\kappa U_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})&U_{-1}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})\\
U_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})&U_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $U_{l}({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})=\sum_{n=0}^{2}e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}ln}e^{-i\boldsymbol{q}_{n}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}_{n}={\boldsymbol{q}}_{n}(k_{\theta})$ is given by $q_{n,x}+iq_{n,y}=-ik_{\theta}e^{2\pi in/3}$ . It is convenient to use the fact that $T({\boldsymbol{r}},k_{\theta})=T({\boldsymbol{r}}k_{\theta},1)=\tilde{T}(\tilde{{\boldsymbol{r}}})$ only depends on the combination ${\boldsymbol{r}}k_{\theta}$ to re-scale (74) so that it depends on $\theta$ more explicitly and not through the unit cell size. We obtain

$$ \displaystyle H_{\mathrm{BM}}(\theta) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}-ivk_{\theta}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\tilde{{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}}&\tilde{T}(\tilde{{\boldsymbol{r}}})\\
\tilde{T}(\tilde{{\boldsymbol{r}}})&-ivk_{\theta}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\tilde{{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}}\end{pmatrix} \displaystyle=H_{\mathrm{BM}}(\theta_{M})+(\theta-\theta_{M})k_{D}I^{\rm layer}_{2\times 2}(-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\tilde{{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}}), $$

where we have separated the “magic angle” Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{BM}}(\theta_{M})$ from part corresponding to the deviation from the magic angle, where the second part has a simple, layer-independent, from. We now wish to project (76) onto our explicit model wavefunctions (5). We neglect the first term by hypothesis (the BM dispersion is known to be small at the magic angle) but compute the second term explicitly. Undoing the scale transformation leads to $\frac{(\theta-\theta_{M})}{\theta}(-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}})$ such that we must evaluate

$$ h_{\mathrm{BM}}^{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\frac{\theta-\theta_{M}}{\theta}v\bra{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\gamma}}(-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}})\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\gamma^{\prime}}}. $$

We recall that our wavefunctions are sublattice polarized (we have neglected the corresponding off-diagonal part of the form factor) and the Chern sector is given by $\gamma_{z}=\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}$ , where $\sigma_{z}$ is the sublattice matrix within each valley and $\tau_{z}=\pm 1=K,K^{\prime}$ is the graphene valley and we are focusing on the $K$ valley. Thus, in (77) we may identify $\gamma$ and $\sigma$ . Moreover, $-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}$ anticommutes with $\sigma_{z}$ while the wavefunctions are eigenstates of $\sigma_{z}$ : this observation implies that the diagonal terms, with $\gamma=\gamma^{\prime}$ , vanish. We can then focus on $\gamma^{\prime}=-\gamma=+$ and obtain $\gamma=-\gamma=-$ through $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ , which acts as $\sigma_{x}K$ and ${\boldsymbol{r}}\to-{\boldsymbol{r}}$ . Since $\bra{\sigma=-}(-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}})\ket{\sigma+}=-2i\overline{\partial}$ , where $\overline{\partial}=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}+i\partial_{y}$ ) is the derivative with respect to $\overline{z}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\bra{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-}}(-i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}})\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{+}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}}\int_{\mathrm{UC}}\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}}\overline{\left(1+\frac{\overline{z}/\delta}{i\overline{k}/s}\right)}\left(1+\frac{z/\delta}{ik/s}\right) \displaystyle\times e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}^{\dagger}(-2i\overline{\partial})\left[e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})\right]. $$

Here we plugged in the wavefunctions (5) with $\psi^{-}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\overline{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{+}(-{\boldsymbol{r}})}$ by $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ . We also used that we can move the derivative $\overline{\partial}$ past $z$ . The above expression is sufficient to extract the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ dependence, up to an overall coefficient with a layer-spinor dependent integral that can be in principle evaluated. Note that, for this calculation, we have not replaced $\chi_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})\to\chi_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}}=0)$ as in the main text because otherwise the integral above vanishes. In practice the overall scale of the BM dispersion can be matched to numerics on the BM model or symmetry-preserving generalizations, so we will focus on extracting the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependence. For this purpose it is sufficient to use $C_{3}$ symmetry under which $z$ and $\overline{\partial}$ have angular momentum one and the other parts of the wavefunction have angular momentum zero. The only terms that survives the $C_{3}$ symmetric integral over the UC is then the angular momentum $3\equiv 0$ part with two factors of $z$ . We then obtain

$$ \displaystyle h^{-+}_{\mathrm{BM}} \displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{BM}}\frac{k^{-2}}{1+2s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{-2}} \displaystyle E_{\mathrm{BM}} \displaystyle=\frac{\theta-\theta_{M}}{\theta}\int_{\mathrm{UC}}\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{\delta^{2}}e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}^{\dagger}(-2iv\overline{\partial})\left[e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})\right]. $$

After using $h^{+-}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\overline{h^{-+}({\boldsymbol{k}})}$ by $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ we arrive at the expression quoted in the main text.

### B.2 Strain dispersion

We now move on to the strain dispersion. To leading order, strain couples to the BM Hamiltonian (74) as $-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\to-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}-\mu_{z}{\boldsymbol{A}}$ where $\mu_{z}=\pm$ labels the top and bottom graphene layer and ${\boldsymbol{A}}=\frac{\beta\sqrt{3}}{2a}(\epsilon_{xx}-\epsilon_{yy},-2\epsilon_{xy})$ [147, 148, 149, 150, 151] where the tensor $\epsilon$ is the dimensionless strain tensor, $a$ is the graphene lattice constant, and $\beta\approx 3.14$ is a dimensionless parameter associated with the graphene hopping as a function of distance[99, 43, 97]. We note that there is a layer dependent distortion matrix as well, described in other works[99, 106, 105], which captures the energetic effects associated with distorting the moiré unit cell. Its effect is of order $\theta\epsilon\ll\epsilon$ or $\epsilon^{2}$ , and so we regard it as subleading here. It may be included in a very similar calculation, however.

It follows that we must project $v\mu_{z}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{A}}$ onto the wavefunctions (5). As with the BM dispersion, only the off-diagonal in Chern sector terms are nonzero, and we may begin with the $\gamma^{\prime}=-\gamma=+$ component.

$$ \displaystyle h^{+-}_{\rm strain} \displaystyle=({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{A}})_{+-}\chi_{0}^{\dagger}\mu_{z}\chi_{0}\frac{1}{N_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}} \displaystyle\times\int_{\mathrm{UC}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\overline{\left(1+\frac{\overline{z}/\delta}{i\overline{k}/s}\right)}\left(1+\frac{z/\delta}{ik/s}\right)\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{r}}\right\rvert^{2}}{2\delta^{2}}}}{2\pi\delta^{2}} $$

Here, the terms proportional to $z$ vanish under the unit cell integral and we obtain

$$ h_{\rm strain}=v{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\chi_{0}^{\dagger}\mu_{z})\chi_{0}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}. $$

where we used time reversal symmetry to deduce that the final result is the same in both valleys, and thus replaced ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\to\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ . This is the same form we quoted in the main text.

Note that the orbital coupling of an in-plane magnetic field in TBG has the same form as strain in the $K$ valley, but is odd under time reversal symmetry such that it couples oppositely to strain in the $K^{\prime}$ valley. We therefore obtain the same result except with an extra factor of $\tau_{z}$ that accounts for the valley sign change. This orbital coupling can generally not be ignored in TBG, since the g-factor is roughly the same as Zeeman. However, in alternating twist trilayer graphene, an in-plane field is odd under the $M_{z}$ symmetry that exchanges the top and bottom layer; as a result it does not directly project to the active flat bands and the orbital coupling dominates.

## Appendix C Wannier State Asymptotic Forms

In this section we calculate Wannier state wavefunctions analytially for the various regimes: ${\boldsymbol{R}}=0$ , $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll s^{-1}$ , and $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\gg s^{-1}$ . The Wannier states are related by translation, $w_{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}})=w_{{\boldsymbol{R}}=0}^{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{R}})$ , so we will focus on the Wannier state centered at ${\boldsymbol{R}}=0$ . Additionally, time reversal implies that we may choose $w_{\boldsymbol{R}}^{-}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\overline{w_{\boldsymbol{R}}^{+}({\boldsymbol{r}})}$ , so we will focus only on $\gamma=+$ and drop the $\gamma$ label for the rest of the section. Finally since $\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is exponentially suppressed away from AA sites, we may evaluate it in the neighborhood of each AA site and use the Bloch periodicity $\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}\approx{\boldsymbol{R}})=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}\approx 0)$ . We therefore have

$$ \displaystyle w_{{\boldsymbol{R}}=0}({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}\frac{1+\frac{(z-R)/\delta}{ik/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}}\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert z-R\right\rvert^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}\left(c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}})+c_{z}({\boldsymbol{R}})\frac{z-R}{\sqrt{2}\delta}\right)\frac{e^{-\frac{\left\lvert z-R\right\rvert^{2}}{4s^{2}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\frac{e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}} \displaystyle c_{z}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{ik}\frac{e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}} $$

Note that we have used $\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}=A_{\mathrm{UC}}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}$ with $A_{\mathrm{UC}}=2\pi\ell^{2}=2\pi$ . For ${\boldsymbol{R}}=0$ we have $c_{z}=0$ by symmetry whereas

$$ \displaystyle c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}}=0) \displaystyle=1-\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\left(1-\frac{\left\lvert k\right\rvert}{\sqrt{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}}\right) \displaystyle=1-2s^{2}\log s^{-1}, $$

where for the first term we used that the area of the Brillouin Zone is $2\pi$ . For ${\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0$ , the integrals are all dominated by the $k\approx 0$ region and have a circular symmetry. We can perform the integral over $\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ , leading to Bessel functions $J_{0,1}(u)$ for $u=\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert$ .

$$ \displaystyle c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}du\frac{u^{2}J_{0}(u)}{\sqrt{u^{2}+2s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2}}}, \displaystyle=-2s^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}du\frac{uJ_{1}(u)}{(u^{2}+2s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2})^{3/2}}, \displaystyle c_{z}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2}se^{-i\theta_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert}\int_{0}^{\infty}du\frac{uJ_{1}(u)}{\sqrt{u^{2}+2s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2}}}. $$

To go from the first to second line above we integrated by parts and used $\frac{d}{du}(uJ_{1}(u))=uJ_{0}(u)$ . We can now evaluate the asymptotoics of $c_{1}$ and $c_{z}$ by replacing $(u^{2}+2s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2})$ with $u^{2}$ and $s^{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2}$ , for $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll s^{-1}$ and $\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\gg s^{-1}$ respectively. The resulting Bessel function integrals can mostly be computed straightforwardly through integration by parts, $\frac{d}{du}J_{0}(u)=-J_{1}(u)$ , and $\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{m}(u)du=1$ . For $c_{1}(\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll s^{-1})$ , however, this procedure leads to $-2s^{2}\int J_{1}(u)/u^{2}$ . This integral is logarithmically divergent as $u\to 0$ because $J_{1}(u)\approx u/2$ for small $u$ . The divergence is cut off at $u\sim s\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll 1$ leading to $-s^{2}\log(s\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert)^{-1}$ . We therefore conclude

$$ \displaystyle c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}1-2s^{2}\log s^{-1},\quad R=0\\
-s^{2}\log(s\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert)^{-1},\quad\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll s^{-1}\\
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}s\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{3}},\quad R\gg s^{-1}\end{cases} \displaystyle c_{z}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=e^{-i\theta_{\boldsymbol{R}}}\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert},\quad\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\ll s^{-1}\\
\frac{1}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert^{2}},\quad\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{R}}\right\rvert\gg s^{-1}\end{cases} $$

The near complete weight of the Wannier state at its center implies that the density operator is nearly-diagonal in the Wannier basis, since the Wannier state overlap is parametrically small. An explicit calculation yields

$$ \displaystyle\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}} \displaystyle e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\braket{u_{k}|u_{k+q}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}-{\boldsymbol{R}})} \displaystyle=e^{-\left\lvert q\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}/2}\begin{cases}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}+O(s^{2})\text{ for }{\boldsymbol{R}}={\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}\\
(c_{1}({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})-\frac{iq\delta}{\sqrt{2}})e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}}\\
+(c.c,{\boldsymbol{R}}\leftrightarrow{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}\leftrightarrow-{\boldsymbol{q}})\text{ for }{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}\end{cases} $$

such that off diagonal elements are suppressed by $O(s^{2})$ relative to diagonal ones. We will now use this fact to bound the entropy at any filling.

## Appendix D Entropy Bound Calculations

In this section we describe the calculations associated with the entropy bounds (23) and (31). We begin by explicitly computing the exchange energy scales without strain, Eq. (20), and with strain, Eq. (28). Later we will address the ground state energy lower bounds (21), (30).

### D.1 Exchange Energy Scale

We copy the exchange Hamiltonian below for readability

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}{\boldsymbol{R}}}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}} \displaystyle\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\langle w_{\boldsymbol{R}}|e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}|w_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\frac{e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

Before taking expectation values, we use the standard exchange-interaction procedure of grouping the fermion operators at the same site together and using the Fierz identity for $\mathrm{SU}(8)$ generators $r^{\mu}_{\alpha\beta}$ , where $\mu$ labels the generator and $\alpha,\beta$ labels the band index. The Fierz identity reads $r^{\mu}_{\alpha\beta}r^{\mu}_{\gamma\delta}+\frac{1}{8}\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\gamma\delta}=\delta_{\beta\gamma}\delta_{\alpha\delta}$ , where the generators satisfy $\tr r^{\mu}r^{\nu}=\delta^{\mu\nu}$ . To obtain interactions in terms of the flavor operators $R^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{R}})=c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}r^{\mu}c_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}$ . We obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}},{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}\right\rvert^{2}n_{\boldsymbol{R}}(1-\frac{n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}}{8}) \displaystyle-\tr(r^{\mu}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}r^{\nu}\Lambda^{{\dagger}{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}_{\boldsymbol{q}})R^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{R}})R^{\nu}({\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}). $$

Note that we cannot set $\mu=\nu$ because $\Lambda$ is not the identity matrix (it is different between the Chern sectors for ${\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}$ .)

#### D.1.1 Strain-free

We now compute the zero-strain $NJ_{\rm ex}\Tr\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rho_{0}=\langle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}$ where we recall $\rho_{0}$ is the equal weight density matrix of states $\ket{\Psi}$ that satisfy $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}\ket{\Psi}=(n+\nu)\ket{\Psi}$ . Products of such flavor operators at distinct sites have zero expectation value under $\rho_{0}$ because $\rho_{0}$ is symmetric under local $\mathrm{SU}(8)$ rotations. Thus, the last line in (89) has zero expectation value. We therefore have

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm ex}=\langle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rangle_{\rho_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{N}{8}(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}J({\boldsymbol{R}}) $$

where we have identified

$$ J({\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0)=\frac{2}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}},0}\right\rvert^{2} $$

as the $\mathrm{SU}(8)$ symmetric part of the exchange coupling at distance ${\boldsymbol{R}}$ (we will counter other parts in the strain calculation). We can further evaluate, using the Plancherel theorem

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}J({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4N}(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}|\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}|^{2}, $$

which is the general form that we quoted in (20). Note we have not yet had to assume $s\ll 1$ .

For $s\ll 1$ we can show $J_{\rm ex}\propto s^{2}$ up to a log. To see this, note that there are only two order $s^{2}$ areas of phase space, ${\boldsymbol{k}}\approx\Gamma$ and ${\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}\approx\Gamma$ , where $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is appreciably distinct from $\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ . We can explicitly evaluate the expression by evaluating $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ in these two areas, using (68), and integrating.

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}|\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}|^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2}\left(\left\lvert\frac{1+\frac{\overline{q}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}}-1\right\rvert^{2}+\left\lvert\frac{1-\frac{q\delta}{([k+q])/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}-1\right\rvert^{2}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2}\left\lvert\frac{1+\frac{\overline{q}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}}-1\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle=2s^{2}\log s^{-1}\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}\delta^{2}e^{-\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2}\right\rvert\delta^{2}} \displaystyle=2U_{\Gamma}s^{2}\log s^{-1}, $$

Between the second and third line above we did the change of variables $[k+q]\to k$ in the summation over $k$ (done before the integration over ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ ). We also dropped terms subleading to $\log s^{-1}$ , and used the circular symmetry to drop terms that would vanish under the ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ integration. We therefore conclude

$$ J_{\rm ex}=2(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})U_{\Gamma}s^{2}\log s^{-1}, $$

as claimed in the main text (20).

#### D.1.2 With Strain

We now derive the strainful case (28). Again beginning with (89), we take the expectation value in the density matrix $\rho_{0}$ where now $\rho_{0}$ is an equal weight density matrix of states $\ket{\Psi}$ that satisfy $n_{\boldsymbol{R}}\ket{\Psi}=(4+\nu)\ket{\Psi}$ as well as $c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}\ket{\Psi}=(4-\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert)\ket{\Psi}$ .

The expectation value is more complicated now because some of the terms in the second line of (89), involving $r^{\mu}\propto\gamma_{x}$ , have nonzero expectation value in $\rho$ (the first line is equivalent to the strain-free case). We therefore split the $\mathrm{SU}(8)$ generator index $\mu\to(i,a)$ and write $r^{\mu}=\frac{\gamma^{i}}{\sqrt{2}}t^{a}$ . Here $\gamma^{i}$ are the $2\times 2$ Chern-sector Pauli matrices, while $t^{a}$ are the generators of $\mathrm{SU}(4)$ rotations in spin-valley space.

We must first evaluate the expectation value, for ${\boldsymbol{R}}\neq{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}$ . It is zero unless $i=j$ and $a=b=0$ where $t^{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}I_{4\times 4}$ by the symmetry of $\rho_{0}$ . For these indices we have

$$ \langle R^{x0}({\boldsymbol{R}})R^{x0}({\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})\rangle_{\rho_{0}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{4}\left(4-\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\right)^{2} $$

Next we need to evaluate the trace $\tr(r^{ia}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}r^{jb}\Lambda^{{\dagger}{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}_{\boldsymbol{q}})$ , where we can replace $i,j\to x$ and $a,b\to 0$ since otherwise the expectation value vanishes. We obtain

$$ \tr(r^{x0}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}r^{x0}\Lambda^{{\dagger}{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}_{\boldsymbol{q}})=\Re(\lambda^{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}})^{2}, $$

where we used that $\Lambda=(\lambda I_{4\times 4},\overline{\lambda}I_{4\times 4})$ . If the form factors were ${\rm U}(8)$ symmetric we would have obtained the modulus squared instead of the real part as in the strain-free case. We identify the inter-chern exchange coupling

$$ J({\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0)=\frac{2}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\Re(\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{{\boldsymbol{R}},0}\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{0,{\boldsymbol{R}}})^{2}. $$

Putting these sub-computations together, and computing the first term in $\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}$ identically to the strain free case, we have

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm ex} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\langle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ex}\rangle_{\rho_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}(4-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4})\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}J({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{8}\frac{1}{4}(4-\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert)^{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}\tilde{J}({\boldsymbol{R}}) \displaystyle=4(J_{s}-\tilde{J}_{s})+2\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\tilde{J}_{s}-\frac{\nu^{2}}{4}(J_{s}+\tilde{J}_{s}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle J_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}J({\boldsymbol{R}})=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\left\lvert\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}, \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}\neq 0}\tilde{J}({\boldsymbol{R}})=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Re(\lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}})^{2}. $$

We have already evaluated $J_{s}$ in (93). We can similarly integrate

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{J}_{s} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2} \displaystyle\times\Re\left(\left[\frac{1+\frac{\overline{q}\delta}{\overline{k}/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert k\right\rvert^{2}}}}-1\right]^{2}+\left[\frac{1-\frac{q\delta}{([k+q])/s}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{\left\lvert[k+q]\right\rvert^{2}}}}-1\right]^{2}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2NA}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{2s^{2}}{|k|^{2}}}}-1\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}^{2}(\log(4)-1)s^{2} \displaystyle=(\log(4)-1)Us^{2} $$

where we redefined ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ in the second big bracket term to map it to the first and used that the integration over $q$ leads to many terms dropping by circular symmetry.

### D.2 Ground State Energy Lower Bounds

We now discuss the lower bounds of ground state energy (21) (30). It suffices to prove the latter strainful bound, since it reduces to the former for $E_{\rm str}\to 0$ .

For readability we restate the interacting Hamiltonian in the presence of strain

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}h_{\rm{str}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle=\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}-4\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{G}}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}} \displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\qquad\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

For the purpose of lower bounding the ground state energy, relative to $E_{\rm cl}$ we will rewrite the Hamiltonian by separating out the reciprocal lattice vector wavevectors from the ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ sum, since they alone contribute to the $E_{\rm cl}$ at integer filling. Among the reciprocal lattice vector density operators, we will also separate out the part corresponding to the classical energy by splitting the form factor $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}+(\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}})$ and

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{G}}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\alpha}(\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}. $$

Finally, we will find it convenient to work in a space with fixed total particle number $N\nu$ so that we can replace $\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}(c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}-4)\to N_{\nu}$ in various Hamiltonian terms. For example

$$ \delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{G}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}-4)+\tilde{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{G}}\to N\nu+\tilde{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{G}}. $$

With this splitting, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}]\neq 0}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle+\frac{N}{2A_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}\right\rvert^{2}\nu^{2} \displaystyle+\tilde{H}_{\rm H} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\tilde{\rho}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\tilde{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}, \displaystyle+\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}}h_{\rm str}^{\rm av}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{R}}, \displaystyle+\tilde{H}_{\rm str}. $$

We define and discuss the terms in (104) line by line. In the first term, which is positive semidefinite, we sum over all ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ that are not reciprocal lattice vectors. The terms in the sum that did include reciprocal lattice vectors were split between the second, third, and fourth lines. The second term is exactly the interaction contribution to $E_{\rm cl}$ ,

$$ \frac{N}{2A_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}\right\rvert^{2}\nu^{2}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}}{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})\nu^{2}, $$

where we recall $U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})}$ . The third term contains the cross terms and can be expressed in terms of the dispersive part of Hartree

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{\rm H} \displaystyle=\frac{\nu}{A_{\mathrm{UC}}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\tilde{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\nu}{A_{\mathrm{UC}}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}(\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\xi_{\boldsymbol{G}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}, \displaystyle=\nu\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}(h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{H}^{\rm{av}})(c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}-4), $$

and the fourth term is positive semidefinite. The fifth term is the classical part of the strain Hamiltonian, while the sixth is the dispersive part of strain

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{\rm str} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}(h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av})c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$

We are now ready to bound the ground state energy from below. Let us take the expectation value of (104) in the ground state. Then we have

$$ E_{\text{GS}}=\bra{\Psi_{\text{GS}}}\mathcal{H}\ket{\Psi_{\text{GS}}}\geq E_{\rm cl}+\bra{\Psi_{\text{GS}}}\tilde{H}_{\rm H}+\tilde{H}_{\rm str}\ket{\Psi_{\text{GS}}}. $$

Here we used that the second and fifth terms in (104) are equal and minimized respectively by their respective contributions to $E_{\rm cl}$ , while the first and fourth terms are positive semidefinite.

It suffices to lower bound the expectation value on the right hand side of (108). We begin with the Hartree term

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{H}_{\rm H}\rangle \displaystyle=\nu\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}(h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{H}^{\rm{avg}})\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\alpha}c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\alpha}-4\rangle \displaystyle\geq-4\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\left\lvert h_{H}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{H}^{\rm{avg}}\right\rvert=-NJ_{H}. $$

Similarly

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{H}_{\rm str}\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}(h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av})\langle c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{x}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle \displaystyle\geq-4\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\left\lvert(h_{\rm str}({\boldsymbol{k}})-h_{\rm str}^{\rm av})\right\rvert=-NJ_{\rm str}. $$

Combining the above two bounds with (108) we obtain (30) as claimed.

In the small $s$ limit we have the following expressions for $J_{H}$ and $J_{\rm str}$ that we quoted in the main text:

$$ \displaystyle J_{H} \displaystyle=4\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\left\lvert 2U-\frac{2U_{\Gamma}}{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}+2s^{2}}-2U\right\rvert \displaystyle=8\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert U_{\Gamma}\int_{0}^{\Lambda\sim 1}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert d\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert}{1+\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{2s^{2}}} \displaystyle=16\left\lvert\nu\right\rvert U_{\Gamma}s^{2}\log s^{-1}, $$

and similarly

$$ J_{\rm str}=4E_{\rm str}\int_{0}^{\Lambda\sim 1}\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert d\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert}{1+\frac{\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\rvert^{2}}{2s^{2}}}=8E_{\rm str}s^{2}\log s^{-1}. $$

## Appendix E Schwinger-Dyson Calculation of Spectral Function

In this section we show how 1PI correlation functions, such as the self energy, can be calculated non-perturbatively (i.e. without resorting to “all orders in perturbation theory in $U$ ” arguments given in the main text) through the Schwinger-Dyson equations. In particular we will prove

$$ \tilde{\Sigma}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=-\frac{1}{\beta^{2}A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}, $$

as argued for in the main text diagrammatically in the text surrounding (46). Also explained in the main text diagrammatically is the approximation $\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}(*)$ for $T\gg Us^{2}$ and the prescription that $\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}(*)$ can be evaluated in real space in a classical, topologically trivial, model (18). In this appendix, we will also explain this approximation and prescription from the non-perturbative Schwinger-Dyson perspective.

### E.1 Effective Action and Schwinger Dyson Formalism

We begin by reviewing the quantum effective action approach and deriving the Schwinger-Dyson equations that we will use. The formulas in this subsection are more or less common to any fermionic system interacting via density-density interactions. We will reserve the usage and explanation of $s\ll 1$ approximations for the next subsection. We begin by restating the partition functions and coupling it to source fields.

$$ \displaystyle Z[\eta,\overline{\eta},J] \displaystyle=\int D\overline{\psi}D\psi D\phi e^{-S[\overline{\psi},\psi,\phi]-S_{\rm src}} \displaystyle S \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n} \displaystyle+\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n,m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\delta^{\nu}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},n}V^{-1}({\boldsymbol{q}})\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}},-n} \displaystyle\delta^{\nu}\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},m+n}-(4+\nu)\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}],0}\delta_{m,0}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle S_{\rm src} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\overline{\eta}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}+\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\eta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}+\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}J_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m} $$

We additionally use the quantum effective action $\Gamma[\overline{\psi},\psi,\phi]$ , also referred to as the 1PI effective action as its power series expansion coefficients correspond to the irredicible vertices. In other words, $\Gamma$ can be defined as the action under which every correlation function can be evaluated at tree level; its terms can in principle be computed by evaluating such correlation functions through other means. It is also commonly defined, non-perturbatively, as the Legendre transform of the generator of connected correlation functions $W[\eta,\overline{\eta},J]$ , where $e^{iW}=Z$ is the partition function (114). Generally, the quantum effective action contains infinitely many terms and is not local in space or time. However, it may be expanded in powers of the fields, and since it is exact at tree level only a few terms (irreducible vertices) enter any given correlation function. The first few terms are

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}n}G^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}n} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\beta A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}},-m}D^{-1}({\boldsymbol{q}},i\omega_{m})\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m} \displaystyle+\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{q}}mn}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m} \displaystyle\times\left(\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\Gamma^{(3),{\boldsymbol{k}},n}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},m+n}-(4+\nu)\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}],0}\delta_{m,0}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{3!\beta^{2}A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime\prime}m^{\prime\prime}}\tilde{\Gamma}^{(3)}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime\prime}m^{\prime\prime}} \displaystyle\times\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime\prime}m^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}+{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime\prime}],0}\delta_{m+m^{\prime}+m^{\prime\prime},0} \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2\beta^{2}A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{q}}{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}mm^{\prime}n}\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},-m^{\prime}}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m} \displaystyle\times\left(\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},n-m^{\prime}}\Gamma^{(4),{\boldsymbol{k}},n}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}n-m}-(4+\nu)\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{q}}],[{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}]}\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right) \displaystyle+\cdots. $$

Of course, the coefficients of the effective action are generally unknown and, generically, too complex to determine by symmetry. They are in principle determined through the Schwinger Dyson equations (SDEs). The SDEs are an infinite hierarchy that relate lower order correlations to successively higher order correlation functions (we will review their derivation soon). When the correlation functions in the SDEs are evaluated using the effective action $\Gamma$ , one obtains related SDEs which relate lower order vertices to successively higher order vertices. Typically, this hierarchy is still impossible to solve, though here we will find it amenable to phase space approximations for $s\ll 1$ as described in the next subsection.

We begin by deriving the SD equations that we need. Shift $\overline{\psi}\to\overline{\psi}+\overline{\varepsilon}$ in the path integral, take a derivative with respect to $\overline{\varepsilon}$ , and set $\overline{\varepsilon}\to 0$ . Since the partition function does not change under such a change of variables we have

$$ 0=\int D\overline{\psi}D\psi D\phi\left(\frac{\delta}{\delta\overline{\epsilon}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}}S[\overline{\psi}+\overline{\varepsilon},\psi,\phi]+\eta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\right)e^{-S-S_{\rm{src}}} $$

Using

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta\overline{\varepsilon}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}}S[\overline{\psi}+\overline{\varepsilon},\psi,\phi] \displaystyle=G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}+\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\Lambda^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},m+n}, $$

and the fact that we can replace factors of $\psi$ and $\phi$ with derivatives with respect to $\overline{\eta}$ and $J$ respectively, we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle\bigg( \displaystyle G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}})_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\delta}{\delta\overline{\eta}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}^{\beta}} \displaystyle+\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta J_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\delta\overline{\eta}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},m+n}^{\beta}} \displaystyle+\eta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}^{\alpha}\bigg)Z[\eta,\overline{\eta},J]=0 $$

We could have also varied $\psi$ instead of $\overline{\psi}$ ; following the same steps leads to

$$ \displaystyle\bigg( \displaystyle-\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}}G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle-\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta J_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\delta\eta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},n-m}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}) \displaystyle+\overline{\eta}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\bigg)Z[\eta,\overline{\eta},J]=0 $$

where we suppressed the matrix-vector multiplications in the flavor indicies for concision.

Now we differentiate (119) respect to $\overline{\eta}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}$ and set all the sources to zero. We then obtain

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{\alpha\beta} \displaystyle=[G({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})G_{0}^{-1}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})]_{\alpha\beta} \displaystyle-\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\langle\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}^{\alpha}[\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},n-m}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}})]^{\beta}\rangle $$

where $G_{\alpha\beta}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})=-\langle\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n,\alpha}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n,\beta}\rangle$ is the full Green’s function. The expression $\psi\overline{\psi}$ will, from now on, refer to the outer product in flavor indices $\psi_{\alpha}\overline{\psi}_{\beta}$ as indicated explicitly above. We could have also differentiated (118) instead, which exchanges the arguments of $\psi$ and $\overline{\psi}$ and switches $\Lambda$ to the right side. This yields two expressions for the self energy

$$ \displaystyle G^{-1} \displaystyle=G_{0}^{-1}-\tilde{\Sigma} \displaystyle\tilde{\Sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n} \displaystyle=\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m}G^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\langle\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},n-m}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\rangle\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}) \displaystyle=\frac{i}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m}\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\langle\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}},-m}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},n-m}\overline{\psi}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}\rangle G^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n}. $$

### E.2 Phase space approximations to the SDEs

Let us step back and comment on the nature of the Schwinger Dyson equations we have derived; specifically Eqs (122), which relates the self energy to the three-point vertex $\Gamma^{(3)}$ , and (127), which relates the three-point vertex to itself and higher-point vertices. We could of course keep going and obtain equations relating higher point vertices to successively higher point vertices. While such equations are generically difficult to solve, here we are fortunate to posess a self-consistent solution to the SDEs associated with the trivial classical model

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm{cl}} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{R}},{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}U({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})(n_{\boldsymbol{R}}-4)(n_{{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime}}-4), \displaystyle U({\boldsymbol{R}})=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\left\lvert\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}\right\rvert^{2}e^{i{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{R}}-{\boldsymbol{R}}^{\prime})}, $$

which corresponds to formally replacing $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to\xi_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ . Since (129) is commuting, and especially simple at integer filling, in principle all correlation functions and irreducible vertices associated with it can be computed, and they will satisfy the various SDEs self-consistently. We now explain how we make use of this classical solution to solve for the 1PI vertices of the topological model, which of course differ non-perturbatively.

In each SDE, (122), (127) there is a sum over a momentum transfer, ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ or ${\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}$ , on the right hand side. This momentum transfer shifts the momentum of one of the external legs by adding an additional bare vertex. The external vertex that the leg initially touched becomes internal. As such, this process of going higher in the SDE hierarchy is capable of making external vertices internal. This is useful because to leading order in $Us^{2}\ll T$ , we can neglect the contributions from internal momenta near the $\Gamma$ point; such contributions are suppressed by factors of $s^{2}$ due to small phase space. In (122) and (127), this results in

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Sigma}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},n} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}m}D_{{\boldsymbol{q}},m}\Gamma^{(3)}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}-m}({\boldsymbol{k}},i\omega_{n})G_{*,n}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}) \displaystyle-i \displaystyle\Gamma^{(3)}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-i\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle+\frac{i}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}G_{*}D_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Gamma^{(3),*}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}G_{*}\Gamma^{(3),*}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}G_{*}D_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Gamma^{(3)*}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}D_{{\boldsymbol{q}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\tilde{\Gamma}^{(3)}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle-\frac{i}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}G_{*}D_{{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}\Gamma^{(4)*}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}},-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle=-i\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}(*). $$

In the second equation, we additionally assumed that ${\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}=*$ is not near $\Gamma$ since we forecast plugging into the first equation where ${\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{q}}$ is an internal momentum (summed over).

We may now solve (130), and further SDEs in the hierarchy approximated in the same way, in two steps. First, we argue that quantities with Bloch momenta ${\boldsymbol{k}}=*$ can be evaluated in the trivial classical model (129). To see this, we set ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to*$ . Then all form factors and effective action coefficients in (130) are evaluated far away from ${\boldsymbol{k}}\approx\Gamma$ , not just internal ones. This exactly reproduces the SDEs associated with (129), which we can obtain the solution to through solving the classical model in real space. Intuitively, from the perspective of the topological model, the area of the BZ away from the $\Gamma$ point only rarely scatters into $\Gamma$ ; to leading order in $s^{2}$ it functions as a large ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space bath that predominantly interacts with itself. These bath-bath interactions can be solved for exactly in real space using (129), since they are independent of the topological $\Gamma$ -point region.

Second, quantities with Bloch momenta ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , which can be near $\Gamma$ , can be solved for in terms of irreducible vertices of the classical model; the region away from $\Gamma$ acts as a bath that controls the self energy and dynamics of $\Gamma$ electrons. Indeed, the right hand side of the second SDE in (130) enables us to compute the three point vertex in terms of form factors and classical vertices on the right hand side, because right hand side vertices only involve starred BZ momenta. We can then obtain the self energy from the first equation in (130). This procedure can in principle be carried out, but rather than compute all of the classical vertices individually it is easier to compute $\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}}(*)$ , which includes all of the classical vertices in the correct combination, and then directly evaluate the self energy in terms of $\Xi$ as we did in the main text.
